questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 25-year-old patient presents with fever and weight loss. He gives a history of blood in the stools and vomiting 2 weeks ago. On examination, there is right hypochondriac tenderness and hepatomegaly. Abdominal CT a lesion in the right lobe of the liver with ragged edges, multiple septations, and heterogenous densities. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Amoebic liver abscess

Features of fever, hepatomegaly, and hypochondriac tenderness are suggestive of a liver abscess. A liver abscess in a patient with a history of blood in the stools and vomiting points to a diagnosis of amoebic liver abscess.

Amoebic liver abscess is more common in males in the age group of 20 - 40 years with a history of travel to endemic areas. Ingestion of Entamoeba histolytica cysts causes diarrhea initially. Following this, the trophozoites reach the liver through the portal venous system and cause an amebic liver abscess. 80% of the cases involve the right lobe. The clinical features of amoebic liver abscess are right upper quadrant pain, tenderness, fever, hepatomegaly, and diarrhea.

Enzyme immunoassays detecting the presence of antibodies against the parasite have high sensitivity and specificity. Ultrasonography and CT scans can visualize the liver abscess without a peripheral rim of enhancement.

The mainstay of treatment for amebic abscesses is metronidazole, which is curative in more than 90% of patients. Luminal agents such as diloxanide furoate can be administered to treat the carrier state. Aspiration of abscess is recommended in case of a high risk of rupture. Pigtail catheter drainage is done in patients not responding to intravenous metronidazole in the first 48–72 hours to improve antibiotic penetration.

Option A: Pyogenic liver abscess is usually seen after 50 years of age and is not associated with a history of travel or diarrhea. Jaundice, bacteremia, and positive blood cultures are common in pyogenic liver abscesses compared to amoebic liver abscesses. Serology testing for Entamoeba is negative. A characteristic rim enhancement is noted in the case of a pyogenic abscess on a CECT abdomen and can differentiate it from an amoebic liver abscess.

Option B: Hydatid cyst a zoonotic infection caused by the Echinococcus species of flatworms. Primary hydatid cysts most commonly occur in the liver. Most patients are asymptomatic but when symptomatic, the patient presents with hepatomegaly, pain, and obstructive jaundice. The rupture of a hydatic cyst can result in fever, pruritus, or anaphylaxis. Imaging findings are cystic lesion with multiple daughter cysts within, detachment of the endocyst membrane (water-lily sign on USG shown below), and areas of calcification.

Option D: Hemangiomas are more common in women and are usually asymptomatic. Larger hemangiomas may present with vague upper abdominal symptoms. On contrast-enhanced CT scan, hemangiomas show asymmetrical, nodular peripheral enhancement that is isodense, with large vessels and progressive centripetal enhancement.
questions.learning: Amoebic liver abscess Features of fever, hepatomegaly, and hypochondriac tenderness are suggestive of a liver abscess. A liver abscess in a patient with a history of blood in the stools and vomiting points to a diagnosis of amoebic liver abscess.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A woman with a history of missed abortion subsequently develops amenorrhea, despite having a negative urine pregnancy test. Hysterosalpingography shows the abnormality illustrated in the provided image. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical history of secondary amenorrhea following a pregnancy-related procedure (like curettage for a missed abortion) is highly suggestive of Asherman syndrome (Option C). Asherman syndrome is characterized by the formation of intrauterine adhesions or synechiae that obliterate the uterine cavity. The provided hysterosalpingogram (HSG) confirms this diagnosis, showing characteristic irregular filling defects and a diminished, jagged uterine cavity where the contrast cannot flow smoothly. Pyometra (Option A) involves an accumulation of pus in the uterus, usually presenting with pain and fever. Endometriosis (Option B) involves extra-uterine implants and would not show these specific intra-cavity HSG defects. Sheehan syndrome (Option D) is a form of pituitary necrosis following postpartum hemorrhage that causes amenorrhea through hormonal failure, but the HSG in Sheehan’s would show a normal uterine cavity. Therefore, the structural scarring seen on HSG confirms Asherman’s
questions.learning: The clinical history of secondary amenorrhea following a pregnancy-related procedure (like curettage for a missed abortion) is highly suggestive of Asherman syndrome (Option C).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Villages A and B have different age distributions. Which indicator is most appropriate for comparing the death rates between these two villages?
questions.explanation: When comparing mortality across populations with different age structures, the Age Standardized Death Rate is the most reliable indicator. In this scenario, Village B has a significantly larger elderly population (10,000 people aged 60+) compared to Village A (7,000). Because older people naturally have higher death rates, a direct comparison using the Crude Death Rate (Option A) would be biased, likely showing higher mortality in Village B simply due to its age composition rather than poor health quality. Standardization mathematically "removes" the influence of age by applying observed death rates to a common standard population. Specific death rates (Option C) provide details for a single group but not an overall comparison. Proportional mortality (Option D) measures the percentage of deaths from a specific cause and does not assess overall death risk. Standardization allows epidemiologists to make a fair, "apples-to-apples" comparison between disparate communities to identify true health disparities

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A 35-year-old male presents to the emergency department with difficulty breathing and cyanosis after being exposed to phosphine gas in a garage while repairing a vehicle. Despite receiving 100% oxygen, his oxygen saturation remains low and does not improve. What type of hypoxia is most likely responsible for his symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Histotoxic hypoxia

Phosphine causes histotoxic hypoxia by inhibiting mitochondrial function and disrupting cellular respiration at the tissue level.

Phosphine causes histotoxic hypoxia, and thus, by preventing the O2 utilization at the tissue level, it acts as a powerful stimulus for peripheral chemoreceptors. Phosphine inhibits cytochrome oxidase (Complex IV) in the electron transport chain. This disrupts oxidative phosphorylation, preventing ATP production despite adequate oxygen availability.

In phosphine poisoning the oxygen is present but cells cannot use it due to blocked cellular respiration. This is why simple oxygen supplementation isn't effective as a primary treatment.

Other options:

Option B: Anemic hypoxia occurs due to decreased hemoglobin in the blood capable of carrying oxygen. This can be in the form of a low amount of hemoglobin, defective hemoglobin, or interference with hemoglobin-oxygen binding. Carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning is classified as anemic hypoxia as CO preferentially binds to hemoglobin and reduces the oxygen binding. Treatment involves terminating the exposure to CO and oxygen supplementation.

Option C: Hypoxic hypoxia refers to a reduced partial pressure of oxygen in the arterial blood. It has multiple causes, like high altitude, hypoventilation, right-to-left shunts, diffusion defects, and ventilation-perfusion mismatch. Chronic emphysema is an example of hypoxic hypoxia, as there is alveolar destruction leading to reduced gas exchange and ventilation-perfusion mismatch. In most cases, supplemental oxygen is helpful in treatment.

Option D: Stagnant hypoxia refers to ischemic hypoxia that results from inadequate circulation due to conditions such as heart failure and hypoxia in the setting of shock. In such conditions, administering intravenous fluids can improve the patient's condition because it is the circulation that is affected. If the shock is prolonged it can result in acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), which can be treated with positive pressure ventilation and not simply by increasing oxygen administration.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following statements is false about Cuthbertson's metabolic ebb and flow responses to trauma?
options: The "ebb" phase is associated with a decline in body temperature and oxygen consumption.
The "flow" phase occurs after resuscitation from a state of shock.
The "ebb" phase is aimed at reducing posttraumatic energy depletion.
The "ebb" phase leads to activation of the innate immune system and induction of the hepatic acute-phase response.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. The "ebb" phase leads to activation of the innate immune system and induction of the hepatic acute-phase response.

The "flow" phase (not "ebb") leads to activation of the innate immune system and induction of the hepatic acute-phase response.

Cuthbertson's ebb and flow response to trauma:

The "ebb" phase lasts for a brief duration and is associated with a decline in body temperature and oxygen consumption, aimed at reducing post traumatic energy depletion.

The "flow" phase occurs after resuscitation from a state of shock, which leads to an increased metabolic turnover, activation of the innate immune system and induction of the hepatic acute-phase response. This hypercatabolic condition leads to a significantly increased oxygen consumption and energy expenditure.
questions.learning: The "ebb" phase leads to activation of the innate immune system and induction of the hepatic acute-phase response. The "flow" phase (not "ebb") leads to activation of the innate immune system and induction of the hepatic acute-phase response.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient after RTA had a renal shut down. Work-up shows: FeNa: < 1%, Urine osmolality: 300 mOsm/kg, Urinary sodium: 40 mEq/L. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient’s laboratory findings point toward intrinsic renal damage, specifically Acute Tubular Necrosis (ATN). In ATN, damaged tubules lose the ability to concentrate urine and reabsorb sodium. The urinary sodium of 40 mEq/L is elevated, indicating sodium wasting, and the urine osmolality of ~300 mOsm/kg reflects "isosthenuria," where the kidney can no longer produce concentrated or dilute urine compared to plasma. Although a Fractional Excretion of Sodium (FeNa) < 1% is typically associated with pre-renal states, it can also be seen in early or non-oliguric ATN. Pre-renal AKI (Option B) is characterized by a lower urinary sodium (< 20 mEq/L) and a much higher urine osmolality (> 500 mOsm/kg). Post-renal AKI (Option C) requires evidence of obstruction on imaging. "Renal AKI" (Option D) is a broad category; ATN is the specific pathological diagnosis that matches the electrolyte wasting and osmolality findings
questions.learning: The patient’s laboratory findings point toward intrinsic renal damage, specifically Acute Tubular Necrosis (ATN). In ATN, damaged tubules lose the ability to concentrate urine and reabsorb sodium.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: In which of the following clinical conditions is the use of an intrauterine contraceptive device (IUCD) absolutely contraindicated?
questions.explanation: According to WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria (MEC), active, untreated HIV infection with symptomatic AIDS is classified as a Category 4 contraindication for the insertion of an IUCD. In these immunosuppressed patients, the risk of ascending pelvic infections and subsequent sepsis is unacceptably high. However, if a patient is clinically stable on antiretroviral therapy (ART), IUCD use may be considered Category 2 (benefits outweigh risks). Hypertension (Option A), hyperlipidemia (Option B), and diabetes mellitus (Option C) are not absolute contraindications; copper IUCDs are generally safe to use in these patients unless other severe complications are present. Other absolute contraindications include current PID, pregnancy, and unexplained vaginal bleeding. Thus, in the context of the provided options, symptomatic HIV infection represents the most significant health risk for initial IUCD placement
questions.learning: According to WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria (MEC), active, untreated HIV infection with symptomatic AIDS is classified as a Category 4 contraindication for the insertion of an IUCD.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The risk of cancer that can be reduced with OCP use are all, except? OCP- Oral contraceptive pills
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Breast Cancer

Oral contraceptive pills (OCP) are not protective against breast cancer.

OCPs have no effect on the incidence of Breast Cancer.

OCPs protect against ovarian cancer (Option A). Oral contraceptives cause prolonged suppression of gonadotropin stimulation of ovary on long term use. This may account for lower incidence of ovarian malignancy noted in contraceptive users.

Other benefits of oral contraceptive pills:

* Lesser incidence of endometrial carcinoma due to progestin component in OCP (Option D).

* Regularisation of menstrual cycles results in relief of dysmenorrhea and menorrhagia.

* Reduced incidence and relief of fibrocystic breast disease and ovarian cysts.

* Endometriosis and pelvic inflammatory disease are improved.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 6-year-old child presents with brown discoloration of the incisors, with a history of white patches on the teeth that developed due to excessive intake of a substance. What is the most likely cause of this discoloration?
questions.explanation: The presentation of initial white patches that progress to permanent brown discoloration (mottling) of the tooth enamel is the classic description of dental fluorosis. This occurs due to the excessive chronic ingestion of fluoride (fluorine) during the critical period of enamel formation, typically when the child is under age 6–8. This most often happens in regions where the natural groundwater contains high fluoride levels ( ppm). Vitamin A (Option A) and Riboflavin (Option D) are essential nutrients; while deficiencies in these can affect overall health, they do not cause this specific "mottling" of the teeth. Chlorine (Option B) is used for water disinfection and does not cause dental discoloration. Fluorosis is considered a major public health issue in endemic areas and can also progress to skeletal fluorosis if not managed. Thus, fluoride excess is the definitive cause of the described incisor discoloration
questions.learning: The presentation of initial white patches that progress to permanent brown discoloration (mottling) of the tooth enamel is the classic description of dental fluorosis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Distension of the right atrium leads to an increase in heart rate due to activation of which reflex?
questions.explanation: The Bainbridge reflex, also called the atrial reflex, is an increase in heart rate due to an increase in central venous pressure. When the right atrium is distended by increased blood volume, stretch receptors in the atrial wall are activated, sending signals to the brainstem to increase sympathetic tone and heart rate. This reflex helps to move excess blood out of the venous system into the arterial system. The Bezold-Jarisch reflex (Option A) causes bradycardia and hypotension in response to noxious stimuli in the ventricles. The Cushing reflex (Option C) is a triad of hypertension, bradycardia, and irregular respirations seen in increased intracranial pressure. The J reflex (Option D) or juxtacapillary reflex is triggered by pulmonary congestion, leading to apnea followed by rapid breathing. The Bainbridge reflex is physiological and works in opposition to the baroreceptor reflex to maintain circulatory balance

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 42-year-old female presented with fever, vomiting and right hypochondriac pain that was radiating to the neck. She has had similar on and off episodes in the past.On examination, Murphy's sign is positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Acute cholecystitis

The clinical scenario with positive Murphy's sign is suggestive of acute cholecystitis.

Acute cholecystitis is the inflammation of the gallbladder that develops over hours, usually because a gallstone obstructs the cystic duct. In the majority of cases, the process is limited by the stone slipping back into the body of the gallbladder. Clinical features include:

* Pain in the right hypochondrium with referred pain to the back

* Fever

* Nausea, vomiting, dyspepsia

* Jaundice

* Positive Murphy's sign

* Positive Boas' sign

Murphy's sign: After asking the patient to exhale, the examiner places his hand below the costal margin on the right side at the mid-clavicular line. The patient is then instructed to take deep inspiration. If the patient stops breathing and winces with a ‘catch’ of breath, Murphy’s sign is said to be positive.

Boas' sign: It is the presence of an area of hyperaesthesia at the site where pain is radiated to the back, typically, below the scapula.

An ultrasound scan is sensitive in acute cholecystitis and demonstrates a distended gallbladder with thickened wall, pericholecystic fluid, the presence of gallstone, and the sonographic Murphy's sign. The gold standard investigation of acute cholecystitis is hydroxyiminodiacetic acid (HIDA) scan. The radioisotope used is Technetium-99m ( 99mTc)-a labelled derivative of iminodiacetic acid.

The first-line treatment would be medical conservative management to subside the symptoms. The conservative management includes nil per mouth with intravenous fluid administration, administration of analgesics and antibiotics.

Other Murphy's in surgery:

Murphy's punch sign: This test is performed by the examiner using the fist to make jabbing thrusts over the costovertebral angle. The test is positive for infection, inflammation, or obstruction of the kidney.

Murphy's triad is associated with acute appendicitis.

* Pain in the right illiac fossa

* Vomiting

* Fever

Pearl PF1607: Diagnostic Evaluation of the Gall Bladder

* Gallbladder Ultrasound: Investigation of choice for detection of gall stones

* Abdominal X-ray: Useful in

* Calcified gall stones

* Emphysematous cholecystitis

* Porcelain gallbladder

* Limey bile

* Gallstone ileus

* Radioisotope scans (HIDA/DIDA/DISIDA)

* Indicated for confirmation of suspected acute cholecystitis

* Useful in diagnosis of acalculous cholecystopathy

Abbreviations:

* HIDA: Hepatobiliary IminoDiacetic Acid scan

* DIDA/DISDA: Di-isopropyl IminoDiacetic Acid - Dynamic Tc99m DIDA Cholescintigraphy

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following is involved as a secondary messenger in the mechanism of gastric acid secretion?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. cAMP

cAMP is the secondary messenger involved in the mechanism of gastric acid secretion.

cGMP is not involved in gastric acid secretion. Ach acts on the synapses, and CCK-B receptors interact with gastrin to contribute to gastric acid secretion. They also act via secondary messengers such as IP3 and increased intracellular Ca2+.

Pearl PF0546: Stimuli for gastric secretion

Stimuli

Mechanism

Applied aspects

Vagal stimulation

Direct pathway

Vagus nerve innervates parietal cells and stimulates H+ secretion directly.

The neurotransmitter at these synapses is Ach, the receptor on the parietal cells is muscarinic (M3)

The second messengers for CCK are IP3 and increased intracellular [Ca2+].

Atropine, a cholinergic muscarinic antagonist, inhibits H+ secretion by blocking the direct pathway, which uses ACh as a neurotransmitter. However, it does not block H+ secretion completely because it does not inhibit the indirect pathway, which uses GRP as a neurotransmitter

Indirect pathway

Vagus nerve innervates G cells and stimulates gastrin secretion, which then stimulates H+ secretion.

The neurotransmitter at these synapses is GRP (not ACh).

Vagotomy eliminates both direct and indirect pathways.

Gastrin

Released in response to eating a meal (small peptides, distension of the stomach, vagal stimulation).

Stimulates H+ secretion by interacting with the cholecystokinin B (CCKB) receptor on the parietal cells.

The second messenger for gastrin on the parietal cell is IP3/Ca2+.

Histamine

Released from enterochromaffin-like (ECL) cells in the gastric mucosa and diffuses to the nearby parietal cells.

Stimulates H+ secretion by activating H2 receptors on the parietal cell membrane.

The H2 receptor is coupled to adenylyl cyclase via a Gs protein.

The second messenger for histamine is cAMP.

H2 receptor–blocking drugs, such as cimetidine, inhibit H+ secretion by blocking the stimulatory effect of histamine.
questions.learning: cAMP cAMP is the secondary messenger involved in the mechanism of gastric acid secretion. cGMP is not involved in gastric acid secretion. Ach acts on the synapses, and CCK-B receptors interact with gastrin to contribute to gastric acid secretion.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs increases trabecular outflow?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Netarsudil

The drug that increases trabecular outflow is netarsudil.

Netarsudil is a rho-kinase inhibitor used in the treatment and management of glaucoma and ocular hypertension. It lowers the intra-ocular pressure directly through the relaxation of the trabecular meshwork, leading to an increase in aqueous outflow. It also reduces aqueous humor production.

Netarsudil ophthalmic solution is instilled in one drop into the affected eye once daily in the evening. Adverse effects are conjunctival hyperemia, and corneal verticillata.

Other options:

Option A- Timolol is a non-selective β-blocker that decreases the IOP by reducing the aqueous humor production through the blockade of the β-receptors on the ciliary epithelium. Ocular adverse effects are allergy, decreased corneal sensation, and punctate keratitis.

Option C- Brimonidine is a selective alpha-2 agonist which decreases aqueous synthesis and increases uveoscleral outflow. It can cross the blood-brain barrier and, hence, causes drowsiness and CNS depression. It is contraindicated in infants and children.

Option D- Acetazolamide is a topical carbonic anhydrase inhibitor that decreases IOP by reducing aqueous formation. The main adverse effect is the bitter taste following administration. It is contraindicated in people with allergies to sulfonamide antibiotics.
questions.learning: Netarsudil — The drug that increases trabecular outflow is netarsudil. Netarsudil is a rho-kinase inhibitor used in the treatment and management of glaucoma and ocular hypertension.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A woman presented with confusion, constipation, and headache. Serum calcium was 13.1mg/dL and ALP was elevated. She was diagnosed with primary hyperparathyroidism. Which of the following is the imaging of choice?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Sestamibi scan

Sestamibi scan is the imaging of choice to delineate parathyroid abnormalities.

Sestamibi is a monovalent lipophilic cation. It shows passive diffusion across cell membranes and accumulates in mitochondria. Because of its accumulation in the mitochondria, there is a difference in the rate at which it gets washed out depending upon the number of mitochondria in each tissue.

In parathyroid adenomas, there is a high concentration of oxyphilic cells with high mitochondrial content. The three protocols for sestamibi scanning are:

• Single-isotope dual-phase scan
• Dual-isotope subtraction imaging
• Single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT).

SPECT is commonly used because of its improved spatial resolution. Sestamibi combined with CT can be used to detect smaller parathyroid tissues.

Other imaging modalities for parathyroid localization:

• Ultrasonography:

• It is inexpensive and noninvasive
• Mediastinal parathyroid tissue cannot be detected because USG cannot penetrate the sternum or clavicles.

• Four-dimensional CT:

• It has a very high sensitivity
• Increased radiation exposure than other routine modalities is a potential disadvantage

• Selective venous sampling for PTH can be used for the exact localization of adenomas
questions.learning: Sestamibi scan Sestamibi scan is the imaging of choice to delineate parathyroid abnormalities. Sestamibi is a monovalent lipophilic cation.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Endocrine · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 53-year-old woman presents for a routine health check-up. She has no active complaints. Her medical history is unremarkable except for mild osteoarthritis. Her family history is significant for diabetes mellitus in her father and breast cancer in her mother. On examination, her blood pressure is elevated. Laboratory evaluation reveals fasting plasma glucose levels ≥140 mg/dL on multiple occasions. Which of the following is the most likely cause of death in this patient if her condition remains uncontrolled?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Acute myocardial infarction

Patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus are at markedly increased risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, which is the leading cause of mortality.

Pathophysiology:

• Chronic hyperglycemia → endothelial dysfunction
• ↑ advanced glycation end-products (AGEs)
• ↑ oxidative stress and inflammation
• Accelerated atherosclerosis of coronary arteries

This results in a significantly increased risk of:

• Myocardial infarction (most common cause of death)
• Stroke
• Peripheral arterial disease

Why not other options?

A. Breast cancer → unrelated to diabetes mortality risk

B. HHS → acute complication, less common cause of death overall

D. Renal failure → major morbidity but less common cause of death than CVD

Stroke → common but second to MI
questions.learning: Acute myocardial infarction Patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus are at markedly increased risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, which is the leading cause of mortality.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Type of voice associated with the condition shown in the image below?
questions.explanation: The image shows a lateral skull X-ray with narrowing/obstruction in the nasopharyngeal airway, most consistent with conditions like adenoid hypertrophy. This leads to blockage of nasal airflow, which directly affects speech resonance. In such cases, the voice becomes hyponasal (denasal), a condition known as rhinolalia clausa. Here, nasal sounds like “m” and “n” are reduced or altered, and the patient’s speech appears muffled or congested, similar to speaking with a blocked nose. Key Concept: 1. Rhinolalia clausa → nasal obstruction → decreased nasal resonance 2. Rhinolalia aperta → palatal defect → increased nasal resonance Why other options are incorrect: (B) Rhinolalia aperta : Seen in cleft palate → excessive nasal sound (opposite condition) (C) Hot potato voice : Due to peritonsillar abscess; muffled but not nasal (D) Hypernasality : Feature of rhinolalia aperta, not clausa

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Analyze the results of the electrocardiogram (ECG) provided below.
questions.explanation: The ECG strip shows a regular, rapid rhythm with narrow QRS complexes and a rate typically around 150–250 beats per minute. P waves are either absent or not clearly visible, often buried within or just after the QRS complexes. These features are characteristic of supraventricular tachycardia (SVT), which originates above the ventricles (usually AV nodal re-entry). Why other options are incorrect: (A) Ventricular fibrillation → Chaotic, irregular waveform with no identifiable QRS complexes (not seen here) (B) Atrial fibrillation → Irregularly irregular rhythm with absent P waves (this ECG is regular) (D) Ventricular tachycardia → Wide QRS complexes (>120 ms), unlike the narrow complexes seen here

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A 28 year old software engineer visits a psychiatry clinic as he is suffering from sleep disturbances, low mood, stress in his current job from the past 3 months. He cannot work properly and has difficulty balancing family and work. He has no prior psychiatry history. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Adjustment disorder

The given scenario where a software engineer is stressed in his job from the last 3 months suggests it is an adjustment disorder.

Adjustment disorder is a common psychiatric condition, especially seen in adolescents and women, where an individual develops a maladaptive response to a stressful life event. According to ICD-10, it begins within 1 month of a significant stressor and is typically seen in those with poor coping skills or vulnerable personality traits. The disorder usually lasts less than 6 months, except in cases of prolonged depressive reaction. Subtypes include brief or prolonged depressive reaction, mixed anxiety and depression, or predominant disturbance of emotions or conduct. Supportive psychotherapy is the treatment of choice, and most patients recover within about 3 months.

Diagnosing criteria for adjustment disorder include:

* Development of emotional or behavioural response within 3 months of the onset of the stressor.

* The symptoms or behaviour are clinically significant, where, any one of the following are met:

* The response is out of proportion to the severity or intensity of stressor.

* Significant impairment in social, occupational, or other areas of functioning.

* Stress-related disturbance does not meet criteria for another mental disorder or exacerbation of pre-existing mental disorder.

* The symptoms do not represent normal bereavement.

* Once the stressor is terminated, the symptoms do not persist for more than an additional 6 months.

Other options:

Option B: It is not Generalized anxiety disorder as it requires ≥6 months of symptoms. Here the duration is only 3 months. Generalized anxiety disorder is defined as excessive worry and anxiety about several activities and events for most days during a 6 month period which interferes with various aspects of life.

Option C: Acute stress disorder is characterised by intrusive symptoms like distressing memories, dreams and flashbacks of the event occurring after death, serious injury, or sexual violation lasting less than one month.

Option D: PTSD requires a traumatic event + symptoms persisting >1 month (re-experiencing, avoidance, hyperarousal). The treatment modalities for PTSD and acute stress disorder include trauma-focused cognitive behavioral therapy, eye movement desensitization and reprocessing therapy (EMDR), and SSRIs.

Here, there is no trauma and only job stress, so it's not PTSD.

Pearl PF1277: Differential diagnosis of Trauma and Stress related disorder

PTSD

develop within 6 months and persist more than 1 month

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: The given USG of lung shows:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sea shore sign

The given image shows the seashore sign seen in M-mode imaging of the normal lung.

M-mode is defined as the time-motion display of the ultrasound wave along a chosen ultrasound line. With M-Mode, even rapid motions can be displayed, measured, and recorded.

In the M-mode of USG, the motionless portion of the chest above the pleural line creates horizontal ‘waves', and the sliding below the pleural line creates a granular pattern, the ‘sand’. The resultant picture is one that resembles waves crashing in onto the sand and is therefore called the ‘seashore sign’ and is present in a normal lung.

Option A: Stratosphere sign or barcode sign is a finding in the M-mode seen as parallel horizontal lines above and below the pleural line. This is seen in pneumothorax.

Option C: There is no named sign called troposphere sign.

Option D: Mirror image artifact is seen when there is a highly reflective surface (eg: Diaphragm) in the path of the primary beam.
questions.learning: Sea shore sign — The given image shows the seashore sign seen in M-mode imaging of the normal lung. M-mode is defined as the time-motion display of the ultrasound wave along a chosen ultrasound line.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A child presents with trismus and painful limb spasms following a recent untreated ear infection. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tetanus

A child with trismus (lockjaw) and painful generalized muscle spasms following an untreated infection is most consistent with tetanus, caused by Clostridium tetani.

·         C. tetani produces tetanospasmin toxin

·         Toxin blocks release of inhibitory neurotransmitters (GABA and glycine) in the CNS

·         Leads to unopposed muscle contraction → rigidity and spasms

Clinical features:

·         Trismus (lockjaw) – earliest sign

·         Painful muscle spasms

·         Risus sardonicus (facial grimace)

·         Opisthotonus (arching of back)

Why other options are incorrect:

·         Meningitis: Fever, neck stiffness, altered sensorium (no trismus/spasms)

·         Sigmoid sinus thrombosis: Headache, papilledema, sepsis features

·         Bezold’s abscess: Neck swelling due to mastoiditis

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which nerve damage would most likely cause sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot and the medial four toes, along with impaired eversion of the foot?
questions.explanation: The symptoms described pinpoint a lesion of the superficial peroneal nerve. This nerve provides motor innervation to the peroneus longus and peroneus brevis muscles, which are the primary evertors of the foot; hence, injury causes eversion difficulty. Sensorial, it supplies the majority of the dorsum of the foot and the dorsal aspects of the medial four toes, excluding the first web space. The deep peroneal nerve (Option A) supplies the first web space and the extensors responsible for dorsiflexion; its injury results in foot drop. The common peroneal nerve (Option C) is the parent trunk; a lesion here would cause both foot drop and eversion loss. The posterior tibial nerve (Option D) supplies the calf muscles and the sole of the foot, which are unrelated to these specific dorsal symptoms. Therefore, the isolated loss of eversion and specific dorsal sensation confirms superficial peroneal nerve damage
questions.learning: The symptoms described pinpoint a lesion of the superficial peroneal nerve. This nerve provides motor innervation to the peroneus longus and peroneus brevis muscles, which are the primary evertors of the foot; hence, injury causes eversion difficulty.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which gene mutation is most commonly associated with Burkitt's lymphoma?
questions.explanation: Burkitt's lymphoma is a highly aggressive B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma that is characteristically associated with translocations of the MYC gene on chromosome 8, most commonly t(8;14). This translocation leads to the overexpression of the C-myc protein, driving rapid cell proliferation. P-21 (Option B) is a cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor that regulates the cell cycle but is not a primary driver of this lymphoma. The Rb gene (Option C) is a tumor suppressor associated with retinoblastoma and osteosarcoma. The p53 gene (Option D) is the most common tumor suppressor mutated in many human cancers, but it is not the defining genetic hallmark of Burkitt's. Burkitt's lymphoma has three subtypes: endemic (linked to EBV and malaria), sporadic, and immunodeficiency-associated. Almost all endemic cases are latently infected with the Epstein-Barr virus
questions.learning: Burkitt's lymphoma is a highly aggressive B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma that is characteristically associated with translocations of the MYC gene on chromosome 8, most commonly t(8;14).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient with a pituitary tumor that overproduced growth hormone underwent surgical removal of the tumor. The resection was found to be incomplete. What is the first-line treatment for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Octreotide

The above scenario with a pituitary tumor producing growth hormone is likely to cause acromegaly in the patient. Octreotide is the first-line treatment for this condition.

Octreotide is a synthetic analog of somatostatin.

Octreotide can be used in the following conditions:

• Acromegaly
• Secretory diarrheas associated with carcinoid, AIDS, cancer chemotherapy, or diabetes- by suppression of hormones that enhance intestinal mucosal secretion.
• Bleeding esophageal varices- reduces hepatic blood flow and helps stop bleeding.
• Dumping syndrome in post gastric surgery patients

Adverse effects of octreotide are:

• Abdominal pain
• Nausea
• Steatorrhea
• Gall stones (due to biliary stasis)
• Hyperglycemia

Other options:

Option A: Leuprolide is a long-acting GnRH agonist. It is used for palliation of carcinoma prostate, uterine fibroids, endometriosis, and precocious puberty. Side effects include hot flashes, decreased bone mineral density, vaginal dryness, and erectile dysfunction.

Option B: Goserelin is also a GnRH agonist used for the treatment of endometriosis, dysfunctional uterine bleeding, and for prostate and breast cancer.

Option C: Nafarelin is a long-acting GnRH agonist. It is used for the treatment of endometriosis, uterine fibroids, and central precocious puberty.
questions.learning: Octreotide — The above scenario with a pituitary tumor producing growth hormone is likely to cause acromegaly in the patient. Octreotide is the first-line treatment for this condition.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following ECG finding is characteristically found in Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Wide QRS

Characteristic ECG findings in Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome is Wide QRS interval.

Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome is a form of atrioventricular reentry phenomenon characterized by the presence of accessory conducting pathways between the atria and ventricles that are separate from the AV node and Purkinje tissue.

The tachycardia is usually produced by the conduction of a normal impulse from the ventricles to the atria via the accessory pathway (bundle of Kent). This is the orthodromic pathway. Less often, a premature atrial beat travels down the accessory pathway (while AV Node is still in refractory period) leading to premature ventricular activation. This is the antidromic pathway.

The classic ECG features in WPW are as follows:

*

A shortened PR interval (typically <120 ms)

*

A slurring and the slow rise of the initial upstroke of the QRS complex (delta wave)

*

A widened QRS complex (total duration >0.12 seconds)

*

ST-segment–T wave (repolarization) changes, generally directed opposite the major delta wave and QRS complex, reflecting altered depolarization

Pearl PF1816: Wolff Parkinson White Syndrome

Wolff Parkinson White Syndrome (WPW) is characterized by an abnormal accessory pathway in the heart leading to arrhythmias.

Pathology- Born with an accessory pathway, the bundle of Kent which connects the atria and ventricle. The electrical impulses from the SA node reach the ventricles earlier via the accessory pathway as there is no AV nodal delay in this pathway. This leads to the preexcitation of the ventricle and initiation of ventricular contraction. This ventricular contraction is prolonged when the impulse via the AV nodal pathway reaches the ventricles.

Most common location of the accessory pathway- between the left atrium and free wall of the left ventricle

ECG changes:

Shortened PR interval- because of the early initiation of ventricular depolarization

Prolonged QRS duration- because of the AV nodal impulse reaching the ventricles after the aberrant impulse.

Delta waves- slurred upstroke of QRS complex

The given ECG shows delta waves marked with red arrows:

Treatment:

* Catheter ablation is the treatment of choice.

* Anti-arrhythmic drugs like procainamide, amiodarone, quinidine, propafenone, dofetilide are used in slowing conduction in the accessory pathway (prolong refractory period).

* IV procainamide is the drug of choice in a hemodynamically stable WPW presenting with atrial fibrillation.

* DC cardioversion is done in hemodynamically unstable patients.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The remnants of Wolffian ducts in females are located in________.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Leaves of broad ligament

The Gartner's duct is a remnant of the Wolffian ducts in women. These are located in the broad ligament and the vagina.

The Gartner's duct is an embryological remnant of the mesonephric duct/Wolffian duct formed during the development of the urinary and reproductive organs. It runs parallel to, but below, the fallopian tube in the mesosalpinx. The duct passes downwards by the side of the uterus to the level of the internal os where it passes into the tissues of the cervix. It then runs forwards to reach the anterolateral aspect of the vaginal wall and may reach as far down as the hymen.

The duct can sometimes form a cyst in the broad ligament or in the vagina. It is called Gartner’s cyst. It is a benign condition and can be treated with marsupialization.
questions.learning: Leaves of broad ligament — The Gartner's duct is a remnant of the Wolffian ducts in women. These are located in the broad ligament and the vagina.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which classification is used for Barrett esophagus?
questions.explanation: The Prague C & M criteria is the internationally recognized endoscopic classification system used to standardize the reporting of Barrett's esophagus. In this system, "C" represents the circumferential extent of the metaplastic mucosa, and "M" represents the maximal extent (including "tongues" of mucosa) from the gastroesophageal junction. This allows for accurate monitoring and surveillance of the disease. Savary-Miller classification (Option B) is used to grade the severity of reflux esophagitis based on erosions. Johnson classification (Option C) categorizes types of gastric ulcers. Forrest classification (Option D) is used in the setting of acute upper GI bleeding to categorize peptic ulcers based on their bleeding stigmata and to predict the risk of rebleeding. Therefore, for the specific anatomical measurement of Barrett's mucosa, the Prague classification is the only correct choice
questions.learning: The Prague C & M criteria is the internationally recognized endoscopic classification system used to standardize the reporting of Barrett's esophagus.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text:
A patient presents to you with fever, jaundice, and malaise. What is the most likely diagnosis based on the serology reports given below?

Anti-HBc (IgM): Positive

HBsAg: Positive

Anti-HBs: Negative

Anti-HCV antibodies: Negative
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Acute hepatitis B

The given clinical scenario along with the serology reports suggest a diagnosis of acute hepatitis B.

Acute hepatitis B presents after an incubation period of 30-180 days with symptoms such as anorexia, malaise, and myalgias. A low-grade fever can also be associated. These symptoms can precede jaundice by 1-2 weeks. Mild weight loss and tender hepatomegaly are other features.

The presence of HBsAg (hepatitis B surface antigen), also known as Australia antigen, IgM anti-HBc antibodies (antibodies against hepatitis B core antigen), and the absence of anti-HBs is the characteristic picture seen in acute hepatitis B with high infectivity. The absence of anti-HCV antibodies excludes a diagnosis of hepatitis C.

Aspartate transaminase (AST) and alanine transaminase (ALT) values are usually elevated along with bilirubin levels. Serological markers vary according to the phase of the disease process as shown below.

Most cases undergo spontaneous recovery. Prophylaxis can be carried out with the use of vaccines containing HbsAg. Anti-HBs titres ≥ 10mIU/mL are protective.

Acute viral hepatitis can be due to due to any of the five agents - hepatitis A virus (HAV), hepatitis B virus (HBV), hepatitis C virus (HCV), hepatitis D virus (HDV), and hepatitis E virus (HEV). Clinical features of all acute viral hepatitis are similar. A patient suspected to have acute hepatitis should be tested for HBsAg, IgM anti-HAV, IgM anti-HBc, and anti-HCV.

Other options:

Option B: Acute hepatitis C is caused by HCV which is an RNA virus. It is a blood-borne infection. Detection of anti-HCV and HCV RNA is used for diagnosis. HCV-RNA appears before anti-HCV and persists for the entire duration of the disease.

Option C: Chronic hepatitis B is a late complication of acute hepatitis B. Persistence of HBeAg for >3 months or HBsAg for >6 months is suggestive of the development of the condition. Investigations show the presence of HBsAg, IgG anti-HBc, HBeAg, and HBV DNA. Fatigue and intermittent jaundice are the main features. It can progress to cirrhosis or hepatocellular carcinoma. Hepatitis D superinfection can accelerate this progression.

Option D: Chronic hepatitis C is a common complication of acute hepatitis C. It can progress to cirrhosis or hepatocellular carcinoma HCV-RNA and anti-HCV can be detected on serology.
questions.learning: Acute hepatitis B — The given clinical scenario along with the serology reports suggest a diagnosis of acute hepatitis B. Acute hepatitis B presents after an incubation period of 30-180 days with symptoms such as anorexia, malaise, and myalgias.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An elderly man presents with lower back pain, a mobile mass in the lumbar region that becomes more prominent on inspiration, and generalized weakness. Urine examination reveals the presence of red blood cells without pus cells. Based on these clinical and laboratory findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The triad of flank pain, hematuria (RBCs in urine without pus), and a palpable mass is the "classic triad" of renal cell carcinoma (RCC), although it is only seen in about 10% of patients. The fact that the mass moves with respiration indicates it is likely arising from the kidney, which is a retroperitoneal organ. Polycystic kidney disease (Option A) usually presents with bilateral masses and a strong family history. Hydronephrosis (Option B) is a secondary finding of obstruction and rarely presents as a large, primary palpable mass unless severe and chronic. Chronic pyelonephritis (Option D) would typically show pus cells (pyuria) and evidence of chronic infection rather than a solitary movable mass and hematuria. RCC is the most common primary renal malignancy in adults, frequently presenting as an incidental finding on imaging. The general weakness noted may be part of a paraneoplastic syndrome or anemia of chronic disease associated with malignancy
questions.learning: The triad of flank pain, hematuria (RBCs in urine without pus), and a palpable mass is the "classic triad" of renal cell carcinoma (RCC), although it is only seen in about 10% of patients.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A student presented with urticaria after she ate some seafood. She wants a non-sedating drug as she has an exam to study for. Which of the following drugs would you prefer to prescribe to her?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Fexofenadine

The student is suffering from urticaria and fexofenadine can be prescribed to her. This is preferred as it is a second-generation antihistamine having minimal/no sedative effects as it cannot cross the blood-brain barrier easily.

Pheniramine, promethazine, and hydroxyzine are first-generation antihistamines that should not be prescribed to drivers and heavy machine workers because these can cause sedation.

Highly sedative first-generation antihistamines:

* Diphenhydramine

* Dimenhydrinate

* Promethazine

* Hydroxyzine

Second-generation antihistamines- They are less sedative because of less central nervous system penetration and do not block autonomic receptors. They include:

* Fexofenadine

* Loratadine, Desloratadine

* Cetirizine, Levocetirizine

* Azelastine, Mizolastine, Ebastine

* Olopatadine

* Rupatadine
questions.learning: Fexofenadine — The student is suffering from urticaria and fexofenadine can be prescribed to her. This is preferred as it is a second-generation antihistamine having minimal/no sedative effects as it cannot cross the blood-brain barrier easily.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Arrange the ECGs in order: Atrial flutter, Atrial fibrillation, PSVT, and Ventricular Tachycardia.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. ii, i, iii, iv

The correct order of the ECGs based on the arrhythmias provided is:

1. Atrial fibrillation (i): This ECG shows the classic irregularly irregular rhythm with no distinct P waves, characteristic of atrial fibrillation.
2. Atrial flutter (ii): This ECG displays a sawtooth pattern of atrial activity, which is indicative of atrial flutter. This appearance is due to the rapid, regular atrial contractions.
3. PSVT (iii): Paroxysmal Supraventricular Tachycardia (PSVT) is represented by a narrow complex tachycardia without discernible P waves, often seen in reentrant tachycardias like AVNRT (Atrioventricular Nodal Reentrant Tachycardia).
4. Ventricular Tachycardia (VTACH) (iv): The final ECG shows a monomorphic ventricular tachycardia, characterized by wide QRS complexes and a regular, rapid rhythm.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following hormones will be secreted in high amounts by the ovarian granulosa cells during the follicular phase of the menstrual cycle?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Estrogen

During the follicular phase of the menstrual cycle, estrogen is secreted in high amounts by the ovarian granulosa cell.

Follicular phase (days 0–14)

• A primordial follicle develops to the Graafian stage, with atresia of neighboring follicles.
• LH and FSH receptors are up-regulated in theca and granulosa cells.
• Estradiol levels increase and cause the proliferation of the uterus.
• FSH and LH levels are suppressed by the negative feedback effect of estradiol on the anterior pituitary.
• Progesterone levels are low.

Ovulation (day 14)

• Occurs 14 days before menses, regardless of cycle length.
• A burst of estradiol synthesis at the end of the follicular phase has a positive feedback effect on the secretion of FSH and LH (LH surge).
• Ovulation occurs as a result of the estrogen-induced LH surge.
• Estrogen levels decrease just after ovulation (but rise again during the luteal phase).
• Cervical mucus increases in quantity; it becomes less viscous and more penetrable by sperm.

Luteal phase (days 14–28)

• The corpus luteum begins to develop, and it predominantly synthesizes progesterone. Vascularity and secretory activity of the endometrium increase to prepare for receipt of a fertilized egg.
• Basal body temperature increases because of the effect of progesterone on the hypothalamic thermoregulatory center.
• If fertilization does not occur, the corpus luteum regresses at the end of the luteal phase. As a result, estradiol and progesterone levels decrease abruptly.

Menses (days 0–4)

• The endometrium is sloughed because of the abrupt withdrawal of estradiol and progesterone

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Hepatic angiosarcoma is associated with which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Arsenic

Hepatic angiosarcoma is associated with arsenic, thorotrast, and vinyl chloride.

Angiosarcoma is a malignant endothelial neoplasm. There is equal gender predilection. The tumor may occur at any site, but most often involves skin, soft tissue, breast, and liver.

Hepatic tumors and associated agents

Hepatocellular adenoma

Oral contraceptives, anabolic steroids

Hepatocellular carcinoma

Alcohol, thorotrast

Cholangiocarcinoma

Thorotrast

Angiosarcoma

Thorotrast, vinyl chloride, Arsenic

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A woman experiences a difficult labor and, seven days after surgery, complains of continuous dribbling of urine. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical scenario of continuous, involuntary dribbling of urine following a difficult or obstructed labor is the classic presentation of a Vesicovaginal Fistula (VVF). VVF is an abnormal passage between the bladder and the vagina, usually caused by tissue necrosis from prolonged compression by the fetal head. In developing countries, obstructed labor is the most common cause. Ureterovaginal fistula (Option B) is more common following gynecological surgeries like hysterectomy rather than labor. Rectovaginal fistula (Option C) results in the passage of feces or gas through the vagina, not urine. Vesicouterine fistula (Option D) involves a connection to the uterus and often presents with menstrual blood in the urine (menouria). Diagnosis is usually confirmed via a dye test (methylene blue) or cystoscopy. Thus, the history of difficult labor combined with urinary incontinence makes VVF the most likely diagnosis
questions.learning: The clinical scenario of continuous, involuntary dribbling of urine following a difficult or obstructed labor is the classic presentation of a Vesicovaginal Fistula (VVF).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 23-year-old female presented with complaints of neck swelling, difficulty swallowing, and hoarseness of voice. Radiological evaluation revealed a mass compressing the trachea. Biopsy showed cells arranged in nests with amyloid deposits. What is the origin of these cells?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Parafollicular cells

The clinical scenario along with biopsy showing cells arranged in nests along with amyloid deposits is suggestive of medullary carcinoma of the thyroid. Medullary carcinoma of the thyroid (MTC) arises from the parafollicular C cells.

Histopathology shows polygonal to spindle-shaped cells which form nests, trabeculae, or follicles. Amyloid deposits that are derived from the altered calcitonin molecules are present in the stroma. Calcitonin in the tumor cells and stroma is easily demonstratable by immunohistochemistry.

Features of MTC:

• Painful neck mass with cervical lymphadenopathy
• Dysphagia, dysphonia, or dyspnea if there is local invasion
• Diarrhea due to increased intestinal motility
• Cushingoid habitus due to ectopic ACTH production
• Blood-borne metastasis

Diagnosis is by careful family history, physical examination, raised calcitonin and CEA levels, and fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the mass.

Other options:

Option C and D: A Hurthle cell is a cell in the thyroid that is often associated with Hashimoto's thyroiditis as well as benign and malignant tumors (Hürthle cell adenoma and Hürthle cell carcinoma). Ashkanazy cells are another name given to the cells with Hurthle bodies in Hashimoto's thyroiditis.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: General Physiology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 59-year-old man presents with progressively worsening proximal muscle weakness over several weeks. He reports difficulty rising from a chair and climbing stairs, which improves with continued activity. He also complains of dry mouth, erectile dysfunction, and intermittent diplopia. On examination, there is reduced strength in the hip flexors and diminished deep tendon reflexes. After brief repetitive muscle contraction, both muscle strength and reflexes improve significantly. Which of the following underlying conditions is most likely associated with this patient’s disorder?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Small cell lung carcinoma

This is a classic presentation of Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS):

• Proximal muscle weakness
• Improves with activity (facilitation)
• Hyporeflexia that improves after exercise
• Autonomic symptoms (dry mouth, erectile dysfunction)
• Ocular involvement (milder than myasthenia gravis)

Pathophysiology:

• Autoantibodies against presynaptic P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels
• ↓ Acetylcholine release at neuromuscular junction

Strongly associated with paraneoplastic syndrome of small cell lung carcinoma

Why not other options?

A. Campylobacter jejuni → Associated with Guillain-Barré syndrome (ascending paralysis, areflexia, no facilitation)

B. Giant cell arteritis → Headache, jaw claudication, vision loss

C. Medullary thyroid carcinoma → MEN2 syndrome, calcitonin secretion

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 62-year-old man presents with pain and swelling of the left leg for the past five days. His D-dimer test is positive, and duplex ultrasonography confirms an extensive deep vein thrombosis involving the left femoral and popliteal veins. What is the most appropriate initial management in this case?
questions.explanation: For the initial management of acute Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT), starting with Low-Molecular-Weight Heparin (LMWH) and transitioning to an oral anticoagulant (such as a Factor Xa inhibitor) is the current standard of care. LMWH provides rapid anticoagulation without the need for constant monitoring. This approach allows for safer management compared to the traditional unfractionated heparin and warfarin regimen (Option A), which requires hospitalization and frequent INR monitoring. Catheter-directed thrombolysis (Option C) is reserved for massive, limb-threatening iliofemoral DVT due to a higher bleeding risk. IVC filters (Option D) are only indicated when anticoagulation is strictly contraindicated; they do not treat the existing thrombus and carry long-term risks. Therefore, LMWH followed by an oral anticoagulant offers the best balance of efficacy and safety for stabilizing this patient
questions.learning: For the initial management of acute Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT), starting with Low-Molecular-Weight Heparin (LMWH) and transitioning to an oral anticoagulant (such as a Factor Xa inhibitor) is the current standard of care.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child presents with recurrent sinusitis and repeated pulmonary infections, and genetic analysis reveals a mutation in the CFTR gene. Which diagnostic test is considered the gold standard for confirming this condition?
questions.explanation: The gold standard for confirming a diagnosis of Cystic Fibrosis (CF) is the quantitative pilocarpine iontophoresis sweat chloride test. In CF patients, the chloride concentration in sweat is pathologically elevated, with levels ≥60 mMol/L being diagnostic. CF is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the CFTR gene, leading to thick secretions that cause recurrent sinusitis and pulmonary infections. A lung biopsy (Option B) is highly invasive and not used for CF diagnosis. A chest X-ray (Option C) may show non-specific findings like hyperinflation or bronchiectasis but cannot confirm the disease. A nasal swab culture (Option D) may detect colonizing bacteria such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa but is not diagnostic of the underlying genetic defect. Pancreatic insufficiency is another hallmark present in over 85% of cases
questions.learning: The gold standard for confirming a diagnosis of Cystic Fibrosis (CF) is the quantitative pilocarpine iontophoresis sweat chloride test. In CF patients, the chloride concentration in sweat is pathologically elevated, with levels ≥60 mMol/L being diagnostic.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A person is planning to move from Nigeria to the USA. He is advised to have a vaccine certificate that is valid. Which vaccine certificate will be validated by the US Embassy for VISA purposes?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 17D vaccine

The International Health Regulations (IHR, 2005) mandate that travellers from endemic countries (such as Nigeria) must produce a valid yellow fever vaccination certificate when entering countries like the USA.

The strain used for the yellow fever vaccination is the 17D vaccine. The 17D vaccine is a live attenuated vaccine, administered subcutaneously.  It is valid for a lifetime beginning 10 days after vaccination.  The incubation period of yellow fever is 3–6 days. Unvaccinated people are required to remain quarantined for 6 days (maximum period of incubation).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following statements is correct about triage?
questions.explanation: Triage is the process of prioritizing patients based on the severity of their condition during mass casualty incidents. The Yellow category is for "delayed" priority, representing patients who are stable but require medical care and observation; their treatment can be safely postponed for a short time. The Red category (Option A) is for "immediate" priority—patients with life-threatening but treatable injuries, such as airway obstruction or tension pneumothorax. The Green category (Option D) is for the "walking wounded" or ambulatory patients with minor injuries. The Black category (Option C) is for the deceased or those whose injuries are so extensive that survival is unlikely even with maximal care. Efficient triage ensures the greatest good for the greatest number of people when resources are overwhelmed. Correct color-coding allows rapid visual identification of priority by responding medical teams. Knowledge of these categories is a fundamental skill in emergency and disaster medicine

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: What is the duration of short term memory?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 30-300 seconds

Short-term memory lasts for seconds to minutes, hence of the given 4 options, 30-300 seconds is the most appropriate answer.

Memory is usually divided into two forms: Explicit or declarative memory which is associated with consciousness or awareness. Implicit or nondeclarative memory does not involve awareness and its retention does not usually involve processing in the hippocampus.

Explicit and many forms of implicit memory involve

• Short-term memory and
• Long-term memory.

Short-term memory:

It lasts seconds to minutes; the encoding process for short-term explicit memory involves the hippocampus. It lasts only till the person continues to think about the number or facts.

Working memory is a form of short-term memory that keeps information available, usually for very short periods of time, until the individual plans action based on it.

Long-term memory:

It stores memories that can be recollected after years or even for a lifetime. These memories are stored in various parts of the neocortex. The various parts of the memories such as, visual, auditory, olfactory, etc., are localised to the cortical regions concerned with these functions. All these parts of the memories are brought together by long-term changes in the strength of transmission at relevant synaptic junctions so that all the components are brought to consciousness when that particular memory is recalled.

Neural basis of memory:

The basis of memory is the alteration in the strength of the selected synaptic connections. Second messenger systems contribute to the changes in the neural circuits which are required for learning and memory. Alterations in the cellular membrane channels also contribute to it.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: In the treatment of Thalamic Dejerine syndrome, which of the following drugs is least effective or least useful in its management?
questions.explanation: Thalamic Dejerine Syndrome (or Dejerine-Roussy syndrome) is a condition of central post-stroke pain resulting from a lesion in the sensory nuclei of the thalamus. It is characterized by severe, often burning, paroxysmal pain and allodynia on the contralateral side of the body. Because the pain is neuropathic (central) in origin, NSAID analgesics (Option D) like ibuprofen are least useful and generally ineffective as they target peripheral inflammatory pathways rather than central neurotransmission. In contrast, medications that modulate neurotransmitters in the CNS are the mainstay of treatment. Pregabalin (Option A) and Gabapentin (Option C) are first-line agents that bind to calcium channels to reduce neuronal hyperexcitability. Carbamazepine (Option B), an anticonvulsant, is also effective for shooting or paroxysmal components of central pain. Other useful classes include TCAs or SNRIs. This syndrome is notorious for being difficult to treat and often requires a multimodal approach combining pharmacological therapy with psychological support and physical rehabilitation
questions.learning: Thalamic Dejerine Syndrome (or Dejerine-Roussy syndrome) is a condition of central post-stroke pain resulting from a lesion in the sensory nuclei of the thalamus.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In a woman who has sustained third- and fourth- degree burns over her back, what is the correct sequence of management steps that should be followed during treatment?
options: Resuscitation - debridement - allograft or auto- graft
questions.explanation: Resuscitation - debridement - allograft or autograft The management of severe burns (third and fourth degree) follows a critical surgical hierarchy. The absolute first step is always Resuscitation (Option B) to maintain hemodynamic stability and prevent burn shock using the Parkland formula. Once the patient is stabilized, the next priority is Debridement, which involves the removal of dead, necrotic tissue (eschar) to prevent infection. Finally, the open wound must be covered to prevent fluid loss and promote healing, typically using an allograft (temporary donor skin) or an autograft (the patient's own skin). Options A, C, and D are incorrect because reconstruction cannot occur before debridement, and debridement should not precede hemodynamic stabilization. Following this sequential path—Resuscitation, Debridement, and Grafting—is the established standard of care in burn centers to ensure patient survival and maximize functional outcomes after such severe injuries.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text:
An 18-year-old girl was brought to the OPD. Genital examination revealed the findings as given below. These findings are indicative of:

Labia majora - separated

Labia minora- flabby

Fourchette tear present

Roomy vagina seen with intact hymen
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. False virgin

The given findings are suggestive of a false virgin.

The examination findings of a separated labia majora, a flabby labia minora, and a fourchette tear are indicative of forceful penetration.

Hymen usually gets ruptured with the first act of sexual intercourse. However, in some cases, hymen remains intact in spite of sexual intercourse. It is indicative of a false virgin.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Identify the true statement regarding the point marked on the myocardial action potential curve.
options: Due to opening of Na+ and closure of fast K+ channels
Due to slow but prolonged opening of Ca2+ channels
Due to closure of Na+ and opening of slow K+ channel
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Due to slow but prolonged opening of Ca2+ channels

The myocardial action potential curve marked above represents the plateau phase, which is due to the slower and prolonged opening of calcium channels.

Two types of voltage-gated Ca2+ channels (T- and L-types) are present in myocardial cells. The opening of the slower L-type Ca2+ channels is mostly responsible for changes in the action potential. The action potential curve of cardiac muscles consists of 5 phases, as shown below.

Phase 0: Depolarization - Opening of voltage-gated sodium channels (fast sodium channels) leads to sodium influx.

Phase 1: Initial repolarization - Closure of Na+ channels and opening up of K+ channels leads to potassium efflux.

Phase 2: Plateau - Slower but prolonged opening of voltage-gated Ca2+ channels, leading to calcium influx and reduced permeability of K+ channels, causes the graph to plateau

Phase 3: Rapid Repolarization - The closure of Ca2+ channels and opening of K+ at the end of the plateau phase causes repolarization.

Phase 4: Resting membrane potential - Is reached at the end of phase 3
questions.learning: Due to slow but prolonged opening of Ca2+ channels — The myocardial action potential curve marked above represents the plateau phase, which is due to the slower and prolonged opening of calcium channels.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following conditions are associated with oligohydramnios?
questions.explanation: Oligohydramnios is defined as an abnormally low volume of amniotic fluid. Since fetal urine is the primary source of amniotic fluid in the second and third trimesters, any condition that impairs fetal urine production leads to oligohydramnios. "Renal agenesis" (the absence of kidneys) is a classic cause, often resulting in Potter’s sequence due to compression of the fetus. Neural tube defects (Option B) and esophageal atresia (Option C) are characteristically associated with polyhydramnios because the fetus cannot effectively swallow the fluid (swallowing is the primary way amniotic fluid is removed). Premature birth (Option D) itself is not a primary cause, though preterm premature rupture of membranes (PPROM) is a common clinical cause of low fluid. Other causes of oligohydramnios include placental insufficiency and posterior urethral valves. Monitoring via ultrasound is essential to prevent complications like pulmonary hypoplasia or limb deformities in the fetus
questions.learning: Oligohydramnios is defined as an abnormally low volume of amniotic fluid. Since fetal urine is the primary source of amniotic fluid in the second and third trimesters, any condition that impairs fetal urine production leads to oligohydramnios.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A fetus with intrauterine growth restriction was born prematurely with jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly, microcephaly, and diffuse petechiae at birth. A brain CT was done which revealed periventricular calcifications. What is the best method for the diagnosis of the etiological agent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Urine examination

Periventricular calcifications and microcephaly in a baby with suspected congenital infection point toward cytomegalovirus (CMV). The best diagnostic method for CMV is PCR or viral culture on urine.

Since not all affected infants are viremic at birth, urine is a more reliable sample than blood.

Intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR), prematurity, and hepatosplenomegaly raise the suspicion of congenital infection. Hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, pneumonitis, petechiae, and meningoencephalitis are common to toxoplasmosis, rubella, CMV, herpes simplex virus (HSV), enteroviruses and syphilis. Hydrocephalus is seen in CMV, toxoplasmosis, HSV, and rubella.

The triad of congenital CMV infection includes intracranial calcifications (periventricular), microcephaly, and chorioretinitis.

Most CMV transmission occurs in the first trimester. The risk of transmission is high in the third trimester. 90% of the infected babies are asymptomatic and have lesser chances of having late sequelae.

In symptomatic individuals, ganciclovir can limit hearing loss and improve the developmental outcome, while there is no definitive management for congenital CMV infection.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: General Physiology · Basics Of Cell Cytoskeleton
questions.text: Which of the following transport mechanism doesn’t require ATP? Select the correct answer
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2, 3

The image shows four different transport mechanisms across cell membranes:

1. Simple diffusion through membrane: This shows direct diffusion of molecules through the lipid bilayer from high concentration to low concentration. This is also passive transport that doesn't require ATP.
2. Simple diffusion through channels: This shows molecules moving through a protein channel from high concentration to low concentration. This is passive transport that follows the concentration gradient without requiring ATP. Channels have gates that simply open or close without configurational changes, allowing molecules to pass according to their concentration gradient.
3. Paracellular transport: This shows molecules moving between cells through the spaces between adjacent cells, not through the cells themselves. This is passive movement along the concentration gradient and doesn't require ATP.

| Mechanism | ATP Required | Example | Key Feature

| --------- | ------------ | ------- | -----------

| Simple diffusion | ❌ | O₂, CO₂ | No protein needed

| Facilitated diffusion | ❌ | GLUT-4 | Uses carrier

| Secondary active | ❌ (indirect) | SGLT | Uses Na⁺ gradient

| Primary active | ✅ | Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase | Direct ATP use

| Type | Example

| ---- | -------

| Symport | SGLT (Na⁺ + glucose)

| Antiport | Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger

Other Option:

1. Active transport: This shows fewer molecules on one side and more on the other side, indicating movement against the concentration gradient (from low to high concentration). This requires energy in the form of ATP to power the transport proteins.
questions.learning: 1, 2, 3 The image shows four different transport mechanisms across cell membranes: 1. Simple diffusion through membrane: This shows direct diffusion of molecules through the lipid bilayer from high concentration to low concentration.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A histology slide from a large blood vessel demonstrates a very thick tunica media composed of numerous concentric elastic lamellae with relatively inconspicuous adventitia. Which of the following vessels is most likely represented?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Aorta

The aorta is the prototype of an elastic artery. Its hallmark histological feature is a thick tunica media containing multiple concentric elastic lamellae interspersed with smooth muscle cells. These elastic fibers allow the aorta to expand during systole and recoil during diastole, maintaining continuous blood flow (Windkessel effect). Compared with veins, the adventitia is relatively thinner.

Why not the other options?

• B. Brachiocephalic vein: A large vein with a thin tunica media and thick adventitia containing abundant collagen and longitudinal smooth muscle.
• C. Azygos vein: Also a large vein; characterized by a relatively thin media and prominent adventitia, lacking the numerous elastic lamellae seen in the aorta.
• D. Inferior vena cava: The largest vein, with a thin tunica media and a very thick adventitia containing longitudinal bundles of smooth muscle, unlike the elastic media of the aorta.

High-yield pearl:

• Elastic arteries (e.g., aorta): Thick tunica media with many elastic lamellae.
questions.learning: Aorta — The aorta is the prototype of an elastic artery. Its hallmark histological feature is a thick tunica media containing multiple concentric elastic lamellae interspersed with smooth muscle cells.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 28-year-old primigravida with a dichorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy undergoes vaginal delivery. The first twin is delivered cephalically without complications. Ultrasound immediately after delivery confirms that the second twin is in breech presentation, fetal heart rate is reassuring, membranes are intact, and the cervix is fully dilated. What is the preferred method of delivery for the second twin?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Assisted breech delivery

When the first twin is delivered cephalically, vaginal delivery is appropriate regardless of the presentation of the second twin, provided there are no contraindications. If the second twin is breech, assisted breech delivery is the preferred technique. The breech is allowed to descend spontaneously until the umbilicus is visible ("hands off the breech"), after which maneuvers such as Lovset (for the arms) and Burns–Marshall or Mauriceau–Smellie–Veit (for the after-coming head) are used.

Why not the other options?

• A. Lower segment cesarean section (LSCS ) – Not routinely required. Combined vaginal–cesarean delivery has higher maternal morbidity and is reserved for failed vaginal delivery or fetal compromise.
• B. Internal podalic version (IPV) – Indicated for a transverse or oblique lie of the second twin, not for a fetus already presenting by the breech.
• C. Breech extraction – Involves immediate traction on the fetal feet from the outset and is reserved for selected situations such as fetal distress or after internal podalic version, not for a spontaneously descending breech.

High-Yield Pearl:

Second twin breech with full cervical dilatation:

• Assisted breech delivery = Wait, then assist.
• Breech extraction = Pull from the start.
questions.learning: Assisted breech delivery When the first twin is delivered cephalically, vaginal delivery is appropriate regardless of the presentation of the second twin, provided there are no contraindications.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient being treated for hypertriglyceridemia developed flushing, gout, hyperglycemia, and raised liver enzymes. Which drug is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Nicotinamide

Niacin (Vitamin B3) is a lipid-lowering drug that:

• Reduces triglycerides
• Increases HDL
• Decreases LDL moderately

Mechanism: Inhibits hormone-sensitive lipase in adipose tissue

This reduces release of free fatty acids to the liver, decreasing VLDL synthesis.

Nicotinamide (niacin) is used to treat hypertriglyceridemia and is known for flushing due to prostaglandin release.

It can cause hyperuricemia leading to gout, hyperglycemia, and elevated liver enzymes.

Niacin has several very characteristic side effects, often tested in exams.

| Side Effect | Mechanism

| ----------- | ---------

| Flushing | Prostaglandin-mediated vasodilation

| Hyperglycemia | Reduced insulin sensitivity

| Hyperuricemia → gout | Reduced uric acid excretion

| Hepatotoxicity | Liver metabolism

These adverse effects are characteristic and dose-related.

Statins, fibrates, and ezetimibe do not produce this combination of side effects.

A) Atorvastatin

Statins mainly cause:

• Myopathy
• Elevated liver enzymes

But flushing and gout are not typical.

B) Fenofibrate

Fibrates cause:

• Gallstones
• Myopathy (with statins)

But not flushing.

D) Ezetimibe

Mechanism: Inhibits intestinal cholesterol absorption (NPC1L1).

Side effects are minimal.
