questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A diabetic truck driver presents to you with cough and breathlessness. A diagnosis of pneumonia was confirmed, and histopathological examination revealed dichotomous branching, as shown below. What is the likely causative agent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Aspergillus

The most likely causative agent based on the clinical features and image showing dichotomous branching at acute angles given is Aspergillus.

Aspergillus fumigatus is the most common pathogenic species. It can cause invasive aspergillosis in immunocompromised patients. This can be due to prolonged treatment with steroids or retro-positive status. It starts as pneumonia, which can later spread to involve other organs. Voriconazole is the drug of choice.

Other manifestations include allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis where central bronchiectasis is usually seen. Aspergilloma and superficial infections like otomycosis or mycotic keratitis are the other presentations.

Histopathological examination of the tissue section shows characteristic dichotomous branching at an acute angle. The hyphae stain poorly with hematoxylin and eosin, so periodic acid–Schiff (PAS) stain is used.

Other methods for diagnosis include detection of galactomannan (Aspergillus cell-wall component) and culture isolation. Aspergillus fumigatus grows dark green colonies, while Aspergillus niger appears black. Yellow-green colonies are seen in case of Aspergillus flavus. Microscopic examination of colonies stained with lactophenol cotton blue would show septate hyphae and conidiophores.

Other options:

Options A and B - Rhizopus and Mucor are zygomycetes that are responsible for mucormycosis. Non-septate, broad hyphae are seen on tissue samples stained with hematoxylin and eosin.

The image below shows broad aseptate and irregularly-branched non-septate hyphae of Mucor.

Option C - Candida, the causative agent for candidiasis, appear as budding gram-positive cells on wet films and smears. Mycelial forms suggest colonization. Culture colonies are creamy-white and have a yeasty odor. Candida albicans, the most commonly implicated pathogenic species, form chlamydospores on corn meal agar.

The image below shows candidal hyphae and chlamydospores.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A person has suffered from chest trauma resulting in fracture of 2-6th ribs. He is being given pain relief by IV analgesic agents. Which of these blocks will be helpful in pain relief?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Thoracic epidural

Rib fractures from T2–T6 produce severe chest wall pain best relieved by thoracic epidural, which provides segmental analgesia to the corresponding dermatomes. Cervical and supraclavicular blocks do not cover thoracic levels, and lumbar epidural is too low to provide effective analgesia for upper thoracic ribs.
questions.learning: Thoracic epidural Rib fractures from T2–T6 produce severe chest wall pain best relieved by thoracic epidural, which provides segmental analgesia to the corresponding dermatomes.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: In negative feedback, feedback gain of infinity is seen in which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Blood volume control by kidney

In negative feedback, feedback gain of infinity could be seen in blood volume control by the kidney.

When the blood volume falls below the equilibrium, the renal–body fluid mechanism causes the blood volume returns back to the equilibrium point resulting in zero error and hence the gain of kidney in its ability to regulate blood volume is infinity (∞).

The degree of effectiveness with which a regulatory system maintains constant conditions is determined by the gain of the negative feedback system.

Gain= Correction/Error

Example: If an external or internal factor led to a decrease in mean blood pressure from 100 mm Hg to 80 mm Hg. Activation of a negative feedback mechanism i.e. baroreflex leads to a correction of blood pressure to 96 mm Hg. So in this case,

• Correction = 16 mm Hg
• Error = 4 mm Hg
• Gain = Correction/Error = 16/4 = 4

Note: A gain of 0 would imply a total failure of the regulatory system and a gain of infinity (∞) would indicate complete restoration of the regulated variable.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Two vacccines - Measles and the pentavalent vaccine are used during an immunisation programme. Which of these vaccines has to be discarded?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Measles

Open vial policy is not applicable for BCG, JE, Measles vaccines and Rota virus.

All open vials of BCG, measles and JE must be destroyed after 48 hours or before next session, whichever is earlier.

Open vial policy  is applicable for DPT, TT, hepatitis B vaccine, OPV and liquid pentavalent vaccine.

Pearl PF2122: Open Vial Policy

Open vial policy allows for reuse of partially used multidose vials of applicable vaccines under the Universal Immunization Programme in subsequent sessions up to 4 weeks subject to certain conditions and thereby reducing vaccine wastage.

It is applicable only for DPT, TT, hepatitis B vaccine, OPV, liquid pentavalent vaccine, rotavirus vaccine(new version with the VVM on the side), and JE vaccines (inactivated). It is not applicable to BCG and measles vaccines.

Vaccine vials opened in session-site can be used in more than one session up to four weeks if expiry date has not passed, if storage and transport was appropriate, no contamination has occurred in vial septum, asepsis in withdrawing was practiced and if vaccine vial monitor has not reached discard point.

Open vials should not be submerged in water. All open vials should have a record of date and time of opening. At the end of a session, all vaccines should be returned to the cold chain point and segregated as re-usable and non-reusable. All open vials of BCG, measles must be destroyed after 48 hours or before next session, whichever is earlier.

In case of any adverse events following immunization, all open vials should not be discarded until investigation is complete. All vials must be transported in zipper bags in the vaccine carrier and recorded in stock register. Ice packs used should be well sealed.
questions.learning: Measles Open vial policy is not applicable for BCG, JE, Measles vaccines and Rota virus. All open vials of BCG, measles and JE must be destroyed after 48 hours or before next session, whichever is earlier.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text:
A patient presented with ipsilateral Horner's syndrome, ipsilateral loss of pain and temperature sensations in the face, vertigo with numbness and loss of sweating and dysarthria on the contralateral side. All these symptoms are caused due to a lesion in:

A. Medial medulla
B. Lateral medulla
C. Ventromedial medulla
D. Lateral medulla including nucleus ambiguus and spinothalamic tract
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. B and D

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of lateral medullary syndrome/Wallenberg syndrome. This may result from a stroke affecting the ipsilateral vertebral artery.

Lateral medullary syndrome: The clinical findings correspond to the neuroanatomical structures affected in the lateral portion of the medulla:

• Descending tract and nucleus of CN V (trigeminal)- loss of pain and sensation over the ipsilateral half of the face.
• Inferior cerebellar peduncle – ipsilateral ataxia (gait and limb)
• Lateral spinothalamic tract – loss of pain and temperature sensation over the contralateral half of the body.
• IX and X CN - ipsilateral paralysis of palate, vocal cord, diminished gag reflex giving rise to dysphagia, dysarthria.
• Vestibular nucleus - Nystagmus, diplopia, vertigo, nausea
• Descending sympathetic tract – ipsilateral Horner’s syndrome (miosis, ptosis, and anhidrosis).
questions.learning: B and D — The given clinical scenario is suggestive of lateral medullary syndrome/Wallenberg syndrome. This may result from a stroke affecting the ipsilateral vertebral artery.

questions.text: Modified Robson's classification class 1 includes:
options: Multiparous without previous CS, spontaneous labour
Multiparous without previous CS, induced/CS before labour
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Nulliparous, singleton, cephalic, spontaneous labour

Class 1 of modified Robson's classification includes nullipara, equal to or >37 weeks, single, cephalic, spontaneous labor.

It is the most widely accepted classification system available for analyzing characteristics of delivering women worldwide. It consists of 10 patient population categories. The basis for these categories include:

• Parity
• Onset of labor and mode of delivery
• Gestational age
• Fetal presentation
• No. of fetuses

Class 2

Nullipara, equal to or >37 weeks, single, cephalic

2a: induced labor  2b: CS before labor

Class 3
Multipara, equal to or >37 weeks, single, cephalic, spontaneous labor (excludes previous CS)

Class 4
Multipara, equal to or >37 weeks, single, cephalic   4a: induced labor 4b: CS before labor

Class 5
Multipara, previous CS, equal to or >37 weeks, single, cephalic

Class 6
Nullipara, single, breech

Class 7
Multipara, single, breech (including previous CS)

Class 8

Class 9

Class 10
Single, cephalic <37 weeks (including previous CS)

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A lady came to the hospital after fighting with her husband. She reports that she is unable to speak. However, all neurological and physical examinations are normal, and she does not seem concerned about her condition. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. La-belle indifference

La-belle indifference is seen in conversion disorder. It is the absence of concern towards one’s problem despite the apparent severe disability.

Conversion disorder is also called functional neurological symptom disorder, and there is no bodily cause involved in this condition. A conversion reaction is an acute and temporary loss or alteration in motor or sensory function triggered by psychosocial stress. Most of the patients have a history of a traumatic event in childhood. The symptoms or deficits of conversion disorder are not intentionally produced. It is more commonly seen in females.

Primary gain refers to keeping internal conflicts outside of awareness and the relief from stress. Secondary gain refers to the attention gained by the patient (from bystanders) as a result of being sick. If the secondary gain is intentional, then it would lead to the diagnosis of malingering. A related phenomenon is la belle indifference, in which the patient is not concerned about the serious symptoms.

Symptoms of conversion disorder:

* One or two neurologic symptoms affecting the voluntary or sensory function

* Must have psychologic factors associated with the onset or exacerbation of the symptoms.

* Mutism, blindness, and paralysis are the most common symptoms.

* Sensory system: Anesthesia and paresthesia

* Motor system: Abnormal movements, gait disturbance (astasia abasia), weakness, paralysis, tics, jerks, etc.

* Central nervous system: Pseudo-seizures

Other Options:

Option A: Adjustment reaction is a psychological response to an identifiable stressor that results in the development of clinically significant emotional or behavioral symptoms. The condition develops within 3 months of exposure to the stressor and lasts no longer than 6 months after the stressor or its consequences have ended. Notably, the emotional or behavioral symptoms must be out of proportion to the stressor when considering cultural and contextual factors.

Option B: Somatic symptom disorder is the presence of one or more somatic symptoms for more than 6 months in the absence of an organic cause is suggestive of somatic symptom disorder. It is characterized by the fear of having a serious illness based on the person's misinterpretation of bodily symptoms.

Option C:Malingering is the intentional falsification of physical or psychological symptoms to achieve some practical gain such as financial compensation, avoidance of criminal responsibility or military service, or leave from work.

Pearl PF1521: Conversion Disorder

Conversion disorder: Also called functional neurological symptom disorder.

Common presenting symptoms:

* Weakness and/or paralysis

* Non-epileptic seizures

* Movement disorders

* Speech or visual impairment

* Swallowing difficulty

* Sensory disturbances

* Cognitive symptoms

Diagnostic criteria:

* Symptoms of altered neurological function-voluntary motor or sensory

* Often precipitated by a psychological stressor (the temporal relationship between stressor and symptoms is present)

* Not feigned or intentionally produced (as in factitious disorder or malingering)

* Findings incompatible with a recognized neurological condition

* Symptoms cause significant social or occupational impairment

Other important features:

* Presence of primary and secondary gain

* La-belle indifference: refers to an absence of concern towards one’s problem despite severe disability

Management options:

* First-line: Education and self-help technique

* Second-line: Cognitive-behavioral therapy

* Physical therapy for motor symptoms
questions.learning: La-belle indifference La-belle indifference is seen in conversion disorder. It is the absence of concern towards one’s problem despite the apparent severe disability.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which component is the main constituent of Tamm-Horsfall mucoprotein?
questions.explanation: Tamm-Horsfall protein, also known as uromodulin, is a high-molecular-weight glycoprotein secreted exclusively by the thick ascending limb of the Henle's loop and the early distal tubule. It is the most abundant protein in normal human urine. Crucially, Tamm-Horsfall protein serves as the essential matrix for the formation of renal casts. When the urinary flow is slow or the urine is highly concentrated, this protein gels and traps other elements, such as cells or debris, creating the cylindrical structures seen in urine microscopy. Hyaline casts consist purely of Tamm-Horsfall protein. Mural thrombi (Option A) are blood clots attached to the heart or vessel walls. Curschmann spirals (Option B) are found in the sputum of asthma patients. Bence-Jones proteins (Option D) are monoclonal light chains found in the urine of multiple myeloma patients. Understanding the role of Tamm-Horsfall protein is vital for interpreting urinalysis, as casts provide a "microscopic window" into the health and function of the renal tubules
questions.learning: Tamm-Horsfall protein, also known as uromodulin, is a high-molecular-weight glycoprotein secreted exclusively by the thick ascending limb of the Henle's loop and the early distal tubule.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Nasal polyps are commonly associated with:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Intrinsic asthma

Nasal polyps are associated with intrinsic asthma.

Intrinsic asthma is characterized by the presence of asthma with negative skin prick tests for common antigens. The association of nasal polyps with asthma is described by Samter’s triad (intrinsic asthma + aspirin hypersensitivity + nasal polyposis). Asthma is usually severe, persistent, and adult-onset.

Other options:

Option B: Brittle asthma refers to a severe variant of asthma where patients have very serious and often, life-threatening attacks despite appropriate therapy.

Option C: Extrinsic asthma is also referred to as atopic asthma. It is allergen mediated.

Option D: Exercise-induced asthma is airway narrowing due to strenuous physical activity. Symptoms typically start after the exercise has ended and last for around 30 minutes.
questions.learning: Intrinsic asthma Nasal polyps are associated with intrinsic asthma. Intrinsic asthma is characterized by the presence of asthma with negative skin prick tests for common antigens.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Identify the type of wound from the image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Defense wounds

The given image shows irregular and ragged cut wounds over the palmar surface of the hands and fingers, which is suggestive of defense wounds.

Defense wounds are the wounds that occur as a result of the victim's attempt to save himself from an injury.

It can be active or passive. Active defense wounds occur when the victim tries to grasp the weapon, while passive wounds result when the victim raises the hands, arms, or legs in an attempt to protect the eyes, head, or neck.

The morphology of the wound depends upon the type of weapon and the attack. In a sharp injury due to a single-edged weapon, a single cut may be seen on the palm or the bends of fingers. In the case of a double-edged sharp weapon, cuts are seen on both palm and fingers. The cuts are irregular in-depth and are ragged.

The defense wounds signify homicide, and in females, they often indicate sexual assault.

Other options:

Options B and C: Antemortem and postmortem wounds are of medicolegal importance while evaluating trauma. They can be differentiated by the following features:

Feature
Antemortem wounds
Postmortem wounds

Edges
Swollen edges with wound gapes
Closely approximated with no wound gapes

Hemorrhage
Arterial type of hemorrhage
Venous hemorrhage

Spurting
Spurting of blood seen with firmly coagulated blood
No spurts and no clotting

Vital reaction
Inflammation and repair seen
No signs of inflammation and repair

Option D: Hesitation cuts are a feature of self-inflicted wounds or suicide. It typically appears as multiple, small, and superficial wounds on the skin, at the beginning of an incised wound. The common sites are the throat, wrist, and front of the chest.
questions.learning: Defense wounds — The given image shows irregular and ragged cut wounds over the palmar surface of the hands and fingers, which is suggestive of defense wounds.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 35-year-old man sustained a spinal cord injury as a result of a road traffic accident. On examination, his blood pressure is found to be 90/60 mmHg. The patient most likely suffered from which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Neurogenic shock

The clinical scenario of the presence of hypotension associated with the spinal cord injury is suggestive of neurogenic shock.

Neurogenic shock refers to reduced tissue perfusion due to loss of vasomotor tone to peripheral arterial beds. Neurogenic shock is usually secondary to spinal cord injuries due to vertebral body fractures of the cervical or high thoracic region that disrupts the sympathetic regulation of peripheral vascular tone. Loss of vasoconstrictor impulses results in increased vascular capacitance, decreased venous return and decreased cardiac output.

Primary injury in neurogenic shock occurs due to damage to axons and the membrane of neurons. Secondary injury occurs doe to vascular damage hours to days after the primary insult.

The clinical features are bradycardia, temperature dysregulation, hypotension and autonomic dysreflexia. The skin often appears warm and flushed and there is also presence of radiological evidence of vertebral fracture.

Treatment involves securing of airways, adequate ventilation and perfusion with fluids and blood products followed by administration of vasoconstrictors to improve vascular tone.

Other options:

Option A: Cardiogenic shock is caused due to the failure of the myocardial pump.

Option B: Septic shock is not likely in this clinical scenario, as there is no evidence of any infection.

Option D: Hypovolemic shock is caused due to a significant decrease in blood or plasma volume, caused by the loss of fluid from the vascular compartment. Haemorrhage, fluid loss from severe burns, diarrhea, excessive urine formation, perspiration, and trauma are some of the major mechanisms of fluid loss that can lead to hypovolemic shock.
questions.learning: Neurogenic shock — The clinical scenario of the presence of hypotension associated with the spinal cord injury is suggestive of neurogenic shock. Neurogenic shock refers to reduced tissue perfusion due to loss of vasomotor tone to peripheral arterial beds.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following about the enteric nervous regulation system is false? 1. Interstitial cells of Cajal are pacemakers 2. It can function independently of the brain and spinal cord 3. All the afferents are from the vagus nerve 4. Myenteric plexus is in the Lamina propria
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 3, 4

The Enteric Nervous System (ENS) is like a quiet maestro conducting digestion:

• Coordinates motility, secretion, and blood flow
• Works independently of CNS (but can be modulated by it)

Can function independently of CNS input. Interstitial cells of Cajal act as pacemakers generating slow waves. Afferents are not exclusively vagal; significant intrinsic and spinal afferents exist.

| Feature | Myenteric (Auerbach) | Submucosal (Meissner)

| ------- | -------------------- | ---------------------

| Location | Between muscle layers | Submucosa

| Function | Motility | Secretion, blood flow

| Extent | Entire GI tract | Mainly small intestine

Clinical correlations

| Disease | Defect

| ------- | ------

| Hirschsprung disease | Absence of ganglion cells

| Achalasia | Loss of inhibitory neurons

| IBS | Dysregulated ENS
questions.learning: 3, 4 The Enteric Nervous System (ENS) is like a quiet maestro conducting digestion: • Coordinates motility, secretion, and blood flow • Works independently of CNS (but can be modulated by it) Can function independently of CNS input.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is the smallest pelvic diameter at the brim?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Obstetric conjugate

The obstetric conjugate is the smallest pelvic diameter at the brim.

It is the distance between the midpoint of the sacral promontory to the prominent bony projection in the midline on the inner surface of the symphysis pubis. It is the shortest anteroposterior diameter in the anteroposterior plane of the inlet and measures 10 cm. It represents the narrowest fixed diameter of the pelvic inlet that the fetal head must navigate. It cannot be measured directly during a pelvic exam but is estimated using the diagonal conjugate.

Other Options:

Option B: Diagonal Conjugate:  It is the distance between the lower border of the symphysis pubis to the midpoint on the sacral promontory. It measures 12 cm. Obstetric conjugate is derived by subtracting 1.5–2 cm from the diagonal conjugate depending upon the height, thickness and inclination of the symphysis pubis.

Option C and D : True conjugate: Also called anatomical conjugate, is the distance between the midpoint of the sacral promontory to the inner margin of the upper border of the symphysis pubis and measures 11 cm.
questions.learning: Obstetric conjugate — The obstetric conjugate is the smallest pelvic diameter at the brim. It is the distance between the midpoint of the sacral promontory to the prominent bony projection in the midline on the inner surface of the symphysis pubis.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What is the required thickness of a lead apron used for radiation protection?
questions.explanation: For healthcare workers exposed to ionizing radiation (such as in X-ray rooms or cardiac catheterization labs), lead aprons are a critical part of personal protective equipment (PPE). According to standard radiation safety guidelines, a lead apron must have a minimum thickness equivalent of 0.5 mm (Option C). This thickness is designed to attenuate approximately 90% or more of the scattered X-ray radiation. A thickness of 1 mm (Option A) would provide even more protection but is often too heavy for practical daily use. Options B and D are not the standard regulatory requirements for personal aprons . Lead aprons must be regularly inspected for cracks using fluoroscopy and stored flat or on specialized hangers to prevent damage to the internal shielding. Therefore, 0.5 mm is the universally accepted standard for providing a balance between effective radiation protection and ergonomic feasibility for medical personnel
questions.learning: For healthcare workers exposed to ionizing radiation (such as in X-ray rooms or cardiac catheterization labs), lead aprons are a critical part of personal protective equipment (PPE).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Among the listed conditions, which is typically associated with the presence of a B tympanogram?
questions.explanation: Tympanometry measures the compliance of the tympanic membrane under varying air pressure. A Type B tympanogram is a "flat" curve indicating significantly restricted mobility of the eardrum. This is most commonly seen in Serous Otitis Media (Otitis Media with Effusion), where fluid in the middle ear space prevents the membrane from vibrating. It can also be seen in cases of a perforated eardrum or a completely occluded ear canal. Option A (Ossicular dislocation) typically produces a Type Ad (deep) tympanogram due to hypermobility. Option B (Otosclerosis) results in a Type As (stiff/shallow) tympanogram, as the stapes is fixed but the drum can still move slightly. Option D (Normal ear) produces a Type A tympanogram with normal peak pressure and compliance. Understanding these patterns is essential for diagnosing hearing loss; a Type B tympanogram in a child often indicates the need for medical management or the insertion of pressure-equalizing tubes
questions.learning: Tympanometry measures the compliance of the tympanic membrane under varying air pressure. A Type B tympanogram is a "flat" curve indicating significantly restricted mobility of the eardrum.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What is the ideal thickness of lead aprons to be worn by workers associated with radiographical procedures?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 0.5mm

The lead apron to be worn by workers associated with radiographical procedures should contain 0.5 mm of lead.
questions.learning: 0.5mm The lead apron to be worn by workers associated with radiographical procedures should contain 0.5 mm of lead.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The remnants of Wolffian ducts in females are located in: (NEET PG 2020)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Leaves of broad ligament

In females, remnants of the mesonephric (Wolffian) ducts persist within the leaves of the broad ligament. Important Wolffian duct remnants:

• Epoophoron
• Paroophoron
• Gartner duct cysts

Locations:

• Epoophoron and paroophoron → broad ligament near ovary and fallopian tube
• Gartner duct cyst → lateral wall of vagina

Embryologic concept:

• In females, absence of testosterone causes regression of the Wolffian ducts
• Müllerian ducts develop into:

• Fallopian tubes
• Uterus
• Upper vagina

• Wolffian duct remnants can form cysts, especially Gartner duct cysts

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 28-year-old woman presents with left breast pain and swelling, accompanied by erythema, warmth, tenderness, and fever. Based on these findings, what is the most common causative organism responsible for acute mastitis?
questions.explanation: Acute mastitis is most commonly a lactational infection seen in breastfeeding women. The clinical signs of erythema, localized warmth, tenderness, and fever are hallmarks of this inflammatory condition. The primary entry point for pathogens, most frequently Staphylococcus aureus, is a crack or fissure in the nipple (Option D). These skin abrasions, often caused by poor infant latching, allow bacteria from the infant's oropharynx or maternal skin to invade the mammary tissue. Breast engorgement (Option A) can lead to stasis which predisposes a patient to infection, but it is a physiological state rather than the direct portal of entry. Hormonal influence (Option B) is related to cyclic breast pain, not acute infectious mastitis. Absence of lactation (Option C) makes infectious mastitis much less likely, as non-lactational mastitis usually involves different pathogens or underlying pathology like duct ectasia. Therefore, a crack in the nipple is the classic primary cause
questions.learning: Acute mastitis is most commonly a lactational infection seen in breastfeeding women. The clinical signs of erythema, localized warmth, tenderness, and fever are hallmarks of this inflammatory condition.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.topic: General Pharmacology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: All of the following are correctly matched drug-induced liver pathologies, except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Methotrexate – Cholestatic pattern

Methotrexate causes chronic hepatotoxicity characterized by hepatic fibrosis, cirrhosis, and macrovesicular steatosis, especially with long-term use. A cholestatic pattern is not its typical liver injury profile, making this pairing incorrect.

Why other options are incorrect (i.e., correctly matched):

A. Valproate – Microvesicular steatosis: Valproate impairs mitochondrial β-oxidation, leading to microvesicular fatty change.

B. Halothane – Massive necrosis: Halothane can cause immune-mediated fulminant hepatic necrosis (“halothane hepatitis”).

D. Allopurinol – Fibrin ring granulomas: Allopurinol is classically associated with granulomatous hepatitis featuring fibrin ring granulomas.

| Pathology/Pattern | Causative Agents | High-Yield Pearl

| ----------------- | ---------------- | ----------------

| Cholestatic pattern | OCPs, anabolic steroids | ↑ ALP, ↑ bilirubin; bland canalicular cholestasis, minimal inflammation

| Spotty hepatocyte necrosis | Methyldopa, phenytoin | Hypersensitivity-type injury; scattered single-cell necrosis with mild inflammation

| Massive necrosis | Acetaminophen, halothane | Acetaminophen → centrilobular (Zone 3) necrosis via NAPQI; can cause fulminant hepatic failure

| Chronic hepatitis | Isoniazid | Mimics autoimmune/viral hepatitis histologically; risk ↑ with age, alcohol use

| Microvesicular steatosis | Valproate, tetracycline, aspirin (Reye syndrome), ART (esp. NRTIs) | Mitochondrial β-oxidation injury; small fat droplets, nucleus stays central (vs macrovesicular)

| Fibrosis and cirrhosis | Alcohol, methotrexate, enalapril, vitamin A | MTX → periportal fibrosis; monitor with liver biopsy/elastography on long-term therapy

| Noncaseating epithelioid granulomas | Sulfonamides, amiodarone, isoniazid, allopurinol (also implicated), methyldopa | Granulomatous hepatitis; think drug cause if no infectious/sarcoid etiology found

| Fibrin ring granulomas | Allopurinol | Classic association; also seen in Q fever (Coxiella), EBV, CMV — important differential trap
questions.learning: Methotrexate – Cholestatic pattern Methotrexate causes chronic hepatotoxicity characterized by hepatic fibrosis, cirrhosis, and macrovesicular steatosis, especially with long-term use.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following anaesthetic agents is most suitable for cataract surgery?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2 % lignocaine

2% Lignocaine (Lidocaine) is the infiltrative anaesthetic suitable for this patient due to its moderate duration of action, which lasts for 30–60 minutes.

Lidocaine is a local anaesthetic that can be used for peripheral nerve blockade, and topical, infiltrative, spinal, and epidural anaesthesia. The duration of infiltration anaesthesia can be prolonged by the addition of epinephrine to lidocaine (up to 120 minutes). It is also used for intravenous regional anaesthesia (IVRA) in short surgical procedures (<90 minutes) on the limbs.

It is metabolized by CYP enzymes in the liver. Large amounts of lidocaine can exacerbate symptoms of myasthenia gravis and cardiac toxicity, as well as transient neurological symptoms.

Bupivacaine, ropivacaine, and tetracaine are all long-acting drugs. (option B,C & D)

Intermediate duration ( 60-120 minutes):

* Lidocaine

* Mepivacaine

* Prilocaine

Long duration (400-450 minutes):

* Tetracaine

* Bupivacaine

* Ropivacaine

* Etidocaine

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A confirmed case of which of the following viral haemorrhagic fevers was found in India?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Crimean congo hemorrhagic fever

Crimean Congo hemorrhagic fever has been found in India.

Four cases were first described in India in 2011 in the state of Gujarat. It is a severe form of viral hemorrhagic fever caused by negative sense ssRNA Nairovirus species. It is zoonotic in origin with Ixodes ticks as vectors with livestock as primary reservoirs. The outbreak was caused due to person-to-person transmission in a tertiary care hospital where the index patient (first identified case) was admitted.
questions.learning: Crimean congo hemorrhagic fever Crimean Congo hemorrhagic fever has been found in India. Four cases were first described in India in 2011 in the state of Gujarat.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Identify the anaplerotic reaction among the following?
options: Conversion of pyruvate to Acetyl CoA
Conversion of pyruvate to Lactic acid
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Conversion of pyruvate to Oxaloacetate

The conversion of pyruvate to oxaloacetate is an anaplerotic reaction. It is catalyzed by pyruvate carboxylase.

Anaplerotic reactions are chemical reactions that form intermediates of a metabolic pathway. The above reaction is important in maintaining an adequate concentration of oxaloacetate for the condensation reaction with acetyl-CoA. If acetyl-CoA accumulates, it acts as an activator of pyruvate carboxylase and an inhibitor of pyruvate dehydrogenase, thereby ensuring an adequate supply of oxaloacetate.

Other anaplerotic reactions are:

• Compounds that are metabolized to yield propionyl CoA, which can be then carboxylated and isomerized to succinyl CoA.
• Glutamate and glutamine are important anaplerotic substrates because they yield α-ketoglutarate as a result of the reactions catalyzed by glutaminase and glutamate dehydrogenase.
• Transamination of aspartate leads directly to the formation of oxaloacetate.
questions.learning: Conversion of pyruvate to Oxaloacetate — The conversion of pyruvate to oxaloacetate is an anaplerotic reaction. It is catalyzed by pyruvate carboxylase.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A child presents with the findings shown in the image below. Which structure is most likely involved in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cranial nerve 7

The given clinical findings are suggestive of Bell's palsy which is a paralysis of the facial nerve.

Facial nerve paralysis can be central or peripheral. Peripheral is more common and is usually idiopathic.

Bell's palsy is an acute onset idiopathic, peripheral facial paralysis. It is a lower motor neuron lesion of the facial nerve and involves the ipsilateral side of the upper and lower halves of the face.

It presents an inability to close the eye, and if the patient attempts to close it, it turns up and out. This is known as the Bell's phenomenon. Other features include drooling of saliva and facial asymmetry. There may be noise intolerance and a loss of taste sensation.

Bell's palsy is a diagnosis of exclusion. Investigations should rule out all other possible causes of facial paralysis.

Treatment of Bell's palsy involves prednisone 60-80 mg daily during the first 5 days and then tapered over the next 5 days. Tape to depress the upper eyelid during sleep and artificial tears can be used to prevent corneal drying. Most patients recover within a few weeks or months.

Other options:

Option B: In oculomotor nerve (CN 3) palsy, there is ptosis, a dilated pupil, and the eye appears to be down and out due to the unopposed lateral rectus and superior oblique action.

Option C: Orbicularis oculi palsy refers to weakness or paralysis of the muscle responsible for closing the eyelids. This condition can lead to incomplete eyelid closure, resulting in exposure keratitis and difficulty blinking.

Option D: Erb's palsy is a paralysis of the arm caused by injury to the upper brachial plexus (C5-C6 nerves), often during birth. It results in weakness or loss of movement in the shoulder and arm, commonly presenting as a "waiter's tip" deformity as shown in the image below.
questions.learning: Cranial nerve 7 — The given clinical findings are suggestive of Bell's palsy which is a paralysis of the facial nerve. Facial nerve paralysis can be central or peripheral.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: The pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor classically associated with necrolytic migratory erythema is glucagonoma.
questions.explanation: Glucagonoma is a rare neuroendocrine tumor of the pancreatic alpha cells that secretes excessive glucagon. It is clinically defined by a classic "4D" syndrome: Diabetes mellitus, Dermatitis (specifically Necrolytic Migratory Erythema), DVT (venous thrombosis), and Depression. Necrolytic migratory erythema (NME) is the pathognomonic skin rash, appearing as painful or itchy red plaques that blister and crust, typically around the groin and limbs. Insulinoma (Option A) presents with the Whipple triad of fasting hypoglycemia. Somatostatinoma (Option C) presents with a triad of diabetes, gallstones, and steatorrhea. VIPoma (Option D) causes "pancreatic cholera," characterized by profuse watery diarrhea, hypokalemia, and achlorhydria (WDHA syndrome). Because NME is uniquely and specifically linked to excessive glucagon levels, glucagonoma is the definitive diagnosis. Treatment involves somatostatin analogs and surgical resection to control the hormone excess and resolve the characteristic skin lesions
questions.learning: Glucagonoma is a rare neuroendocrine tumor of the pancreatic alpha cells that secretes excessive glucagon. It is clinically defined by a classic "4D" syndrome: Diabetes mellitus, Dermatitis (specifically Necrolytic Migratory Erythema), DVT (venous…

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A child is infected with a negative sense RNA virus which also contains neuraminidase receptors. What is the causative organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Influenza virus

Influenza virus is a segmented, negative-sense/negative-strand RNA virus with neuraminidase receptors/peplomers projecting from the envelope. It belongs to the family of orthomyxoviruses. The hemagglutinin and neuraminidase receptors are present as two different spikes on the envelope.

Parainfluenza virus, Newcastle disease virus, and Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) are negative-sense single-stranded RNA viruses with a linear genome. No neuraminidase is seen.
questions.learning: Influenza virus Influenza virus is a segmented, negative-sense/negative-strand RNA virus with neuraminidase receptors/peplomers projecting from the envelope.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A senior resident in the hospital is performing the following clinical examination as shown in the image below. Which of the following structures will not be visible to him?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Arytenoids

The senior resident would not be visualizing the arytenoids as he is performing a posterior rhinoscopy indicated by the post-nasal mirror that he is holding.

The posterior rhinoscopy mirror (St. Clair Thompson mirror) has two bends in the shaft and is bayonet shaped.

The structures seen in the posterior rhinoscopy are:

• Adenoids
• Posterior ends of nasal turbinates
• Opening of the Eustachian tube
• The posterior border of the nasal septum
• Fossa of Rosenmuller
• Torus tubarius
• The upper surface of the soft palate

The images below show the posterior rhinoscopy mirror and structures seen in the posterior rhinoscopy:

Indirect laryngoscopy is done using a laryngeal mirror. It is straight without any bends with a mirror at the end.

Structures seen during indirect laryngoscopy (in order):

• Oropharynx: Base of the tongue, lingual tonsils, valleculae, medial and lateral glossoepiglottic folds.
• Laryngopharynx: Both piriform fossae, post cricoid region, posterior wall of laryngopharynx.
• Larynx: Epiglottis, aryepiglottic folds, arytenoids, cuneiform and corniculate cartilages, glossoepiglottic folds, pharyngoepiglottic folds, aryepiglottic fold, true and false vocal cords, anterior commissure, posterior commissure, subglottis and rings of the trachea.

The images below show the laryngeal mirror and structures seen during indirect laryngoscopy:
