questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A 30-year-old male patient was intubated for surgery by a final-year resident. Which of the following is the best method to confirm the position of the endotracheal tube?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. End-tidal CO2 concentration

The best method to confirm the position of the endotracheal tube is the end-tidal CO2 concentration assessed by capnography.

Capnography is a non-invasive method of measurement and graphical display of partial pressure of carbon dioxide (CO2) in exhaled breath or the end-tidal CO2. Capnograph is the device used for measurement and capnogram is the CO2 waveform that is displayed. It is the most reliable indicator of endotracheal tube placement.

The proper placement of the endotracheal tube is indicated by a normal CO2 waveform for at least three breaths.

Other signs to confirm proper endotracheal intubation are:

Symmetrical chest rise, presence of equal bilateral breath sounds, absent breath sounds over the epigastrium, visible condensation in the ETT, large exhaled tidal volume, and appropriate compliance of the reservoir bag during manual ventilation.

Absent CO2 waveform tracing despite correct ETT intubation is seen in the following conditions:

• Severe bronchospasm,
• Equipment malfunction,
• Cardiac arrest, or hemodynamic collapse

Clinical relevance:

• Capnography does not differentiate endotracheal from endobronchial intubation. Signs of endobronchial intubation include increased peak expiratory pressure, hypoxemia, increased airway pressures, asymmetric chest expansion and the absence of breath sounds over one lung, generally the left.
• In esophageal intubation, the capnograph can initially detect some CO2 in the stomach from swallowing expired air. But after a few breaths, this CO2  will be washed out and ETCO2 will become zero.
• The most sensitive and earliest indicator of malignant hyperthermia is a persistent increase in ETCO2.
questions.learning: End-tidal CO2 concentration — The best method to confirm the position of the endotracheal tube is the end-tidal CO2 concentration assessed by capnography.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The enzymes that convert pyruvate to acetyl CoA are given in the diagram. What are the enzymes marked as E1 and E2 respectively?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pyruvate dehydrogenase and dihydrolipoyl transacetylase

E1 is pyruvate dehydrogenase and E2 is dihydrolipoyl transacetylase in the image showing oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate. This is catalyzed by the pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) complex where E1, E2, and E3 are the three enzyme components of the complex.

The pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) complex is a multienzyme complex that is associated with the inner mitochondrial membrane. It catalyzes the oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA which enters the citric acid/Kreb’s cycle.

Enzyme components of PDH complex
Co-factors

Pyruvate dehydrogenase (E1)
Thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP)

Dihydrolipoyl transacetylase (E2)

Lipoic acid

Coenzyme A

Dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase (E3)

Flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD)

Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+)

Steps of pyruvate decarboxylation:

• Pyruvate is transported into the mitochondria by a proton symporter.
• Pyruvate is decarboxylated by pyruvate dehydrogenase (E1). TPP is required for this step. The decarboxylated pyruvate remains bound to the enzyme, as hydroxyethyl thiamine pyrophosphate.
• The hydroxyethyl group is oxidized to form an acetyl group. It is then transferred from TPP to lipoamide to form acetyl lipoamide. This step is catalyzed by dihydrolipoyl transacetylase (E2).
• Acetyl lipoamide reacts with coenzyme A to form acetyl-CoA and reduced lipoamide.
• The reduced lipoamide is reoxidized by FAD-dependent dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase (E3).

The overall reaction is : Pyruvate + NAD+ + CoA → Acetyl-CoA + NADH + H+ + CO2

Clinical significance:

1. Dietary deficiency of thiamine inhibits PDH. Chronic alcoholics may develop potentially fatal pyruvic and lactic acidosis. Lactic acidosis is a common presentation in patients with inherited pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency too.
2. In arsenic and mercury poisoning, the heavy metal ions react with -SH groups of lipoic acid and inhibit pyruvate dehydrogenase.

Other multienzyme complexes include alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase and branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase. All the five coenzymes of PDH are common to these two complexes too.
questions.learning: Pyruvate dehydrogenase and dihydrolipoyl transacetylase E1 is pyruvate dehydrogenase and E2 is dihydrolipoyl transacetylase in the image showing oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which one of the following can be used for developmental screening for use in community to identify children (aged 0–6 years) with developmental delay?
options: Revised Denver Development Screening Test (Denver II)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Trivandrum Development Screening Chart

The Trivandrum Development Screening Chart (TDSC) is a simple, rapid developmental screening tool designed for community use to identify developmental delay in children aged 0–6 years. It is easy to administer by primary healthcare workers and is widely used in community screening programs in India.

Why not the other options?

• A. Revised Denver Development Screening Test (Denver II): Comprehensive developmental screening test but not specifically designed for community-level screening.
• B. Ages and Stages Questionnaire (ASQ-3): Parent-completed screening tool; not the standard community screening tool used in India.
• C. Phatak’s Baroda Development Screening Test: Used for developmental assessment but TDSC is the preferred community screening tool for children 0–6 years.
questions.learning: Trivandrum Development Screening Chart — The Trivandrum Development Screening Chart (TDSC) is a simple, rapid developmental screening tool designed for community use to identify developmental delay in children aged 0–6 years.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A 45-year-old man with a long history of heavy alcohol use stopped drinking abruptly and has been abstinent for about 72 hours. Which withdrawal symptoms is he most likely to exhibit at this stage?
questions.explanation: Alcohol withdrawal progresses through distinct stages. Minor symptoms like tremors (Option C) appear within 6–12 hours. Seizures (Option A) typically occur within 12–48 hours. Alcoholic hallucinations (Option D) usually occur 12–24 hours after the last drink. Delirium Tremens (DT) is the most severe stage and classically occurs 48 to 96 hours (3 to 4 days) after cessation . Since this patient has reached the 72-hour mark, he is in the peak period for developing DT. DT is characterized by clouding of consciousness (delirium), autonomic hyperactivity (tachycardia, hypertension), and prominent visual or tactile hallucinations. It is a medical emergency with a high mortality rate if untreated. Therefore, based on the specific timeline of 72 hours, Delirium Tremens is the most likely and dangerous withdrawal symptom the patient will exhibit. Management involves high doses of benzodiazepines and supportive care in an ICU setting. **************
questions.learning: Alcohol withdrawal progresses through distinct stages. Minor symptoms like tremors (Option C) appear within 6–12 hours.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which disorder is characterized by the accumulation of tau protein inclusions?
questions.explanation: Alzheimer's disease (Option A) is the most common cause of dementia and is characterized by two specific proteinaceous brain lesions: extracellular amyloid-beta plaques and intracellular neurofibrillary tangles. These neurofibrillary tangles are composed of hyperphosphorylated tau protein, a microtubule-associated protein. When tau is misfolded, it aggregates into insoluble inclusions that disrupt neuronal transport and lead to cell death. Huntington's disease (Option B) is associated with huntingtin protein inclusions caused by CAG repeat expansions. Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (Option C) is frequently associated with TDP-43 or SOD1 protein inclusions, not primary tauopathy. CNS lymphoma (Option D) is a malignancy of B-lymphocytes and does not involve protein inclusion bodies. Other "tauopathies" besides Alzheimer’s include Pick's disease and progressive supranuclear palsy. Therefore, tau protein inclusions are a hallmark of Alzheimer’s neurodegeneration
questions.learning: Alzheimer's disease (Option A) is the most common cause of dementia and is characterized by two specific proteinaceous brain lesions: extracellular amyloid-beta plaques and intracellular neurofibrillary tangles.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 52-year-old diabetic patient suffered from drug-induced hypoglycemia. Which of the following drugs is most likely responsible for her hypoglycemic episode?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Glimepride

Among the following options, Glimepiride which is a sulphonylurea is known to cause hypoglycemia.

Glimepiride is a sulfonylurea that also stimulates insulin secretion. They bind to a specific site on the β cell K-ATP channel complex and inhibit its activity. This causes cell membrane to depolarize and leads to a cascade of events resulting in insulin secretion.

Antidiabetic drugs with a risk of hypoglycemia (insulin secretagogues):

* Sulfonylureas

* Meglitinides: Nateglinide, Repaglinide

Drugs that do not directly stimulate insulin and rarely cause hypoglycemia:

* Metformin

* Alpha-glucosidase inhibitors

* Pioglitazone

* DPP-4 inhibitors: Sitagliptin

Note: Although alpha-glucosidase inhibitors alone rarely cause hypoglycemia, the risk increases if they are combined with insulin or other insulin secretagogues.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient who is a teacher by profession presents to the clinic with hoarseness of voice. The fiberoptic laryngoscopy image is given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Vocal nodule

The swollen area in the given image and the clinical scenario is suggestive of vocal nodules.

Vocal nodules are also known as singer’s or screamer's nodes. It is present at the junction of anterior one-third with the posterior two thirds. It is the area of maximum vibration of the cord and thus is subjected to maximum trauma.

Vocal nodules occur due to vocal trauma when person speaks in unnatural low tones for prolonged periods or at high intensities. They mostly affect teachers, actors, vendors or pop singers.

Nodule:

* Early stages soft, reddish and oedematous swellings

* Later stages - greyish or white in colour

Symptoms:

* Hoarseness

* Vocal fatigue

* Pain in the neck on prolonged phonation

Treatment:

* Educating the patient in proper use of voice.

* Surgery is required for large nodules or nodules of long standing in adults. They are excised with precision.

Other options:

Option A: Vocal polyp is caused by sudden shouting which results in hemorrhage and edema of the vocal cord.Affected individuals present with hoarseness of voice and diplophonia(double voice). Other factors associated with it are allergy and cigarette smoking. It presents as a benign swelling on the free edge of the vocal cord.

Option B: Vocal cysts: These are retention cysts due to blockage of seromucinous glands of the laryngeal mucosa. They occur in the false vocal cords.

Option D: Reinke's edema is the collection of fluid in Reinke's space. Affected individuals present with diffuse swelling of the vocal cords. Treatment involves the removal of gelatinous collection by a longitudinal incision on the vocal cord.
questions.learning: Vocal nodule — The swollen area in the given image and the clinical scenario is suggestive of vocal nodules. Vocal nodules are also known as singer’s or screamer's nodes.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 10-year-old child presents with gradual painless diminution of vision since early childhood. Slit-lamp examination is as shown in the image. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Zonular cataract

Zonular (lamellar) cataract is the most common developmental cataract in children. It presents with gradual, painless diminution of vision since early childhood and is characterized by a disc-shaped or lamellar opacity surrounding the fetal nucleus, with clear lens cortex inside and outside the opacity.

The slit-lamp image shows a central lamellar opacity with radial “riders” (cortical spoke-like opacities), which is characteristic of zonular cataract.

• Most common developmental cataract: Zonular (lamellar) cataract
• Etiology: Usually hereditary (autosomal dominant); may also be associated with maternal infections or hypocalcemia during lens development
• Appearance: Disc-shaped opacity around the fetal nucleus with cortical riders
• Symptoms: Reduced vision, glare, amblyopia if visually significant
• Treatment: Cataract extraction with visual rehabilitation when vision is significantly affected

Differentiating from Other Cataracts

• A. Nuclear cataract: Congenital central nuclear opacity; not lamellar.
• B. Posterior subcapsular cataract: Posterior pole opacity, common in steroids/diabetes; causes glare, usually in adults.
• D. Mature cortical cataract: Entire cortex becomes opaque (white cataract), typically seen in the elderly.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 20-year-old presented with gradual loss of vision at night and a fundoscopy image is shown. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Retinitis pigmentosa

The fundus shows a pale waxy disc, attenuated arteries, and bony spicules along with gradual loss of vision which implies that it is case of retinitis pigmentosa (RP).

Retinitis pigmentosa (RP) is a dystrophy of rods and cones, with rods being primarily affected. It is a genetic disease. The non-hereditary/sporadic type is most common. Among the hereditary type, it can occur in an autosomal dominant (AD), autosomal recessive (AR), or X-linked recessive (XLR) pattern. AD disease generally has the best prognosis.

The presenting feature is night blindness.

Investigations:

• Perimetry- the initial stage will have ring scotoma, which further develops into tunnel vision.
• Electroretinography- reveals a decreased amplitude of both "a" and "b" waves.

Atypical types of RP are as follows:

• Sectoral RP
• Pericentric/Inverse RP
• RP sine pigmento
• RP punctata albescens

There is no effective treatment for RP.
questions.learning: Retinitis pigmentosa — The fundus shows a pale waxy disc, attenuated arteries, and bony spicules along with gradual loss of vision which implies that it is case of retinitis pigmentosa (RP).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 14-year-old patient presents with a congenital deformity of the neck and upper back. Examination shows an elevated, medially rotated scapula with an equilateral triangle appearance and restricted neck movements. The deformity has been present since birth with no improvement over time. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Klippel-Feil deformity is a congenital condition characterized by the fusion of two or more cervical vertebrae. This leads to a short neck, restricted neck movements, and a low hairline. A distinctive feature is the triangular appearance of the neck, which occurs due to elevation and medial rotation of the scapula. Why other options are incorrect: 1. Separated Shoulder Deformity : This refers to a traumatic separation of the clavicle from the acromion. It is not a congenital condition and does not present with a short neck or limited neck mobility. 2. Torticollis (Wry Neck) : In this condition, the head tilts to one side and the chin rotates to the opposite side. Although it may be congenital, it primarily affects head posture rather than causing a short neck or vertebral fusion. 3. Sprengel’s Deformity : This is a congenital condition involving an elevated and medially rotated scapula, leading to shoulder asymmetry. However, it typically does not cause marked restriction of neck movement or vertebral fusion, which are key features of Klippel-Feil deformity
questions.learning: Klippel-Feil deformity is a congenital condition characterized by the fusion of two or more cervical vertebrae. This leads to a short neck, restricted neck movements, and a low hairline.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A pus swab has been sent for microbiological examination to your lab. After testing the sample, how will you discard it?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Yellow bin

The used pus swab should be discarded in the yellow colour bin as it is clinical laboratory waste.

Microbiology, biotechnology, and clinical laboratory waste are collected in autoclave-safe bags. They must be pre-treated before disposal by incineration, plasma pyrolysis, or deep burial.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A 16-year-old girl has intense food cravings. After eating her food in one go, she induces forceful vomiting. Her BMI is 27 kg/m2. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bulimia nervosa

The given scenario of a 16-year-old girl with intense food cravings followed by self-induced vomiting and a BMI of 27 kg/m2, points towards the diagnosis of bulimia nervosa.

Bulimia nervosa is an eating disorder, often seen in young women. It is characterized by binge-eating episodes, followed by inappropriate, compensatory measures to stop weight gain, like self-induced vomiting, laxative abuse, diuretics, enema, and emetic abuse. These binge-eating episodes occur at least once a week and are present for at least 3 months. The patient fears gaining weight and has a relentless drive to be thin.

The weight is normal in most patients with bulimia nervosa. However, few patients may either be overweight or underweight. There is a risk of dehydration and electrolyte imbalance.

Treatment modalities are cognitive behavioral therapy, psychotherapy, and antidepressants such as fluoxetine.

Other options:

Option A: Anorexia nervosa is an eating disorder that is often seen between the ages of 10 and 30. Typical features are self-induced starvation, voluntary and unhealthy reduction in weight, intense drive for thinness, and fear of becoming obese. Associated features can include depression, anxiety, amenorrhea in females, hypothermia, and bradycardia.

Option C: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is a condition where scrupulous individuals are overly concerned that something they thought or did might be a sin or a violation of religious or moral doctrine. The treatment of choice for OCD is cognitive behavioral therapy.

Option D: Binge-eating disorder is the most common eating disorder. It is characterized by rapid intake of abnormally large quantities of food over a short period of time, even when not hungry. There are feelings of guilt about the eating episodes, but these patients do not compensate in any way following the episodes of binge.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 40-year-old female patient came with complaints of chest pain, palpitation, and shortness of breath. On examination, a mid-diastolic murmur was heard, and a prominent 'a' wave was found on JVP. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Tricuspid stenosis

The presence of a mid-diastolic murmur and a prominent a-wave in JVP is suggestive of tricuspid stenosis.

Mid-diastolic murmurs result from obstruction and/or augmented flow at the level of the mitral or tricuspid valve. Thus, both mitral stenosis (MS) and tricuspid stenosis (TS) present with a mid-diastolic murmur. However, the presence of a prominent a-wave in JVP points toward tricuspid stenosis.

Causes for mid-diastolic murmur:

1. Mitral stenosis
2. Tricuspid stenosis
3. Atrial myxomas
4. Austin Flint murmur in severe aortic regurgitation
5. Carey-Coombs murmur in acute rheumatic fever

Tricuspid stenosis:

It always occurs in association with MS and is rheumatic in origin. Mid-diastolic murmur in TS is best heard along the left sternal border and over the xiphoid process. Murmur is augmented during inspiration and reduced during expiration. The jugular veins are distended, and a giant a-wave is seen in JVP. There is a slow y descent due to impedance of right atrial emptying during diastole. ECG shows features of right atrial enlargement, which includes tall, peaked P wave in lead II and a prominent, upright P wave in lead V1.

Other options:

Option A: Mid-diastolic murmur is seen in mitral stenosis (MS). It occurs most commonly in rheumatic fever. Loud S1 (first heart sound) with an opening snap and a following S2 (second heart sound) is heard. S2 is followed by a low-pitched, rumbling, mid-diastolic murmur, which is best heard at the apex with the patient in a lateral recumbent position.

Option C: Holosystolic murmur is seen in mitral regurgitation (MR). The major causes of MR are infective endocarditis, myocardial infarction, rheumatic fever, and cardiomyopathies. Soft S1 with a widely split S2 and a low-pitched S3 (third heart sound) is heard in MR. In addition, a holosystolic murmur is prominent at the apex and radiates to the axilla.

Option D: Holosystolic murmur is seen in tricuspid regurgitation (TR). TR is most commonly due to functional defects such as tricuspid annular dilatation and leaflet tethering caused by rheumatic heart disease, myocardial infarction, etc. The jugular vein is distended. Prominent c-v waves and rapid y descents are seen in severe TR. A blowing holosystolic murmur along the lower left sternal margin, which is augmented during inspiration (Carvallo's sign) and reduced during expiration is seen in TR.
questions.learning: Tricuspid stenosis — The presence of a mid-diastolic murmur and a prominent a-wave in JVP is suggestive of tricuspid stenosis. Mid-diastolic murmurs result from obstruction and/or augmented flow at the level of the mitral or tricuspid valve.

questions.text: A 56-year-old patient suffering from alcoholic cirrhosis receives a healthy liver from his biological son. What is this type of transplant known as?

Transplant of an organ/tissue from a son to a parent is an example of an allograft.

An allograft is transplant of cells/tissues/organs from a genetically non-identical donor of the same species.

Isografts are allografts in which cells/tissues/organs are transplanted from a donor to a genetically identical recipient. (monozygotic twins)

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: In a case where a dead body is found with severely charred burns, how can fractures and internal injuries be identified?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Virtual autopsy

Virtual autopsy (virtopsy) is a non-invasive postmortem imaging technique that uses CT and/or MRI to detect fractures, internal hemorrhage, foreign bodies, gas collections, and internal organ injuries, especially when conventional autopsy is difficult, such as in severely charred, decomposed, or mutilated bodies.

Why not the other options?

• B. Traditional photography: Documents external findings only and cannot identify internal injuries or fractures.
• C. Psychological autopsy: A retrospective assessment of the deceased’s mental state, mainly used in suspected suicides; it does not evaluate physical injuries.
• D. In situ autopsy: Refers to examination of the body at the scene but does not provide detailed internal imaging like virtual autopsy.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which disease causes the lesion shown in the image below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Scrub typhus

The lesion shown in the image is eschar. It is seen in scrub typhus.

Scrub typhus is caused by Orientia tsutsugamushi and transmitted by trombiculid mites.  Humans are infected when they are bitten by the mite larvae known as chiggers. Transovarian transmission of microbes occurs in mites.

The incubation period is 1-3 weeks. The patient typically develops a characteristic eschar which is a punched-out ulcer covered with a blackened scab at the site of the mite bite, with regional lymphadenopathy and maculopapular rash.

Other options:

Option  A: Rocky Mountain spotted fever is a rickettsial infection transmitted by ticks (Dermacentor andersoni). It is the most serious type of fever. Symptoms include fever, headache, Rash, muscle pain and lack of appetite. Early treatment with doxycycline is recommended to prevent death and severe illness.

Option B: Malaria is a protozoal disease caused by Plasmodium species. It is transmitted by the female anopheles mosquito. Here, the definitive host is the anopheles mosquito and humans are the intermediate hosts. Clinical features are periodic bouts of fever with chills and rigors, followed by anemia, splenomegaly, and hepatomegaly.

Option D: COVID-19 is a highly contagious viral disease caused by severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2). The primary mode of transmission is through respiratory droplets. The median incubation period is around 5 days. Patients commonly present with fever, cough, and shortness of breath and less commonly with a sore throat, anosmia, anorexia, nausea, malaise, myalgias, and diarrhea.
questions.learning: Scrub typhus — The lesion shown in the image is eschar. Scrub typhus is caused by Orientia tsutsugamushi and transmitted by trombiculid mites.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 22-year-old college student presents with small depigmented lesions which have been there for over 2 years now as shown in the image below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vitiligo

The image is suggestive of vitiligo. The pathological basis of vitiligo is the loss of melanocytes.

Vitiligo is a common form of localized depigmentation. It is characterized by milky‐white sharply demarcated macules. It is an acquired condition resulting from the autoimmune destruction of dopa-positive melanocytes in the basal layer of the epidermis. It can begin at any age but in the majority of cases becomes apparent in the third decade. The prevalence is most probably the same in both sexes or a slight female preponderance.

Electron microscopy studies confirm the loss of melanocytes. Wood's lamp examination shows milky-white fluorescence. Koebner phenomenon defined as the development of lesions at sites of trauma to uninvolved skin of patients with cutaneous diseases is a well‐known phenomenon in vitiligo.

World Vitiligo day is celebrated every year on 25th June to promote understanding and help vitiligo patients avoid discrimination and become more optimistic in life. The theme for the year 2021 is "Embracing Life with Vitiligo".

Other options:

Option A: Melasma is the most common cause of facial melanosis that manifests as hyperpigmented macules on the face. It is exacerbated by sun exposure and oral contraceptive pills. The condition is predominantly seen in females

Option C: Psoriasis:

* The peak on occurrence is between 16 to 22 years and between 57 to 62 years. They usually present with itching and a papulosquamous rash.

* The lesions are red, and scaly, and have well demarcation from the normal skin.

* They can also be encircled by a clear peripheral zone which is called the Woronoff ring.

* They commonly appear in the scalp, trunk, and extensor surfaces of the limbs.

Option D: Dermatitis herpetiformis:

* Dermatitis herpetiformis is a chronic, intensely pruritic, skin condition associated with gluten‐sensitive enteropathy.

* It typically appears in the 4th decade,  most typically over the extensor surfaces of the elbows, knees, buttocks, and scalp.

* On examination, multiple erythematous papules and vesicles can be seen over the extensor aspects. They appear symmetrical and heal without scarring. The oral cavity may show mucosal abnormalities and enamel pits.
questions.learning: Vitiligo — The image is suggestive of vitiligo. The pathological basis of vitiligo is the loss of melanocytes.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A woman is bitten by a dog that later develops symptoms of rabies and dies within a week. What is the best method for antemortem diagnosis of rabies in this situation?
questions.explanation: The Direct Fluorescent Antibody Test (DFAT) is the gold standard for the rapid antemortem diagnosis of rabies. It uses fluorescent-labeled antibodies to detect rabies virus antigens in accessible tissues such as corneal smears, nuchal skin biopsies (from hair follicles), or saliva. Detection of Negri bodies (Option A) involves identifying eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions in neurons, but this requires brain histology and is strictly a postmortem finding. Seller's staining (Option C) is a microscopic technique specifically used postmortem to highlight Negri bodies in brain tissue. Brain biopsy (Option D) is highly invasive and rarely performed for antemortem diagnosis. Thus, DFAT provides the most rapid, sensitive, and specific results required for clinical management before death occurs

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Lysosomal enzymes are present in___?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cytosol

Lysosomal enzymes (hydrolytic enzymes) are present in the lysosome, which is located in the cytoplasm of the cell. In the given options, cytosol is the best choice.

The interior of lysosomes is more acidic than the rest of the cytoplasm, and external material such as endocytosed bacteria, as well as worn-out cell components, is digested in them. The interior is kept acidic by the action of a proton pump, or H+ ATPase, which uses the energy of ATP to move protons from the cytosol up their electrochemical gradient and keep the lysosome relatively acidic, near pH 5.0.

Lysosomes contain over 40 types of hydrolytic enzymes, which are all acid hydrolases, and they function best at the acidic pH of the lysosomal compartment. This can be a safety feature; if the lysosomes were to break open and release their contents, the enzymes would not be efficient at the near-neutral cytosolic pH of 7.2 and thus would not be able to digest cytosolic targets they may encounter.

When a lysosomal enzyme is congenitally absent, the lysosomes become engorged with the material the enzyme normally degrades and lead to lysosomal storage diseases. e.g., Fabry disease caused by a deficiency in α-galactosidase, Gaucher disease caused by a deficiency in glucocerebrosidase, and Tay-Sachs disease caused by the loss of hexosaminidase A.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient with penicillin allergy presents with fever, burning micturition, ototoxicity and dizziness. Which drug is most appropriate for management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ciprofloxacin

In this patient with symptoms of a urinary tract infection with a penicillin allergy, ototoxicity, and dizziness, Ciprofloxacin is the most appropriate drug of choice.

Ciprofloxacin, a fluoroquinolone, inhibits bacterial DNA replication and prevents the growth of bacteria. DNA gyrase is particularly important in gram-negative bacteria, where it introduces negative supercoils into the DNA to relieve torsional strain. Ciprofloxacin binds to and inhibits this enzyme, preventing the proper replication of bacterial DNA. Additionally, topoisomerase IV is the target of gram-positive bacteria, and its inhibition by ciprofloxacin prevents chromosome segregation during cell division.

Ciprofloxacin is the most appropriate choice as it effectively treats urinary tract infections while having a relatively safe profile in penicillin-allergic patients. The symptoms (fever and burning micturition) suggest a UTI, and Ciprofloxacin achieves high urinary concentrations with good activity against common uropathogens. Ciprofloxacin's oral bioavailability makes it suitable for outpatient

Other Options:

Option A: Macrolides like Azithromycin are not first-line therapy and have lower efficacy compared to fluoroquinolones as well as additionally exhibiting ototoxicity.

Option B: Alternative options which includes aminoglycosides like Amikacin would be contraindicated due to their significant ototoxicity and diziness.

Option D:  Beta-lactams like Amoxicillin-Clavulinic acid would be inappropriate due to the penicillin allergy.
questions.learning: Ciprofloxacin — In this patient with symptoms of a urinary tract infection with a penicillin allergy, ototoxicity, and dizziness, Ciprofloxacin is the most appropriate drug of choice.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 54-year-old man, following binge drinking and a heavy meal, presents to the emergency department with sudden, severe left-sided chest pain radiating to the left shoulder. X-ray shows pneumoperitoneum. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The combination of binge drinking followed by forceful vomiting and sudden severe chest pain is the classic description of Boerhaave Syndrome (spontaneous esophageal perforation). The perforation typically occurs in the left lower esophagus, leading to the leakage of air and gastric contents into the mediastinum or the abdominal cavity, explaining the pneumoperitoneum (air under the diaphragm) noted on the X-ray. While a perforated peptic ulcer (Option D) also causes pneumoperitoneum, it usually presents with severe abdominal pain rather than sudden onset left-sided chest pain radiating to the shoulder. Mediastinal air leak (Option A) is a feature of the perforation rather than the primary diagnosis. Pneumoperitoneum (Option C) is the radiological finding, not the disease itself. Boerhaave syndrome is a surgical emergency with a high mortality rate; diagnosis is often confirmed with a Gastrografin swallow study showing the leak
questions.learning: The combination of binge drinking followed by forceful vomiting and sudden severe chest pain is the classic description of Boerhaave Syndrome (spontaneous esophageal perforation).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with seizures, and CT head imaging reveals multiple parenchymal cysts. What is the appropriate management for this patient?
questions.explanation: A patient presenting with seizures and multiple parenchymal brain cysts most likely has neurocysticercosis, caused by the larval stage of Taenia solium. The standardized management protocol emphasizes that Steroids must be administered followed by (or concurrently with) antiparasitic drugs like albendazole. This sequence is critical because killing the parasites triggers a massive inflammatory response and brain edema, which can exacerbate seizures or cause brain herniation; the steroids serve to suppress this inflammation. Option B is dangerous for this reason. Antiepileptic drugs are the absolute first priority for controlling the seizure but the "steroid-first" rule applies specifically to the targeted cysticidal therapy. Continuing antiepileptics (Option D) is necessary but does not address the underlying infection. Clinicians must also ensure the patient does not have ocular cysticercosis before starting antiparasitics, as inflammation in the eye can lead to permanent blindness. Proper staging of the cysts (vesicular vs. calcified) on imaging determines if antiparasitic therapy is even indicated
questions.learning: A patient presenting with seizures and multiple parenchymal brain cysts most likely has neurocysticercosis, caused by the larval stage of Taenia solium.

questions.text: A 60-year-old woman comes with chronic vulval itching and pain. On examination, there is a vulval lesion suspicious of vulval cancer. Which of the following lymph node/s should be considered for sentinel node biopsy to look for the metastatic spread?

The sentinel lymph node biopsy is helpful for evaluating the spread of vulval cancer.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is a differentiating feature between cardiac tamponade and tension pneumothorax?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Breath sounds

The differentiating feature between cardiac tamponade and tension pneumothorax is breath sounds. The breath sounds are absent in tension pneumothorax while they are present in cardiac tamponade.

The presence of hypotension, distended jugular veins, and muffled heart sounds (Beck's triad) suggest a cardiac tamponade. These features can also be seen in tension pneumothorax. Other clinical features pointing towards tension pneumothorax are absent breath sounds, hyper resonance to percussion, and shift of the mediastinum to the contralateral side.

Heart sounds can be muffled by structures between the stethoscope and the heart, eg, adipose tissue deposition (obesity), fluid accumulation (pericardial effusion, pleural effusion), gas accumulation (pneumothorax, subcutaneous emphysema), soft tissue masses can lead to attenuation of heart sounds.
questions.learning: Breath sounds — The differentiating feature between cardiac tamponade and tension pneumothorax is breath sounds. The breath sounds are absent in tension pneumothorax while they are present in cardiac tamponade.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: In which type of hanging does the weight of the head act as a constricting force?
questions.explanation: Hanging is defined as a form of ligature strangulation where the force is provided by the weight of the body. In "complete hanging," the entire body is suspended and the feet do not touch the ground. In "partial hanging," some part of the body (feet, knees, or even the buttocks) remains in contact with the ground or a supporting surface. In these instances, the full weight of the body is not used; instead, only the weight of the head or the upper torso acts as the constricting force on the ligature around the neck. "Typical hanging" (Option C) refers to the knot being at the occiput. "Atypical hanging" (Option D) refers to the knot being at any other position. Partial hanging is frequently seen in suicidal cases, where individuals use low points of attachment like door handles or bedposts. Forensic examiners must be aware that even a small force (about 2-5 kg) is sufficient to compress the jugular veins and carotid arteries, leading to death
questions.learning: Hanging is defined as a form of ligature strangulation where the force is provided by the weight of the body. In "complete hanging," the entire body is suspended and the feet do not touch the ground.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child presents to the hospital with features of severe malnutrition and marked dehydration, requiring prompt intravenous fluid therapy. To ensure effective rehydration and correction of electrolyte disturbances, which intravenous fluid would be the most appropriate choice for management in this patient?
questions.explanation: For a child suffering from severe acute malnutrition (SAM) with significant dehydration, standard aggressive rehydration protocols must be modified to prevent heart failure and electrolyte overload. The recommended IV fluid in this specific high-risk scenario is Ringer's Lactate (RL) with 5% Dextrose. This fluid provides both volume and glucose to prevent hypoglycemia, which is common in SAM. Standard Normal Saline (Option C) or DNS (Option D) contains too much sodium, which can lead to life-threatening fluid overload in a malnourished heart. ORS (Option A) is the fluid of choice for oral rehydration but is not appropriate for the "immediate medical intervention" of IV resuscitation in a severely dehydrated patient. The IV infusion rate in Sam must be slow and meticulously monitored for signs of respiratory distress or increasing liver size, which indicate early cardiac failure
questions.learning: For a child suffering from severe acute malnutrition (SAM) with significant dehydration, standard aggressive rehydration protocols must be modified to prevent heart failure and electrolyte overload.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which anatomical structure is most likely affected in a man with a history of prolonged crutch use who now experiences tingling and paraesthesia along the medial aspect of the arm, forearm, and hand?
questions.explanation: Prolonged reliance on crutches can lead to compression of neurovascular structures within the axilla, a condition commonly referred to as crutch palsy. When a person bears body weight through the axilla instead of the hands, the intercostobrachial nerve is particularly vulnerable. This nerve arises from the second intercostal nerve (T2) and supplies sensory innervation to the inner (medial) side of the upper arm, with sensations often perceived as tingling or paraesthesia. Because of its superficial course across the axilla, it is easily compressed between the crutch pad and the humerus or chest wall. Compression of this nerve produces sensory symptoms without motor weakness, which matches the clinical presentation described. In the given diagram, structure A corresponds to the intercostobrachial nerve. Other structures shown are deeper components of the brachial plexus or surrounding muscles, which would typically cause motor deficits if significantly compressed. Therefore, based on the mechanism of injury, anatomical location, and pattern of sensory disturbance, structure A is most likely to be impacted
questions.learning: Prolonged reliance on crutches can lead to compression of neurovascular structures within the axilla, a condition commonly referred to as crutch palsy.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which of the following are Amsel’s diagnostic criteria? I. Vaginal pH > 4.5 II. Positive Whiff test III. Presence of clue cells >20% IV. Positive bacterial vaginal culture Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. I, II and III

Amsel’s criteria are the clinical diagnostic criteria for bacterial vaginosis (BV), the most common cause of abnormal vaginal discharge in reproductive-age women. Diagnosis is made when at least 3 of the following 4 criteria are present. The following are Amsel’s criteria:

• I. Vaginal pH > 4.5: Loss of normal Lactobacillus flora results in an elevated vaginal pH (>4.5). ⭐
• II. Positive Whiff test: Addition of 10% potassium hydroxide (KOH) to vaginal discharge releases volatile amines, producing a characteristic fishy odor.
• III. Presence of clue cells >20%: Clue cells (vaginal epithelial cells coated with bacteria) seen on saline wet mount are the hallmark microscopic finding of bacterial vaginosis.

Why is IV incorrect?

• IV. Positive bacterial vaginal culture: Culture is not recommended for diagnosing bacterial vaginosis because it is polymicrobial and Gardnerella vaginalis can be present in healthy women. Diagnosis is based on Amsel’s criteria or Nugent scoring, not culture.
questions.learning: I, II and III Amsel’s criteria are the clinical diagnostic criteria for bacterial vaginosis (BV), the most common cause of abnormal vaginal discharge in reproductive-age women.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A woman presents to the outpatient department with spotting following IUD insertion. No pain or fever was reported. What is the next best step in this scenario? IUD - Intrauterine device
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Give iron tablets and observe

In this scenario of a woman presenting to the outpatient department with spotting following an IUD insertion with no complaints of fever or pain, the next best step would be to give iron tablets and observe.

Spotting is a common side effect after IUD insertion and often resolves on its own without intervention. Since no other complications are present in this patient, there is no need to remove the IUD or prescribe any medications. The patient just needs to be under observation.

It's important to monitor the woman for any signs of heavy bleeding, severe pain, fever, or other unusual symptoms that could indicate complications such as infection or perforation.

Complications following an IUD insertion :

* Pain accounts for 15–40% of IUD removal, hence, it is the most common cause of IUD removal.

* However, bleeding is the most common side-effect reported after IUD insertion.

* Disturbances in menstrual bleeding are very commonly reported in the form of increased blood loss or irregular bleeding.

* Studies have shown that larger non-medicated IUDs cause greater incidences of bleeding than copper devices and hormone-releasing devices.

* Other side effects and complications are pain, pelvic infection, uterine perforation, and ectopic pregnancies.

Contraindications for IUD usage include:

Absolute contraindications
Relative contraindications

• Suspected pregnancy
• PID
• Vaginal bleeding of unknown etiology
• Carcinoma cervix/uterus/adnexa /other pelvic tumours

• Anemia
• Menorrhagia
• History of PID since the last pregnancy
• Purulent cervical discharge
• Distortions of the uterine cavity due to fibroids
• Uterine malformations
• An unmotivated person

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which vertebral level corresponds to Tuffier's line, a clinically relevant anatomical landmark?
questions.explanation: Tuffier's line (also known as the intercristal line) is a horizontal line connecting the highest points of the iliac crests. In most adults, this line passes through either the body of the L4 vertebra or the L4-L5 intervertebral space. This landmark is of critical clinical importance for performing a lumbar puncture or administering spinal and epidural anesthesia. Since the adult spinal cord typically ends (conus medullaris) at the L1-L2 level, inserting a needle at or below Tuffier's line (such as the L3-L4 or L4-L5 spaces) provides a significant safety margin to avoid direct cord injury. Options A (L2-L3), C (L5-S1), and D (L3-L4) are incorrect Anatomical correlates for this specific surface landmark. While the exact level can vary slightly with age or positioning, using Tuffier's line as the primary guide remains the standard practice in clinical neurology and anesthesia to ensure the safe entry into the subarachnoid space
questions.learning: Tuffier's line (also known as the intercristal line) is a horizontal line connecting the highest points of the iliac crests. In most adults, this line passes through either the body of the L4 vertebra or the L4-L5 intervertebral space.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A primigravida came with 6 cm cervical dilatation and a contraction rate of 3/10 minutes. Which stage of labor is she in?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1st stage

In this case, cervical dilatation of 6 cm and contraction rate of 3/10 minutes is indicative of first stage of labor.

The first stage of labor is characterized by dilatation and effacement of cervix and can be divided into latent phase and active labor.

• The onset of latent labor is the point at which the mother perceives regular contractions.
• Cervical dilatation of ≥6 cm in the presence of uterine contractions can be taken to reliably represent the threshold for active labor.

The second stage of labor begins with complete cervical dilatation and ends with fetal delivery.

The third stage of labor is characterized by the delivery of the placenta.

The fourth stage is a stage of observation for at least an hour after the full expulsion of the placenta.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 2-month-old infant was brought by his mother with complaints of inability to open the eyes in light and excessive watering. The clinical picture is given below. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Congenital glaucoma

The clinical history of inability to open eyes in light (photophobia), excessive watering, and the image showing hazy cornea are suggestive of congenital glaucoma.

Primary congenital glaucoma refers to abnormally high intraocular pressure (IOP) which occurs as a result of a developmental anomaly of the angle of the anterior chamber. It is not associated with any other ocular or systemic anomaly. It can be classified as follows:

• True congenital glaucoma: The IOP is elevated during intrauterine life.
• Infantile glaucoma: Manifests prior to age 3.
• Juvenile glaucoma: The IOP rises between 3 and 16 years of age. It is the least common type.

The CYP1B1 gene is implicated in the pathogenesis of congenital glaucoma.

Clinical presentation: Lacrimation, photophobia, and blepharospasm form the classic triad of symptoms of congenital glaucoma. A corneal haze is seen due to diffuse edema secondary to raised IOP. Buphthalmos occur as a result of stretching due to elevated IOP prior to the age of 3 years. Haab striae that are curvilinear healed breaks in Descemet's membrane are seen. Corneal scarring can also occur.

Evaluation under general anesthesia is generally required. IOP measurement, anterior chamber examination, optic disc examination, corneal diameter measurement, gonioscopy, and refraction should be evaluated.

Management is essentially surgical with goniotomy or trabeculotomy. If angle surgery fails, trabeculectomy, tube shunt implantation, and ciliary body ablative procedures are performed.

Other options:

Option A - In ophthalmia neonatorum, there will be inflammation of the conjunctiva. Clinical presentation includes conjunctival discharge, hyperemia chemosis, swollen eyelids, tender eyeball. Corneal involvement is rare which may occur in the form of superficial punctate keratitis.

Option C - In mucopolysaccharidosis, there will be bilateral cloudy cornea.

Option D - In cataract, there will be opacification of lens presenting as whitish reflex/ leukocoria.
questions.learning: Congenital glaucoma — The clinical history of inability to open eyes in light (photophobia), excessive watering, and the image showing hazy cornea are suggestive of congenital glaucoma.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient is admitted with fever and neck stiffness. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis reveals low glucose levels, elevated protein, and a predominance of neutrophils. What is the most appropriate treatment in this case?
questions.explanation: The classic triad of fever, headache, and nuchal rigidity, combined with CSF findings of decreased glucose, elevated protein, and neutrophilic pleocytosis, is diagnostic of bacterial meningitis. Ceftriaxone is the first-line, broad-spectrum antibiotic recommended for empirical treatment in adults. It effectively covers the most common pathogens, Streptococcus pneumoniae and Neisseria meningitidis. Regarding the distractors, Ampicillin (Option A) is specifically added for Listeria monocytogenes in neonates or elderly patients but is not the primary choice for standard adult cases. Penicillin (Option C) is no longer used alone due to rising resistance. Vancomycin (Option D) is often used with Ceftriaxone to cover penicillin-resistant strains but is insufficient as monotherapy. Therefore, Ceftriaxone is the most appropriate first-line agent based on the provided clinical and laboratory profile
questions.learning: The classic triad of fever, headache, and nuchal rigidity, combined with CSF findings of decreased glucose, elevated protein, and neutrophilic pleocytosis, is diagnostic of bacterial meningitis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the correct sequence of Damage control surgery? * Patient selection * Primary exploration * ICU care * Secondary exploration * Abdominal closure
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1,2,3,4,5

The correct answer is option C: 1,2,3,4,5

The correct sequence  of five stages of damage control surgery are:

* Patient selection

* Control of haemorrhage and control of contamination(primary exploration)

* Resuscitation continued in the intensive care unit

* Deﬁnitive surgery(secondary exploration)

* Abdominal closure

Damage control surgery is minimal intervention done to stabilize the patient and do the definite surgery later. It centers on coordinating staged operative interventions with periods of aggressive resuscitation to salvage trauma patients sustaining major injuries. The aim of the DCS is to restore physiology over anatomy. It is applied to trauma patients with combined vascular and visceral injuries.

The phases are:

*

Phase 1 involves recognition of the severity of the injury. Here,rapid-sequence induction of anesthesia and intubation is done. This is followed by early rewarming and prompt movement of the patient to the operating theatre.

*

Phase 2 involves performing immediate laparotomy. Here, the focus is to control bleeding and contamination. Abdominal packing and temporary wound closure are done.

*

Phase 3 involves movement to the intensive care unit (ICU). The aim is to normalize the biochemical and physiological parameters.

*

Phase 4 involves re-exploration in the operating theatre. Here, definitive repair of all injuries is done. Multiple procedures on multiple occasions may be required.

Pearl PF2177: Damage Control Surgery

Five stages of damage control surgery:

1. Patient selection
2. Control of hemorrhage and control of contamination
3. Resuscitation continued in the intensive care unit
4. Deﬁnitive surgery
5. Abdominal closure

Phases of Damage Control Surgery:

Phase 0: Identification of patient for damage control surgery in emergency room
Phase 1: Emergency laparotomy to stop bleeding and prevent contamination
Phase 2: ICU care for resuscitation
Phase 3: Re-laparotomy for definitive repair
Indications for damage control surgery:
Anatomical

* Inability to achieve haemostasis

* Complex abdominal injury, e.g. liver and pancreas

* Combined vascular, solid and hollow organ injury, e.g. aortic or caval injury

* Inaccessible major venous injury, e.g. retrohepatic vena cava

* Demand for non-operative control of other injuries, e.g. fractured pelvis

* Anticipated need for a time-consuming procedure

Physiological (decline of physiological reserve)

* Temperature <34ºC

* pH <7.2

* Serum lactate >5 mmol/L (normal is <2.5 mmol/L)

* Prothrombin time (PT) >16 s

* Partial thromboplastin time (PTT) >60 s

* Blood transfusion approaching 15 units

* Blood pressure <70 mmHg

Environmental

* Operating time >60 min

* Inability to approximate the abdominal incision

* Desire to reassess the intra-abdominal contents (directed relook)

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which organization plays a role in intersectoral coordination under the Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) program?
questions.explanation: The Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) scheme requires extensive intersectoral coordination between the Ministry of Women and Child Development and various health initiatives to provide holistic care for children and mothers. The National Health Mission (NHM) is the primary organization that collaborates with ICDS to provide essential health services, including immunization, health check-ups, and referral services at the village level. NACO (Option B) focuses on AIDS control. NLEP (Option C) is dedicated to leprosy elimination. UNDP (Option D) is an international developmental agency and is not a core part of the domestic intersectoral coordination framework for ICDS. Coordination between NHM and ICDS occurs primarily through the collaboration of Anganwadi Workers and ASHAs. This partnership ensures that nutrition, health education, and medical care are integrated to reduce infant mortality and improve childhood development outcomes. Therefore, NHM is the correct coordinating organization for health-related ICDS goals
questions.learning: The Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) scheme requires extensive intersectoral coordination between the Ministry of Women and Child Development and various health initiatives to provide holistic care for children and mothers.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: In children diagnosed with congenital heart disease, NADA's criteria include all the following, except?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Increased troponin-T

Increased troponin-T is not included in NADA’s criteria.

Nada’s criteria is used to diagnose congenital heart disease in children. The presence of 1 major or 2 minor criteria indicates congenital heart disease.

Major criteria

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: In a patient, the hypothalamic thermostat was reset from point V to point X as shown below. Which of the following happens in stage W compared to stage Y?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Shivering

“Thermostat reset”

• Hypothalamus (preoptic area) acts like a biological thermostat
• Normally maintains temperature around 37°C

In fever (due to pyrogens like IL-1, TNF → PGE₂):

• Set point shifts UPWARD (V → X)

Pyrogens (IL-1, TNF, IL-6)

↓

↑ Prostaglandin E2 (PGE2)

↓

Hypothalamic set point ↑

↓

Body perceives "COLD"

↓

Shivering + Vasoconstriction

↓

Body temperature rises → reaches new set point

Resetting the hypothalamic set-point upward (V → X) produces fever.

To increase temperature:

| Mechanism | Effect

| --------- | ------

| Shivering | Heat production ↑

| Vasoconstriction | Heat loss ↓

| Behavioral (blanket seeking) | Heat conservation

In stage W, body temperature is below the new set-point, so heat-generating mechanisms are activated—most notably shivering.

In stage Y, the set-point falls back to normal, leading to heat loss mechanisms like sweating and vasodilation.

questions.text: Identify the incorrect pair of branch and parent nerve:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Infratrochlear- Maxillary Nerve

Correct nerve–branch relationships:

• Frontal nerve (V1) → supraorbital, supratrochlear
• Nasociliary nerve (V1) → anterior ethmoidal, posterior ethmoidal, long ciliary, infratrochlear
• Maxillary nerve (V2) → infraorbital, zygomatic, superior alveolar nerves

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is implicated in the pathogenesis of rheumatoid arthritis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Autoimmunity

Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic inflammatory disorder of autoimmune origin that principally attacks the joints, producing nonsuppurative, proliferative, and inflammatory synovitis. The inflammation progresses to the destruction of the articular cartilage and ankylosis of the joints.

In RA, the synovium contains germinal centers with secondary follicles and abundant plasma cells, which produce antibodies, some are autoantibodies. Many of the autoantibodies produced in the lymphoid organs are specific for citrullinated peptides (CCPs). 80% of patients have serum IgM or IgA autoantibodies that bind to the Fc portions of their own IgG. These autoantibodies are called rheumatoid factor and may also be deposited in joints as immune complexes.

The characteristic histologic features of RA include:

* Increased vascularity due to angiogenesis

* Dense inflammatory infiltrates

* Synovial cell hyperplasia and proliferation

* Fibrinopurulent exudate (synovial and joint surfaces)

* Subcutaneous nodule: Necrotising granulomas with a central area of fibrinoid necrosis.

* Osteoclastic activity (underlying bone)

This all together leads to a mass of edematous synovium called pannus, which grows over the articular cartilage and causes its erosion.
questions.learning: Autoimmunity Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic inflammatory disorder of autoimmune origin that principally attacks the joints, producing nonsuppurative, proliferative, and inflammatory synovitis.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following options is considered a high-level disinfectant?
questions.explanation: Glutaraldehyde (e.g., Cidex) is classified as a high-level disinfectant. High-level disinfectants are capable of killing all microorganisms, including bacterial spores, when used for a sufficient contact time (chemosterilant). It is widely used for heat-sensitive medical equipment, such as endoscopes and bronchoscopes. Isopropyl alcohol (Option A) is an intermediate-level disinfectant; it kills most bacteria and viruses but is not sporicidal. Iodophors (Option C), like Povidone-iodine, are also intermediate-level disinfectants used primarily as skin antiseptics. Benzalkonium chloride (Option D) is a quaternary ammonium compound, which is a low-level disinfectant that is ineffective against many viruses and spores. High-level disinfection is the minimum requirement for "semi-critical" items that come into contact with mucous membranes. Because glutaraldehyde has a broad spectrum of activity including spores, it is the correct choice
questions.learning: Glutaraldehyde (e.g., Cidex) is classified as a high-level disinfectant. High-level disinfectants are capable of killing all microorganisms, including bacterial spores, when used for a sufficient contact time (chemosterilant).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What are the benefits of transitioning from Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV) to Inactivated Polio Vaccine (IPV)?
options: Less incidence of Vaccine Associated Paralytic Polio
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Less incidence of Vaccine Associated Paralytic Polio

The benefit of transitioning from an Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV) to an Inactivated Polio Vaccine (IPV) is IPV is unlikely to cause VAPP(Vaccine Associated Paralytic Polio ).

There are two types of vaccine that protect against polio: inactivated poliovirus vaccine (IPV) and oral poliovirus vaccine (OPV).

* Sabin (OPV)

*  Salk (IPV)

OPV (Sabin) initially consisted of a mixture of live attenuated poliovirus strains of each of the three serotypes. OPV used in India contained, Type 1 virus 10 lakh, Type 2 virus 2 lakh and Type 3 virus 3 lakh TC ID50 per dose (0.5 ml). Trivalent vaccine has now been replaced by bivalent OPV, by removing the type 2 component from immunisation programmes (OPV switch) as it is implicated in the pathogenesis of cVDPV and occasionally vaccine-associated paralytic polio (VAPP). OPV type 2 was discontinued globally in April 2016.

IPV (Salk)  is produced from wild-type poliovirus strains of each serotype that have been inactivated (killed) with formalin. The Salk vaccine or inactivated polio vaccine is trivalent. It can be administered as an IM, SC, or ID injection. It carries the advantage of not causing Vaccine-associated paralytic poliomyelitis (VAPP) or cVDPV as it is inactivated.

Other options:

Option B: Both OPV (Oral polio vaccine) and IPV (Inactivated polio vaccine) induce humoral IgG and IgM antibodies. OPV also induces local immunity in the lining of the intestine.

Option C: Although polio vaccine related side effects are less in IPV as compared to OPV, this is incorrect because Option A provides a better and precise statement.

Option D: Storage is not a major reason for transitioning from OPV to IPV. The storage conditions are quite similar for both of them

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A patient came to the OPD with complaints of vomiting and diarrhoea along with skin eruptions. He gives the history of similar episodes in the past. After switching to gluten free diet his symptoms resolved. Which marker is useful in diagnosing this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Anti tissue transglutaminase antibody

The given scenario of vomiting, diarrhoea, skin eruptions and resolving symptoms with gluten free diet along with crypt hperplasia, villous atrophy and intra epithelial lymphocyte as seen in histopathology are suggestive of celiac disease. Anti tissue transglutaminase antibody will help in diagnosing this condition.

Small intestinal adenocarcinoma is also associated with celiac disease.

Celiac disease or celiac sprue or gluten-sensitive enteropathy is triggered by the ingestion of gluten, which is the major storage protein of wheat and similar grains. It usually affects the 2nd part of the duodenum or proximal jejunum.

Antibodies associated with celiac disease are:

• Anti-gliadin antibodies
• Anti tissue transglutaminase antibodies
• Anti endomysial antibodies

MARSH's score is used to assess celiac disease histologically.

Dermatitis herpetiformis occurs in about 10% of patients with celiac disease.

Other options :

Option A : Serological markers that are usually positive in patients with Crohn's disease include the anti–Saccharomyces cerevisiae antibody (ASCA).

Option B : Anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA)-associated vasculitis is categorized into 3 distinct forms:  Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA; formerly Wegener granulomatosis), Microscopic polyangiitis (MPA), Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis, formerly called Churg–Strauss syndrome (CSS).

Option D : Anti-parietal cell antibody is positive in patients with Pernicious anemia.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient who wears contact lenses presents with two months of eye watering, redness, and a foreign body sensation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical history of a contact lens wearer with chronic discomfort and foreign body sensation is highly suggestive of an immune response to the lens material or deposits. The pathognomonic visual finding shown in the image—large, flattened papillae on the superior tarsal conjunctiva, often described as a "cobblestone" appearance—is diagnostic of Giant Papillary Conjunctivitis (GPC). GPC is effectively a mechanical and allergic reaction. Acute trachoma (Option A) presents with follicles and scarring, often linked to Chlamydia infection in endemic areas. Follicular conjunctivitis (Option B) shows small, translucent lumps (follicles) rather than these large papillae. Spring catarrh (Option D), or Vernal Keratoconjunctivitis, also shows cobblestone papillae but is typically seen in young boys without a contact lens history. Because the patient specifically has a contact lens risk factor and classic papillary changes, GPC is the correct diagnosis. Management involves discontinuing lens wear and using topical antihistamines
questions.learning: The clinical history of a contact lens wearer with chronic discomfort and foreign body sensation is highly suggestive of an immune response to the lens material or deposits.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 4-year-old child presents with self- mutilating behavior such as biting the lips and fingers, delayed developmental milestones, hyperuricemia, and a family history of similar symptoms in male relatives. Deficiency of which enzyme is most likely responsible for this condition?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of self-mutilation (biting lips and fingers), developmental delay, and hyperuricemia in a young male is diagnostic of Lesch-Nyhan syndrome. This X-linked recessive disorder is caused by a complete deficiency of the enzyme hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyl transferase (HGPRT). HGPRT is essential for the purine salvage pathway; its absence leads to the massive overproduction of uric acid and neurological dysfunction through poorly understood mechanisms. Purine nucleoside phosphorylase deficiency (Option A) and Adenosine deaminase deficiency (Option D) cause forms of Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID), not self-mutilation. Adenine phosphoribosyl transferase deficiency (Option C) results in 2,8-dihydroxyadenine urolithiasis (kidney stones). Lesch-Nyhan is characterized by "orange sand" (uric acid crystals) in the diaper during infancy. Management includes allopurinol to control hyperuricemia and prevent gout/stones, but there is no effective treatment for the severe behavioral and neurological components. The family history in male cousins reinforces the X-linked inheritance pattern
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of self-mutilation (biting lips and fingers), developmental delay, and hyperuricemia in a young male is diagnostic of Lesch-Nyhan syndrome.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A polytrauma patient with femur fracture and massive hemorrhage presents to the emergency department after a road traffic accident. Which of the following is not an immediate treatment consideration in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Internal fixation of femur fracture

The internal fixation of a femur fracture is not an immediate concern in a patient with polytrauma and hemodynamic instability secondary to severe blood loss. Instead, splinting is preferred until the patient has been stabilized.

Damage Control Orthopaedics (DCO) in unstable/borderline polytrauma patients involves 3 components:

• Stage 1: Resuscitative procedures for rapid hemorrhage control
• Stage 2: Restoration of normal physiologic parameters
• Stage 3: Definitive surgical management

The first stage is early temporary stabilization of unstable fractures and the control of the bleeding. In femur fracture, the most suited approach is temporary stabilization using an external fixator.

The second stage involves resuscitation and stabilization of the patients in the ICU.

Finally, the third stage involves delayed definitive fracture management after the patient’s condition becomes suitable. In femur fracture, the definitive procedure is intramedullary nailing which is performed after the patient becomes stable.
questions.learning: Internal fixation of femur fracture — The internal fixation of a femur fracture is not an immediate concern in a patient with polytrauma and hemodynamic instability secondary to severe blood loss.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: What is the daily fluid requirement for a 3-day- old baby with a birth weight of ?
questions.explanation: Fluid requirements in neonates depend on postnatal age, birth weight, and renal maturity. In the first few days of life, especially in low-birth-weight (LBW) infants, fluids are introduced cautiously to allow for physiological weight loss and to prevent complications related to fluid overload. For an LBW baby (≈ 1.5–2 kg): Day 1: ~60–70 ml/kg/day Day 2: ~70–80 ml/kg/day Day 3: 80–90 ml/kg/day Day 4–5: ~100–110 ml/kg/day After Day 7: ~120–150 ml/kg/day (full maintenance) Thus, on Day 3 of life, the recommended daily fluid requirement is 80–90 ml/kg/day. Why other options are incorrect: 1. Option A (100–110 ml/kg/day): Appropriate for Day 4–5, not Day 3 2. Options C & D (120–150 ml/kg/day): Used after the first week, once full maintenance is established Excessive fluids early in LBW neonates increase the risk of PDA, NEC, BPD, and electrolyte imbalance. Therefore, a gradual, step-wise increase in fluids is the standard neonatal practice

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following statements is false about the umbilical cord?
options: It has one artery and two veins
It contains a gelatinous substance called Wharton's jelly
Presence of a single umbilical artery is associated with congenital anomalies
Normal average umbilical cord length is 50-60 cms
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. It has one artery and two veins

The umbilical cord normally has two arteries and one vein. The presence of a single umbilical artery is the most common vascular anomaly of the cord. It is associated with congenital anomalies such as genitourinary and cardiac anomalies.

The umbilical cord is a tube that connects the fetus to the placenta. It contains umbilical vessels and an obliterated allantois duct, all surrounded by Wharton's jelly and contained within an outer layer of amnion. Maternal blood enters the fetus through the umbilical vein, and blood exits the fetus via the two umbilical arteries. Wharton's jelly is a gelatinous mucopolysaccharide that protects the umbilical vessels. Local collections of Wharton's jelly produce false knots in the cord.

The average length of the umbilical cord is between 40-70 cm at term. A long cord can form a loop around the fetus' neck and can cause asphyxia. A short cord can result in cord rupture during labor.
questions.learning: It has one artery and two veins — The umbilical cord normally has two arteries and one vein. The presence of a single umbilical artery is the most common vascular anomaly of the cord.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: In the given barium swallow image, which of the following shows the left atrium impression on the esophagus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 3

In the given barium swallow image, the arrow marking with the number 3 shows the left atrium impression on the esophagus.

The esophagus is a fibromuscular tube that connects the pharynx of the neck to the stomach, passing through the thorax through the superior and posterior mediastinum. It starts below the cricopharyngeus muscle, at the level of C6- the cricoid cartilage's bottom margin. The esophagus is located behind the trachea in the neck. It passes posterior to the left main bronchus, the left atrium, and the aortic arch as it descends through the mediastinum, each of which leaves an impression.

The vagus nerves accompany the esophagus as it travels through the diaphragmatic gap at T10 and finishes at the gastric cardia at T11. The left lobe of the liver is located anterior to the abdominal esophagus. Thus, the esophagus is composed of a short cervical, a long thoracic, and a short abdominal segment.

questions.text: Identify the segment marked in the image below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. V

The liver segment highlighted in green in this CT section is segment V. The section of the CT given is taken below the portal vein as the cross-section of the portal vein before its bifurcation can be viewed.

A horizontal plane known as the portal plane divides the liver where the portal vein bifurcates and becomes horizontal. This divides each section of the liver into superior and inferior segments:

* Left lateral section: segment II above and segment III below the portal plane

* Left medial section: segment IVa above and segment IVb below the portal plane

* Right anterior (or medial) section: segment VIII above and segment V below the portal plane

* Right posterior (or lateral) section: segment VII above and segment VI below the portal plane

Shown below is a section from below the portal plane.

Couinaud classification is the commonly used classification of the liver. It divides the liver is divided into eight segments. It is based on the distribution of portal venous branches in the liver parenchyma. Each segment has its own vascular supply, biliary drainage, and lymphatic drainage.

The Couinaud classification is currently the most widely used system to describe functional liver anatomy.

* Based on the distribution of hepatic portal venous branches in the parenchyma

* Each segment has its own dual vascular inflow, biliary drainage and lymphatic drainage

The image depicts cobra head/ adder head deformity in an IVP of bilateral ureteroceles.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 40-year-old female presented with a history of profuse vaginal discharge. The discharge has a fishy odour. Which of the following best describes the microscopic finding given below?
options: Epithelial cell with bacteria attached on cell surface
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Epithelial cell with bacteria attached on cell surface

The given clinical scenario of women with fishy odor vaginal discharge is suggestive of bacterial vaginosis (BV). The microscopic finding is vaginal epithelial cells with bacteria attached to their surface called clue cells, creating a poorly defined cellular border. They are the most reliable indicators of BV.

Bacterial vaginosis (BV) is characterized by a decrease in lactobacilli and an overgrowth of anaerobic bacterial species, including gardnerella, prevotella,mobiluncus, and bacteroides. Multiple or new sexual partners, having female partners, and engaging in oral sex are associated with a higher risk of BV. They may experience a foul-smelling (fishy odor) thin vaginal discharge.

The clinical diagnosis of BV is based on the presence of three out of four Amsel criteria: elevated vaginal pH (>4.5), thin noninflammatory discharge, >20% clue cells, and a fishy odor (positive whiff test) after adding 10% potassium hydroxide to a vaginal sample. creating a poorly defined cellular border.

BV is associated with adverse pregnancy outcomes such as preterm birth, preterm premature rupture of membranes, and postpartum endometritis. It also increases susceptibility to sexually transmitted infections, including HIV.

The recommended treatment options in nonpregnant women include oral metronidazole, metronidazole gel, or clindamycin cream. Alternative options include oral secnidazole, tinidazole, or clindamycin. Partner treatment is not needed.

questions.text: A patient presents with carcinoma in pyriform Fossa. On laryngoscopy, the lesion is around 5cm and the right vocal folds are not mobile. There is no lymph Node involvement and no distant metastasis. What is the TNM staging for the malignancy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. T3N0M0

The patient has carcinoma hypopharynx as it is a tumor in the pyriform fossa and his staging of the disease is T3N0M0 as he has no nodal mets or involvement of vocal cords.

Staging of carcinoma hypopharynx:

1)Tumour

T1:

* Tumor involves only in one part of the hypopharynx

* is less than <2 cms

T2:

* Tumor involves more than one part of the hypopharynx

* has grown into a nearby area

*  > 2cm but < 4 cm across

* not affected the vocal cords

T3:

* Tumor is > 4 cm across

* Tumor is affecting the movement of the vocal cords

* Tumor has grown into the esophagus

T4a:

* The tumor has grown into thyroid or cricoid cartilage/ hyoid bone/ thyroid gland/nearby muscle or fat.

T4b:

* Tumor grows into Prevertebral Space

* Superior Mediastinum

* Encases carotid artery

2)Nodal staging:

* NX -cannot be assessed

* N0 No regional lymph node metastasis

* N1 Metastasis in a single ipsilateral lymph node, <3 cm

* N2a Metastasis in a single ipsilateral lymph node, >3cm but < 6 cm

* N2b Metastasis in multiple ipsilateral lymph nodes, <6 cm

* N2c Metastasis in bilateral or contralateral lymph nodes, < 6 cm

* N3 Metastasis in a lymph node > 6 cm

* M0- no metastasis

* M1- metastasis present
