questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 47-year-old hypertensive woman came to your clinic complaining of bone pain. She has a history of recurrent renal stones. Which of the following is the most appropriate management for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Thiazide diuretics

Given the clinical picture of a 47-year-old hypertensive woman with bone pain and recurrent renal stones, the most likely diagnosis is hyperparathyroidism (often primary hyperparathyroidism) and the most appropriate management for the given condition is thiazide diuretics.

Thiazides reduce calcium excretion in the urine, which can help prevent the formation of kidney stones in hyperparathyroidism and help manage the hypercalcemia associated with it.

Hyperparathyroidism is a condition characterized by the overproduction of parathyroid hormone (PTH) by the parathyroid glands, leading to elevated levels of calcium in the blood (hypercalcemia). There are two main types: primary hyperparathyroidism, where an abnormality within the parathyroid glands (often an adenoma) causes excessive PTH production, and secondary hyperparathyroidism, typically caused by chronic kidney disease, which leads to low calcium levels and compensatory increased PTH secretion.

Primary hyperparathyroidism
Secondary hyperparathyroidism
Tertiary hyperparathyroidism

an autonomous overproduction of parathyroid hormone (PTH)

compensatory hypersecretion of PTH in response to prolonged hypocalcemia
persistent hypersecretion of PTH even after the cause of prolonged hypocalcemia is corrected

Parathyroid  adenoma or hyperplasia
chronic renal failure
after renal transplant.

Primary hyperparathyroidism is one of the most common endocrine disorders, and it is an important cause of hypercalcemia. Tumours of the parathyroid glands usually come to attention because of excessive secretion of PTH rather than mass effects. It can also be associated with MEN1 and MEN 2A syndromes.

The clinical manifestations of hyperparathyroidism can be summarized as “painful bones, renal stones, abdominal groans, and psychic moans.” Skeletal manifestations of hyperparathyroidism include bone resorption, osteitis fibrosa cystica, and brown tumours. Renal changes include nephrolithiasis (stones) and nephrocalcinosis.

Localisation of parathyroid is difficult. Nuclear medicine scanning with radiolabeled Sestamibi is a widely used technique. Sestamibi accumulates in parathyroid adenomas. This radionuclide is concentrated in the thyroid and parathyroid tissue but usually washes out of normal thyroid tissue in under an hour. It persists in abnormal parathyroid tissue. It is now regarded as the most accurate and reliable method for imaging the parathyroid glands.

Other options:

Option B: Loop diuretic is not an appropriate answer, as it increases calcium excretion and could worsen hypocalcemia.

Option C: Calcitriol is not appropriate in this case, as it is a form of active vitamin D that increases calcium absorption, which could exacerbate hypercalcemia.

Option D: Calcium gluconate is not appropriate here, as calcium gluconate is used to treat hypocalcemia, not hypercalcemia.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient presents with photosensitivity, purpura, and blistering lesions on sun-exposed skin. Biochemical analysis reveals impaired conversion of uroporphyrinogen III to coproporphyrinogen III within the heme biosynthesis pathway. Which of the following enzyme is deficient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase

Porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT) is the most common porphyria and results from uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase (UROD) deficiency. Defective conversion of uroporphyrinogen III to coproporphyrinogen III leads to the accumulation of uroporphyrins, which are photosensitizing compounds. Exposure to sunlight generates reactive oxygen species, causing photosensitivity, skin fragility, blistering lesions, hyperpigmentation, and purpura on sun-exposed areas.

Why not the other options?

• A. Coproporphyrinogen oxidase deficiency: Causes Hereditary coproporphyria, characterized by acute neurovisceral attacks with or without photosensitivity.
• C. Ferrochelatase deficiency: Causes Erythropoietic protoporphyria, presenting with painful photosensitivity without blistering due to protoporphyrin accumulation.
• D. Porphobilinogen deaminase deficiency: Causes Acute intermittent porphyria (AIP), which presents with abdominal pain, neuropsychiatric symptoms, and neuropathy, without photosensitivity.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Ureteric injury is most commonly observed in which population?
questions.explanation: Ureteric injury is a known complication of pelvic surgeries, especially those involving extensive dissection near the ureter. The highest risk occurs during Wertheim’s hysterectomy (radical hysterectomy), which is performed for carcinoma cervix. In this procedure: 1. The ureter is closely related to the uterine artery (“water under the bridge”) 2. Extensive dissection is done near the cardinal and uterosacral ligaments 3. The ureter is mobilized and dissected, increasing the risk of injury Because of this complex anatomy and radical nature of surgery, ureteric injury is most common in Wertheim’s hysterectomy. Why other options are incorrect: (A) Vaginal hysterectomy → Lower risk due to limited dissection (C) Abdominal hysterectomy → Moderate risk, less than radical surgery (D) Emergency C-section → Ureteric injury is rare; bladder injury more common

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the most likely condition affecting the umbilical region of a 39-year-old obese man who has recently begun exercising at the gym?
questions.explanation: The image shows a rounded swelling directly at the umbilicus in an adult obese man who recently started exercising. This is typical of an umbilical hernia, where abdominal contents protrude through a weakness in the umbilical ring. Increased intra-abdominal pressure (such as during exercise or obesity) is a common precipitating factor. Umbilical hernias in adults usually present as a central bulge at the navel, which may become more prominent on straining or standing and may reduce on lying down. Hy other options are incorrect: (A) Omphalocele : A congenital condition in newborns, where abdominal organs herniate into a sac at the umbilicus. Not seen in adults. (B) Gastroschisis : Another congenital defect, where bowel loops protrude outside the abdomen without a covering sac, usually to the right of the umbilicus. Again, only in newborns. (D) Paraumbilical hernia : Occurs adjacent to (not exactly at) the umbilicus. The swelling in the image is clearly central, not lateral

questions.text: A 10-year-old boy rapidly develops hypoglycemia after moderate activity. Blood examination reveals raised levels of ketone bodies, lactic acid, and triglycerides. On examination, the liver and kidneys are found to be enlarged. Which of the following deficiency would be seen in the liver of this child ?

* Osteopenia

* Hepatic adenoma

* Pulmonary hypertension

* Pancreatitis.

* Renal failure.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following elements is not considered a microelement (trace element) required in very small quantities for normal human health?
questions.explanation: In human nutrition, elements are classified based on the required daily intake. Calcium is classified as a macroelement (or macromineral) because the body requires it in large amounts (typically ) for bone structure, muscle contraction, and nerve signaling. In contrast, Copper (Option A), Zinc (Option B), and Selenium (Option D) are all microelements (trace elements). These are essential for health but are required only in minute quantities (typically ), usually acting as cofactors for specific enzymes. Other macroelements include sodium, potassium, and magnesium. Other microelements include iron, iodine, and manganese. Understanding this distinction is vital for clinical nutrition; macroelement deficiencies often manifest with structural or major electrolyte issues, while trace element deficiencies typically present with specific metabolic or enzymatic dysfunctions. Therefore, due to its high daily requirement and structural role in the skeleton, calcium is definitively not a trace element

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 55-year-old hypertensive patient presents with blurred vision and headaches. Retinal examination reveals flame-shaped hemorrhages, cotton wool spots, and disc edema. According to the Keith-Wagener classification, which grade of hypertensive retinopathy does this patient have?
questions.explanation: The Keith-Wagener-Barker classification is used to grade the severity of hypertensive retinopathy based on ophthalmoscopic findings. The presence of disc edema (papilledema), along with the signs of severe retinal damage like flame-shaped hemorrhages and cotton wool spots, is the defining feature of Grade IV retinopathy. This grade signifies malignant hypertension and is a medical emergency, as it indicates significant end-organ damage and a high risk of cardiovascular or neurological events. Grade III (Option C) includes hemorrhages, cotton wool spots, and hard exudates (often in a "macular star" pattern) but lacks disc edema. Grade II (Option B) is characterized by more pronounced arteriolar narrowing and AV nipping. Grade 1 (Option A) involves simple generalized arteriolar narrowing and "silver-wiring". Management of Grade IV retinopathy requires immediate but controlled reduction of blood pressure, usually in an intensive care setting, and urgent neurological evaluation to rule out hypertensive encephalopathy. Retinal findings often improve significantly once blood pressure is stabilized

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: During a household survey, a family includes a 35-year-old man, his wife who is 6 weeks pregnant, and their 3-year-old child, along with the temporary stay of the man’s brother and sister-in-law during winter vacation. How should this household be classified?
questions.explanation: In sociology and public health demography, a Nuclear family is strictly defined as a household consisting of a married couple and their own unmarried children living together. This household includes the man, his wife, and their 3-year-old child. The temporary presence of the man’s brother and his wife for a winter vacation does not change the core classification, as they are not permanent residents of the household. A Joint family (Option A) consists of multiple generations and/or multiple married siblings and their families living together as a single permanent unit. An Extended family (Option C) includes other relatives beyond the nuclear core who live permanently in the household. A Third generation family (Option D) specifically includes grandparents, parents, and children. Categorizing family types is essential for assessing social support networks and health risks. Because the brother's family is only visiting, the primary sociological structure remains that of a nuclear unit, focusing on the parental pair and their child

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which statement regarding a primary healthcare center (PHC) is incorrect?
options: There is 1 PHC per 30,000 population in plain areas.
Type A PHC conducts fewer than 20 deliveries per month.
Provides maternal and child health care, family planning, and MTP.
questions.explanation: The statement that a PHC is the first referral unit (FRU) is incorrect. In India’s public health infrastructure, the Community Health Center (CHC) is designated as the First Referral Unit, as it provides specialist services, blood storage, and emergency obstetric care that a PHC cannot. All other statements are true: there is indeed 1 PHC per 30,000 population in plain areas (and 1 per 20,000 in hilly/tribal areas) (Option A). PHCs are categorized by their delivery load, with Type A centers conducting fewer than 20 deliveries per month (Option B). PHCs serve as the primary hub for maternal and child health (MCH), family planning, and Medical Termination of Pregnancy (MTP) services (Option C). Therefore, the designation of "First Referral Unit" applies to the CHC level, not the PHC

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Identify the blue-colored area shown in the image below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Midpelvis

The blue colored area in the given image shows midpelvis.

Midpelvis is the region of the pelvis that is bounded by the plane of the greatest pelvic dimensions above and the midpelvic plane below.

The plane of greatest pelvic dimensions (most roomy pelvic plane) extends from the middle of the posterior surface of the symphysis pubis to the junction of the second and third sacral vertebrae.

The midpelvic plane extends from the lower margin of the symphysis pubis to the tip of the sacrum at the level of ischial spines (coinciding with the plane of least pelvic dimensions), or from the lower margin of the symphysis pubis to the junction of S4 and S5, making a wedge posteriorly.

Other options:

Option A: Obstetric outlet - It is the region of the pelvis that is bounded by the plane of the least pelvic dimensions above and the anatomical outlet below.

Option B: Anatomical outlet/ bony outlet - It corresponds to the bony outer margin of the pelvis. It is a diamond-shaped region formed by joining two triangular planes with a common base. The anterior triangle is bounded laterally by the ischiopubic rami and the apex is formed by the inferior border of the pubic arch. The posterior triangle is bounded laterally by the ischial tuberosity and sacrotuberous ligament and the apex is formed by the tip of the coccyx. The common base is formed by the line joining the ischial tuberosities.

Option C: Pelvic inlet - It represents the superior plane of the true pelvis. It is bounded by the horizontal pubic rami and the symphysis pubis anteriorly, the linea terminalis laterally, and the promontory and alae of the sacrum posteriorly.
questions.learning: Midpelvis — The blue colored area in the given image shows midpelvis. Midpelvis is the region of the pelvis that is bounded by the plane of the greatest pelvic dimensions above and the midpelvic plane below.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following enzyme is deficient in Von Gierke's disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Glucose-6- phosphatase

Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency causes von Gierke's disease (Type I GSD).

These patients have hepatomegaly, fasting hypoglycemia, and hypotonia overlap. Further, in von Gierke's disease, there are increased serum lactate levels and hyperuricemia.

Other options:

Liver glycogen phosphorylase deficiency causes Her's disease (Type VI GSD). It results in the accumulation of glycogen in the liver causing hepatomegaly and mild hypoglycemia. Hypotonia is not seen.

Muscle glycogen phosphorylase deficiency causes McArdle syndrome (Type V GSD) which presents with poor exercise tolerance, low lactate levels following exercise, and accumulation of glycogen in muscles.

Glycogen debranching enzyme is deficient in Cori's disease - Type III glycogen storage disease (GSD) in which hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly, hypotonia, and growth retardation can be seen.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 20-year-old patient presents with painful swelling in the middle finger around the proximal phalanx. An X-ray was done and it is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Enchondroma

The above clinical vignette and X-ray findings point toward the diagnosis of enchondroma.

Enchondromas are benign tumors consisting of a lobulated mass of cartilage encapsulated by fibrous tissue. It is more commonly seen in 20 to 30 years of age. Small bones of hands and feet are commonly involved followed by the femur and humerus.

The patient usually presents with long-standing swelling from one or more phalanges or metacarpals, without much pain. Diagnosis can be done by X-ray, which can show expanding lytic lesions, occasionally, a biopsy will be required if the diagnosis is unclear. Enchondromas of long bones may undergo malignant transformation into chondrosarcoma.

Treatment is removal by curettage and it is indicated if there is pain or pathological fracture.

Other options:

Option A: Osteosarcoma is the most common primary malignancy of bone that produces osteoid matrix or mineralized bone.  X-ray shows periosteal reaction and it may take the form of a Codman's triangle or it may have a sunburst (sunray) appearance as shown below.

Option B: Ewing's sarcoma is the second most common primary malignancy of bone after osteosarcoma. Onion-peel appearance due to deposition of periosteal reaction in layers is seen on radiology (as shown below) and Homer-Wright rosettes, which are round groupings of cells with a central fibrillary core may be seen histologically.

Option C: Osteoclastoma is also called a giant cell tumour because multinucleated osteoclast-type giant cells are present on histology. The image below shows an X-ray of a giant cell tumor showing an eccentrically located solitary lytic lesion in the epiphysis and the typical soap bubble appearance

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Data obtained from hospital records is not a representative sample of the population. What are the reasons for this? I. Mild cases and subclinical cases may be missed. II. Population served by a hospital usually cannot be defined. III. Cost of hospital care is not recorded. IV. Admission policy for cases can vary from hospital to hospital. Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. I, II and IV

Hospital records are an important source of health data but are not representative of the general population. They are subject to selection bias, as only individuals who seek or require hospital care are included.

The reasons include:

• Mild and subclinical cases are often missed, since they usually do not present to hospitals.
• The population served by a hospital is often ill-defined, making it difficult to calculate population-based disease rates.
• Admission policies differ between hospitals, leading to variations in the types and severity of cases admitted.

Cost of hospital care is not a reason why hospital records are unrepresentative of the population.
questions.learning: I, II and IV Hospital records are an important source of health data but are not representative of the general population. They are subject to selection bias, as only individuals who seek or require hospital care are included.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: In conventional oxygen therapy, which device will deliver highest FiO2?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Non rebreathing mask

Non rebreathing masks provide highest FiO2 during conventional oxygen therapy.

The non-rebreather mask is a low flow device that can be used to deliver oxygen at higher concentrations (FiO2 80-95%). It uses a reservoir bag to let the oxygen get concentrated while a one-way valve doesn't allow to breathe in expired air.

This type of masks are used in patients with significant hypoxia, with relatively normal ventilation, such as victims of trauma or carbon monoxide exposure.

Other options:

A) Venturi mask:

• Venturi mask is a high-flow, fixed-performance oxygen delivery system and the highest oxygen concentration (FiO2) delivered is 60% at a flow rate of 15 L/min.
• It is based on the Bernoulli Principle, which states that in order to maintain a constant flow, a fluid must increase its velocity as it flows through a constriction.
• It is available in different colors, with the green valve venturi mask providing 60% FiO2.
• This is useful with patients who require greater FiO2 such as COPD patients, where it is important to provide controlled oxygenation.

B) Hudson mask:

• Also known as simple face mask
• Low-flow, variable performance device
• They provide an oxygen flow rate of up to 5-10 L/min and provide a variable FiO2.
• The body of the mask functions as reservoir for both oxygen and expired carbon dioxide.
• Used in patients who require oxygen therapy for shorter periods of time.

D) Nasal cannula:

• They are low-flow, variable performance devices, with flow rate of 1-4 L/min.
• Used in patients who require low supplemental oxygen.
• Nasopharynx acts as the reservoir in such cannulas.

Indications of a nasal cannula and other low-flow oxygen delivery systems include

• Minute ventilation < 8–10 L/min
• Breathing frequencies < 20 breaths/min
• Normal inspiratory flow (10–30 L/min).
questions.learning: Non rebreathing mask Non rebreathing masks provide highest FiO2 during conventional oxygen therapy. The non-rebreather mask is a low flow device that can be used to deliver oxygen at higher concentrations (FiO2 80-95%).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: On radiological evaluation of a pregnant woman, the pelvic inlet is noted to be oval in the anteroposterior direction. According to the Caldwell and Moloy classification, this pelvic inlet shape corresponds to which type of pelvis?
questions.explanation: The Caldwell-Moloy system classifies the female pelvis into four types based on the shape of the inlet. The "Anthropoid pelvis" (Option B) is characterized by an inlet that is oval-shaped, where the anteroposterior (AP) diameter is significantly larger than the transverse diameter. This pelvis is common in non-Caucasian populations. The "Gynecoid pelvis" (Option C) is the most common female type, featuring a rounded or slightly transverse-oval inlet. The "Android pelvis" (Option A) has a heart-shaped inlet with a narrow fore-pelvis, resembling a male pelvis. The "Platypelloid pelvis" (Option D) has a flattened, transverse-oval inlet where the transverse diameter is much larger than the AP diameter. In an anthropoid pelvis, the fetus is most likely to engage in the "occipito-posterior" position due to the elongated AP dimension. Understanding pelvic architecture is crucial for predicting the mechanism of labor and the likelihood of successful vaginal delivery versus cephalopelvic disproportion

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which skin condition shows coral-red fluorescence when examined under a Wood’s lamp?
questions.explanation: Erythrasma is a common superficial bacterial infection of the intertriginous areas (axilla, groin) caused by Corynebacterium minutissimum. The pathognomonic diagnostic finding is the presence of coral-red fluorescence when the skin is viewed under a Wood’s lamp. This distinct color is produced by the bacterium's secretion of porphyrins. Acanthosis nigricans (Option B) is a sign of insulin resistance and shows hyperpigmented, velvety plaques. Allergic contact dermatitis (Option C) and Cutaneous candidiasis (Option D) do not exhibit this specific fluorescence pattern. Candidiasis characteristically shows "satellite lesions" and a white curd-like surface. Clinically, erythrasma appears as well-demarcated, reddish-brown, scaly patches that can be mistaken for fungal infections. Treatment typically involves topical or oral macrolide antibiotics like erythromycin or clindamycin. Accurate identification via Wood's lamp allows for rapid bedside diagnosis and prevents unnecessary antifungal therapy for a bacterial condition

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The heart of the activated sludge process is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Aeration tank

The activated sludge process is a part of the secondary sewage treatment and the heart of this process is the aeration tanks.

Pearl PF1009: Modern Sewage Treatment

Primary treatment

* Screening

* A large metal screen is used to intercept large floating objects like dead animals, wood, rags, etc., so as to prevent clogging

* Grit chamber

* It is also called detritus chamber

* It allows for the settlement of heavier solids like gravel or sand and permits the organic matter to flow through

* The grit that is collected at the bottom is then disposed of.

* Primary sedimentation

* In a primary sedimentation tank, sewage is allowed to flow slowly so that suspended matter is sediments to form sludge which is then removed without disturbing the rest of the operation.

* Biological action takes place here and breaks down complex organic solids

* Scum in the form of grease and fat collect on top of the tank

* Sometimes, chemicals like lime are added to the effluent to enhance precipitation

Secondary treatment

* Trickling filter method

* The trickling or percolating filter is a bed of crushed stones or clinker

*  Effluent from the primary sedimentation tank is spread over the filter bed and as it percolates through it, it gets oxidized by bacterial flora. There is no actual filtration that occurs.

* The oxidized sewage forms a light green material called humus and it is then led into secondary sedimentation tanks.

* Activated sludge process

* This is done in place of the trickling filter method. Both are not done together

* The heart of the activated sludge process is the aeration tank

* In these tanks, the effluent from primary sedimentation is mixed with activated or return sludge (sludge from the final settling tank) and is then exposed to aeration for 6 to 8 hours.

* During aeration, organic matter is oxidized into carbon dioxide, nitrates and water with the help of aerobic bacteria in the activated sludge.

* Secondary sedimentation

* From the trickling filters or aeration tanks, the oxidized sewage is allowed into a secondary sedimentation tank where it is held for 2 – 3 hours.

* Here, aerated sludge or activated sludge is formed, part of which is pumped back into an aeration tank

* Sludge digestion

* Sludge digestion can be done by incubating it under favorable conditions to allow anaerobic auto-digestion. This is done in sludge digestion tanks.

* Disposal of sludge is also done by sea disposal

* Sludge can also be disposed of by composting with solid refuse

* Disposal of effluent

* Disposal of effluent can be done by dilution in water bodies which has to then be chlorinated

* Disposal on land is possible if the effluent can be used for irrigation purposes

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman presents to you with complaints of difficulty in hearing in the right ear which is slowly progressive. She also has tinnitus which is pulsatile in nature. On examination, a reddish mass was seen behind the tympanic membrane and an audible bruit is heard over the mastoid when auscultation with a stethoscope. Her Rinnie test was negative. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Glomus tumour

The given clinical picture of a woman with progressive conductive hearing loss, tinnitus , reddis mass behind the tympanic membrane and audible bruit heard over the mastoid suggests a diagnosis of a ‘glomus tumor’.

Glomus tumor:

The cell of origin in the glomus tumor is paraganglionic cells (not perivascular cells). These cells are derived from the neural crest. They are paragangliomas of the glomus bodies found in the mastoid.

Glomus tumor is the most common benign neoplasm of the middle ear.

It is of 2 types:

* Glomus jugulare: Origin is from the dome of the jugular bulb causing neurological signs of IXth to XIIth cranial nerve involvement.

* Glomus tympanicum: Promontory in the  middle eari s the source of Glomus tympanicum. It produces auditory symptoms and occasionally facial paralysis.

The rule of 10 is seen in the glomus tumor. It comprises of

* 10% familial

* 10% multicentric

* 10% functional

It is 5 times more common in women. Common presenting features include:

* Progressive conductive hearing loss

* Tinnitus in glomus tumors is pulsatile, of swishing character, synchronous with a pulse, and can be temporarily stopped by carotid pressure.

* Audible bruit heard over the mastoid with a stethoscope in all stages

Investigations would include:

* Phelp's sign-on CECT scan helps to distinguish glomus tympanicum from the glomus jugulare tumor by identification of caroticojugular spine which is eroded in the latter.

* MRI gives the soft tissue extent of the tumor.

* Four vessel angiography is necessary when the CT head shows the involvement of a jugular bulb, carotid artery, or intradural extension.

* A biopsy is never done since it’s a highly vascular tumor.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Respiratory distress syndrome is due to the deficiency of
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Dipalmitoyl Phosphatidylcholine

Respiratory distress syndrome is due to the deficiency of dipalmitoyl-phosphatidyl-choline(DPPC) /dipalmitoyl lecithin. It is the major pulmonary surfactant.

Clinical relevance- Test to assess fetal lung maturity is L/S ratio - lecithin/sphingomyelin ratio. A ratio of ≥ 2 is considered normal.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 28-year-old primigravida with a low-risk pregnancy presents at 39 weeks + 6 days with labor pains. Her vitals are stable. On PV, her cervix is 3 cm dilated and 60% effaced. The fetal head is at -3 station and membranes are felt as a bag of worms beneath the head. What is the appropriate course of management?
options: Rupture of membranes and confirm cord prolapse
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Emergency Caesarean section

In this patient, the membranes are intact and the 'bag of worms' palpaeted refers to the umbilical cord within the membrane, suggestive of cord presentation. The best course of management would be to take the patient up for an emergency caesarean section.

Cord presentation refers to the presence of the umbilical cord below the presenting part over the internal os, within an intact bag of membranes, whereas in the case of a cord prolapse, the membranes are ruptured and the cord lies externally. The goal of management in the event of a cord presentation is to expedite delivery while keeping the membranes intact, and hence the best option would be to deliver the fetus via emergency LSCS. While the patient is being prepared for surgery, she may be positioned in the exagerrated Sim's position (shown below) to avoid cord compression.

In comparison, the management algorithm of cord prolapse is based on three important factors, which are: living or dead baby, maturity of the baby, degree of cervical dilatation, according to which the following steps are taken:

Other options:

Option A: Oxytocin should not be started as the patient should not be allowed to proceed to deliver via normal vaginal delivery due to the risk of cord prolapse and fetal death.

Option B: The membranes should not be ruptured as this would lead to an overt cord prolapse and complicate the situation further.

Option D: Cord presentation is an obstetric emergency requiring immediate action.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 28-year-old man presents to the emergency department after a crush injury to his hand, sustaining a puncture wound from machinery. He reports receiving a tetanus toxoid (TT) injection at age 20. After thorough wound cleaning, what is the appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation: The patient has sustained a crush injury with a puncture wound, which is classified as a tetanus-prone (dirty) wound due to the high risk of contamination and anaerobic conditions favoring Clostridium tetani. Management depends on both the type of wound and the immunization history. This patient received a tetanus toxoid (TT) injection 8 years ago (at age 20). For dirty wounds, if the last booster was given more than 5 years ago, a booster dose is required. The currently recommended booster is Td (tetanus-diphtheria) rather than TT alone. In addition, Tetanus Immunoglobulin (Ig) is administered to provide immediate passive immunity, especially in high-risk wounds such as crush injuries and puncture wounds, where toxin production risk is high. Why other options are wrong: (A) TT only → lacks passive immunity (B) Td only → insufficient protection in high-risk wound (C) TT with Ig → TT is outdated; Td preferred Thus, the most appropriate management is Td with Ig
questions.learning: The patient has sustained a crush injury with a puncture wound, which is classified as a tetanus-prone (dirty) wound due to the high risk of contamination and anaerobic conditions favoring Clostridium tetani.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A young male had a road traffic accident and was brought to emergency with stable vitals. Which wound is not expected:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Chop wound

In road traffic accidents (RTA), injuries are typically due to blunt force trauma, not sharp weapons.

Common RTA injuries :

• Abrasions (especially graze/brush abrasions) → due to friction with road surface
• Contusions (bruises) → due to impact
• Lacerations → irregular tears from blunt force

Why chop wound is not expected:

• Chop wounds are caused by heavy sharp weapons (e.g., axe).
• Characterised by: Clean-cut margins + underlying bone injury
• Not seen in accidental blunt trauma like RTA.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Cyclooxygenase plays a role in which pathway?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Prostaglandin

Prostaglandins are produced from arachidonic acid present in the membrane phospholipids. This process is mediated by 2 cyclooxygenases: COX-1 and COX-2. Prostaglandins are produced by mast cells, macrophages, and endothelial cells.

COX-1 is commonly found in most tissues. It plays a role in maintaining normal homeostasis. It is also induced by inflammatory stimuli.

COX-2 is found in cells that are involved in inflammatory reactions.

The most important prostaglandins in inflammation are PGE2, PGD2, PGF2a, PGI2 (prostacyclin), and thromboxane A2.

Other options:

Options A: Kreb's cycle is also called the citric acid cycle and tricarboxylic acid cycle. It is the terminal pathway for the oxidative catabolism of carbohydrates, amino acids, and fatty acids.

Option C: Leukotrienes are also produced from arachidonic acid with the help of lipoxygenases.
questions.learning: Prostaglandin Prostaglandins are produced from arachidonic acid present in the membrane phospholipids. This process is mediated by 2 cyclooxygenases: COX-1 and COX-2.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 45-year-old female patient presents with complaints of dryness in the mouth and eyes. She also has dysphagia. On examination, dental caries and enlarged cervical lymph nodes are noted. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Sjogren syndrome

The patient's clinical features of dry eyes, dry mouth and dysphagia along with cervical lymphadenopathy and dental caries are suggestive of Sjögren's syndrome.

Sjögren's syndrome is an autoimmune disorder that involves lymphocytic infiltration of the exocrine glands. This manifests as xerostomia (dry mouth) and keratoconjunctivitis sicca (dry eyes). It is associated with autoantibodies anti-Ro/SS-A and anti-La/SS-B.

Keratoconjunctivitis sicca can be diagnosed by Schirmer's test. This test measures the quantity of tears produced. Two marked strips of paper are placed between the globe and the lower eyelid and the patient is instructed to close their eyes for 5 minutes. The tears produced spread along the paper by capillary action. The distance is measured. A score of more than 10 mm is considered to be normal while that of less than 5 mm is considered deficient.

A number of other systems can be involved as well. For example, atrophic gastritis, esophageal mucosal atrophy, and vaginal dryness. Extraglandular or systemic manifestations can also be present. These manifest as fatigue, arthritis, Raynaud's phenomenon, and myalgia.

Diagnosis of primary Sjögren's syndrome requires the following:

* Eye and/or mouth dryness

* Eye tests disclose keratoconjunctivitis sicca

* Mouth evaluation reveals dry oral mucosa and/or

* Presence of anti-Ro or anti-La autoantibodies

A labial (lip) biopsy is a must to confirm the diagnosis and determine the prognosis.

Treatment of Sjögren's syndrome is directed at treating the symptoms and complications. Artificial tears can be used for dry eyes and propionic acid gel for vaginal dryness. Pilocarpine can help increase oral secretions and hydroxychloroquine can be used to treat arthritis.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 62-year-old man presents with persistent headaches that change location depending on intracranial irritation. MRI shows localized pachymeningitis affecting different cranial fossae at different times. The neurologist explains that each cranial fossa has a different primary sensory innervation of the dura, which helps explain the variation in referred pain patterns. Which combination correctly identifies the major nerve distribution to the dura mater in the three cranial fossae?
options: Anterior cranial fossa – V2; Middle cranial fossa – C1–C3; Posterior cranial fossa – V1
Anterior cranial fossa – V3; Middle cranial fossa – V1; Posterior cranial fossa – C1–C3
Anterior cranial fossa – V1; Middle cranial fossa – V3 (meningeal branches); Posterior cranial fossa – C1–C3
Anterior cranial fossa – V2; Middle cranial fossa – V3 via auriculotemporal nerve only; Posterior cranial fossa – V1
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Anterior cranial fossa – V1; Middle cranial fossa – V3 (meningeal branches); Posterior cranial fossa – C1–C3

The dura mater of the cranial cavity receives sensory innervation from branches of the trigeminal nerve and upper cervical nerves, which explains the pattern of referred headache pain depending on which cranial fossa is involved. Major sensory innervation of cranial fossae:

•

Anterior cranial fossa:

• Mainly supplied by ophthalmic division of trigeminal nerve (V1)
• Especially via anterior and posterior ethmoidal nerves

•

Middle cranial fossa:

• Supplied mainly by meningeal branches of the mandibular division (V3)
• Includes the nervus spinosus (meningeal branch of V3)

•

Posterior cranial fossa:

• Supplied primarily by upper cervical nerves (C1–C3)
• Also contributions from vagus and hypoglossal nerves

Irritation of different dural regions produces distinct headache referral patterns because of these different sensory nerve supplies.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Among the options, the accurate statement regarding pregnancy is-
questions.explanation: During pregnancy, significant physiological changes occur to support fetal growth. One major adaptation is a marked increase in renal plasma flow and the Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR), which increases by about 50% (making Option A incorrect). Because more blood is being filtered, the clearance of waste products is enhanced, resulting in a characteristic decrease in serum creatinine levels (Option C). A "normal" creatinine level for a non-pregnant adult may actually indicate renal impairment in a pregnant woman. Platelet counts typically decrease slightly during pregnancy (gestational thrombocytopenia) due to hemodilution and increased consumption, making Option B inaccurate. Therefore, Option D is also incorrect. Understanding these shifts is vital for interpreting laboratory results correctly; for example, a serum creatinine above in pregnancy should prompt further investigation. These changes return to baseline levels shortly after delivery. Serum creatinine decrease is one of the most reliable indicators of the increased renal workload in a healthy pregnancy

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A pregnant woman is found to have a short cervix and undergoes cervical cerclage. Which specific cerclage procedure is most likely to have been performed?
questions.explanation: A cervical cerclage is used to treat cervical insufficiency in women with a short or incompetent cervix. The Modified Shirodkar procedure is a variation that allows for a high placement of the suture (usually Mersilene tape) at the level of the internal os. This higher placement provides better structural support than the standard McDonald's cerclage (Option B), which is a purse-string suture placed lower at the cervicovaginal junction without dissection. The original Shirodkar technique (Option C) requires extensive bladder and rectal dissection to reach the internal os; the "modified" version is often technically simpler while still maintaining the high-placement advantage. Transabdominal cerclage is reserved for cases where vaginal approaches have failed. In this specific clinical context of significant shortening, the Modified Shirodkar is the most likely definitive procedure for high-level support
questions.learning: A cervical cerclage is used to treat cervical insufficiency in women with a short or incompetent cervix. The Modified Shirodkar procedure is a variation that allows for a high placement of the suture (usually Mersilene tape) at the level of the internal os.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A medical student is studying Meigs syndrome for a class presentation. Which of the following is not a classic feature of Meigs syndrome?
questions.explanation: Meigs syndrome is characterized by a specific clinical triad: a benign ovarian tumor, ascites (Option A), and a hydrothorax (pleural effusion), which is classically right-sided (Option B). The most common benign ovarian tumor associated with this syndrome is an ovarian fibroma (Option C). Dysgerminoma (Option D), while a common germ cell tumor in young women, is NOT a component of the classic Meigs triad . In some cases, other benign tumors like thecomas or cystadenofibromas can also cause the syndrome (sometimes called Pseudo-Meigs). A key feature of Meigs syndrome is that the fluid collections (ascites and hydrothorax) resolve spontaneously once the benign ovarian tumor is surgically removed. Because the syndrome is specifically defined by the association with benign fibromas, the malignant dysgerminoma is the correct "except" choice. Recognizing this syndrome is important to avoid misdiagnosing a treatable benign condition as advanced metastatic cancer
questions.learning: Meigs syndrome is characterized by a specific clinical triad: a benign ovarian tumor, ascites (Option A), and a hydrothorax (pleural effusion), which is classically right-sided (Option B).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What characteristic clinical sign is usually seen following an injury to the hypoglossal nerve?
options: Tongue deviation to the contralateral side
Tongue deviation to the same side
questions.explanation: The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) provides motor innervation to all intrinsic and most extrinsic muscles of the tongue, including the genioglossus. The genioglossus muscle is primarily responsible for protruding the tongue. In a healthy individual, the simultaneous action of both genioglossus muscles results in a straight, midline protrusion. When one hypoglossal nerve is injured, the genioglossus muscle on the affected side becomes paralyzed. Consequently, when the patient attempts to protrude their tongue, the unopposed action of the healthy genioglossus muscle on the intact side pushes the tongue toward the side of the lesion. Deviation to the contralateral side (Option A) is not seen in lower motor neuron hypoglossal injuries. Falling of the tongue (Option C) and total inability in protrusion (Option D) would require bilateral nerve damage. Therefore, ipsilateral tongue deviation is the classic clinical sign of a unilateral hypoglossal nerve injury
questions.learning: The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) provides motor innervation to all intrinsic and most extrinsic muscles of the tongue, including the genioglossus. The genioglossus muscle is primarily responsible for protruding the tongue.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 4-year-old child has a history of biting his lips and fingers. On evaluation, you notice lip lacerations, missing sections of his fingers, and developmental delay. Lab reports reveal hyperuricemia. Which enzyme is most likely deficient in this child?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase

The given clinical scenario of self-mutilating behavior, delayed developmental milestones and hyperuricemia is highly suggestive of Lesch-Nyhan syndrome. It occurs due to the complete deficiency of the enzyme hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT) involved in the salvage pathway.

Purines produced in the body or introduced through diet can be converted to nucleoside triphosphates to be reused by the body. This pathway is called the salvage pathway for purines as shown in the image below.

Lesch-Nyhan syndrome is an X-linked recessive disorder due to a complete deficiency of the HGPRT enzyme. This deficiency results in an inability to salvage hypoxanthine or guanine resulting in increased levels of phospho-ribosyl pyrophosphate (PRPP) and decreased levels of inosine monophosphate (IMP) and guanosine monophosphate (GMP). An increase in guanine and hypoxanthine eventually gets converted into uric acid, There is increased de novo purine synthesis.

The clinical features include compulsive self-mutilation, intellectual disability, delayed milestones, dystonic movements, and hyperuricemia. The excess uric acid can form kidney stones (urolithiasis) or deposits in joints as urate crystals (gouty arthritis).

The treatment of this condition includes:

* Allopurinol or febuxostat for hyperuricemia

* Behavioural management using restraints for self-mutilation

* High fluid intake, reduced fructose and purine intake

Partial deficiency of HGPRT leads to Kelley-Seegmiller syndrome.

Other options:

Option A: Purine nucleoside phosphorylase deficiency leads to severe T-cell deficiency with normal B-cell function. Patients present with autoimmune diseases and opportunistic infections.

Option C: Adenine phosphoribosyltransferase (APRT) is another enzyme along with HGPRT to be involved in the salvage of purine bases to nucleotides.

Option D: Adenosine deaminase deficiency leads to sparse or defective T cells and B cells. Patients suffer from severe immunodeficiency and often succumb to fatal infections.

Pearl PF1567: Purine salvage deficiencies: Lesch-Nyhan syndrome and Adenosine deaminase deficiency(SCID)

Severe Combined Immunodeficiency(SCID):

Adenosine deaminase enzyme deficiency is one of the major cause of SCID. It is also called as Glanzmann–Riniker syndrome.

SCID patients are usually affected by severe bacterial, viral, or fungal infections early in life and often present with interstitial lung disease, chronic diarrhea, and failure to thrive.

Lesch-Nyhan syndrome:

It is due to deficiency of the enzyme Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase(HGPRT). It is an X-linked recessive disease.

Clinical features:

* Intellectual disability

* Self-mutilation

* Aggression

* Hyperuricemia

* Gout

Treatment:

* Allopurinol

* Febuxostat

Enzymes

Reaction

AMP deaminase

AMP to IMP

Adenosine deaminase

Adenosine to Inosine

5'-nucleotidase

IMP & GMP to Inosine & Guanosine respectively

Purine nucleoside phosphorylase

Inosine & Guanosine to Hypoxanthine & guanine respectively

Xanthine oxidase

Hypoxanthine to Xanthine & Xanthine to uric acid

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A study was conducted to compare the incidence of postpartum depression in mothers as compared to the sex of the child. For assessment, Edinburg Depression scaled score (EDSS) was used. The study was divided into mothers with male babies as one group to be compared with mothers with female babies. Which of the following statistical test will be used to determine the association?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Chi square test

The Chi-square test is used to compare qualitative data and compares 2 groups with independent measures. The variables used here are yes/no signifying the presence/absence of postpartum depression. Hence it is the most appropriate test here.

Option A: Student’s t-test is for quantitative data. Here the data is qualitative, hence it can't be used.

Option B: Paired t-test compares paired data or pre-intervention and post-intervention data of the same group. This doesn't apply here as the groups are not paired.

Option C: ANOVA is used to compare more than 2 groups.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following factors are involved in maintaining and regulating calcium levels in the blood?
questions.explanation: Blood calcium homeostasis is a tightly regulated process involving three primary hormones. Parathormone (PTH), secreted by the parathyroid glands, is the most important regulator for "increasing" blood calcium; it stimulates bone resorption, renal calcium reabsorption, and the activation of Vitamin D. Vitamin D (Option C), specifically its active form calcitriol, increases calcium levels by promoting its absorption from the small intestine. Calcitonin (Option A), secreted by the parafollicular C-cells of the thyroid, acts as a physiological antagonist to PTH by "decreasing" blood calcium through the inhibition of bone-resorbing osteoclasts. While calcitonin plays a smaller role in daily human calcium regulation compared to PTH, it is still a recognized component of the regulatory system. Together, these substances ensure that ionized calcium remains within a narrow physiological range, which is critical for muscle contraction, nerve conduction, and blood coagulation. Therefore, the combination of all three factors (Option D) constitutes the complete regulatory machinery for serum calcium

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text:
In a town, there were 1000 live births in a period of 6 months. During the same period, 12 women died due to the following causes. What is the maternal mortality ratio?

Sepsis - 3

Road traffic accidents - 2

Obstructed labor - 2

Postpartum hemorrhage - 3

Snake bite - 2
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 800 per 100000 live births

This town's maternal mortality ratio (MMR) is 800 per 100,000 live births.

Maternal mortality refers to deaths during pregnancy or within 42 days of termination of pregnancy, from causes related to pregnancy. Excluding the deaths from traffic accidents and snake bite, the total number of maternal deaths is 8.

MMR = (Number of maternal deaths in a given year / Number of live births in the same area and year) x 1,00,000 (or 1000).

Hence, MMR = 8 x 100000/1000 = 800 per 100,000 live births.
questions.learning: 800 per 100000 live births This town's maternal mortality ratio (MMR) is 800 per 100,000 live births. Maternal mortality refers to deaths during pregnancy or within 42 days of termination of pregnancy, from causes related to pregnancy.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: When a court calls a member of the public who witnessed an incident to give testimony and record their statement, what type of evidence does this witness provide?
questions.explanation: When a witness who personally observed an incident appears in court to provide a verbal account of their observations, they are providing Oral evidence. Under the Indian Evidence Act, oral evidence must always be direct, meaning it must come from a person who says they personally saw, heard, or perceived the facts through their own senses. Hearsay evidence (Option B) is an indirect account of what the witness heard from someone else and is generally inadmissible in court. A Subpoena (Option C) is the legal document (summons) that compels the witness to appear in court, not the evidence itself. Circumstantial evidence (Option D) is evidence of a series of facts other than the direct fact in issue, from which the fact in issue may be inferred. Oral evidence provided by a direct eyewitness is a foundational component of the legal process. It must be recorded accurately by the court to establish the facts of the case and ensure a fair trial
questions.learning: When a witness who personally observed an incident appears in court to provide a verbal account of their observations, they are providing Oral evidence.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text:
A 30-year-old drowsy male was brought to the casualty. His pulse was 130/min, respiratory rate -30/min. His lab reports are given below. He showed improvement on nasogastric aspiration and administration of sodium bicarbonate, calcium gluconate, and 4-methyl pyrazole. What substance did he most likely consume?

ABG - metabolic acidosis

Total serum calcium - 6.8 mg/dL

Blood Urea – 100 mg/dl

Creatinine – 3.4 mg/dl

Urine analysis - Calcium oxalate crystals.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ethylene glycol

The given scenario point towards ethylene glycol poisoning.

Ethylene glycol is converted to glyoxyaldehyde by alcohol dehydrogenase. Glyoxyaldehyde causes kidney damage.

Methanol is converted to formaldehyde by alcohol dehydrogenase. Formaldehyde causes retinal damage like blurring of vision/loss of vision.

The principles of treatment for both these conditions are the same. It predominantly involves using fomipezole or ethanol to inhibit the metabolic conversion of these relatively non-toxic alcohols to their toxic metabolites.
questions.learning: Ethylene glycol — The given scenario point towards ethylene glycol poisoning. Ethylene glycol is converted to glyoxyaldehyde by alcohol dehydrogenase.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: After examining the left eye shown in the image, what is the most appropriate course of management?
questions.explanation: The clinical image shows a total opaque cornea (corneal scarring or leukoma), likely resulting from the patient's previous eye injury a year ago. This opacity prevents light from reaching the retina, causing total vision loss. The most appropriate management strategy to restore vision is a keratoplasty (corneal transplant), which involves replacing the diseased cornea with a healthy donor cornea. Keratotomy (Option B) is an outdated refractive procedure involving incisions in the cornea. LASIK (Option C) is used for correcting minor refractive errors in a clear cornea and is ineffective for total opacity. DCR (Option D) is a surgery for the tear drainage system and has no impact on corneal clarity. If the posterior segment (retina and optic nerve) is healthy, keratoplasty offers the patient a chance to regain functional vision. Therefore, given the visual evidence of a scarred, opaque cornea, keratoplasty is the definitive therapeutic intervention

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Refsum disease is due to:
options: Absence of alpha oxidation in peroxisomes
Absence of beta oxidation in peroxisomes
Absence of alpha oxidation in lysosomes
Absence of beta oxidation in lysosomes
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Absence of alpha oxidation in peroxisomes

Refsum disease is due to the absence of alpha oxidation in peroxisomes.

Refsum's disease is a rare autosomal recessive disorder. The defective enzyme is phytanoyl CoA hydroxylase, which causes alpha oxidation of fatty acids and leads to elevated levels of phytanic acid in the blood.

Clinical features are dysmorphic facies and severe neurological symptoms such as polyneuropathy, retinitis pigmentosa, nerve deafness, ichthyosis, and cerebellar ataxia.

Restricted dietary intake of phytanic acid reduces the symptoms. Management includes avoiding sources of phytanic acid such as dairy products, meat, nuts, and green leafy vegetables.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 30-year-old patient presents to the emergency department with several weeks of breathlessness, cough, chest pain, and respiratory discomfort, with no significant past medical history. Lung biopsy reveals the presence of asteroid bodies. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The presence of Asteroid bodies within non-caseating granulomas on lung biopsy is a hallmark histological finding for Sarcoidosis. Sarcoidosis is a multisystem granulomatous disease of unknown etiology, characteristically affecting young adults and commonly presenting with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy or pulmonary infiltrates. Asteroid bodies are star-shaped eosinophilic inclusions found within giant cells, though they are not pathognomonic as they can appear in other granulomatous conditions. Other common histological findings include Schaumann bodies (laminated calcified concretions). Rheumatoid Arthritis (Option B), Sjogren syndrome (Option C), and SLE (Option D) are autoimmune disorders that can have pulmonary manifestations but do not typically present with the specific non-caseating granulomas and asteroid bodies seen here. Diagnosis is established by combining clinical findings, radiographic evidence of hilar adenopathy, and histological proof of non-caseating granulomas while ruling out other causes like tuberculosis or fungal infections. Management usually involves corticosteroids for symptomatic or progressive pulmonary involvement to prevent fibrosis and permanent loss of respiratory function

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Ammonia in the brain is detoxified to form _________
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Glutamine

Ammonia in the brain is detoxified to form glutamine.

Glutamine synthetase combines ammonia with glutamate to form glutamine. It requires the hydrolysis of ATP.

Deficiency of glutamine synthetase in neonates results in severe brain damage, multiorgan failure, and death.

Note: Glutamine is the transport form of ammonia from the brain and intestine to the liver; while alanine is the transport form from the muscle.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A middle-aged man presents with a genital ulcer, as seen in the accompanying images. Microscopic examination of a sample taken from the lesion reveals characteristic findings. Based on these observations, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with a genital ulcer that appears beefy red and likely painless, which is characteristic of granuloma inguinale (Donovanosis), a sexually transmitted infection caused by Klebsiella (Calymmatobacterium) granulomatis. A key diagnostic feature is seen on microscopy: Donovan bodies, which are intracellular organisms present within macrophages. These appear as oval, safety-pin shaped inclusions on special stains such as Wright–Giemsa and are pathognomonic for this condition. Other options are incorrect: (B) Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) typically begins with a small, painless ulcer that heals quickly, followed by painful inguinal lymphadenopathy (buboes), not a persistent beefy ulcer. (C) Chancroid presents with a painful, soft ulcer with ragged edges and may show organisms in a “school of fish” pattern, not Donovan bodies. (D) Gonorrhoea usually causes purulent urethral discharge and dysuria rather than genital ulcers. Thus, the presence of a painless beefy red ulcer along with Donovan bodies confirms granuloma inguinale

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: All among the following are ionizing radiations except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. MRI

MRI is a technique that produces topographic images by means of magnetic fields and radiofrequency waves.

The ionizing radiations

• Alpha
• Beta
• Gamma
• X-Rays

The non-Ionizing radiations are:

• Radiofrequency waves
• UV rays
• Microwaves

Alpha and beta rays are particulate radiation (particles) whereas gamma and x-rays are electromagnetic rays. All electromagnetic waves have a constant velocity of 3×108 m/s and no mass. The electromagnetic spectrum, from low frequency to high frequency consists of:

Radiowaves < Microwaves < Infrared < Visible light < Ultraviolet < X-rays < Gamma rays

Note: W. C. Roentgen is the father of X-ray and the first medical X-ray by Roentgen was of his wife Anna Bertha's left hand. Physicists Peter Mansfield and Paul Lauterbur developed MRI-related imaging techniques in medicine and they were awarded the Nobel prize in 2003.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: All of the following disorders are associated with dystonia and basal ganglia involvement. Which among the following needs to be diagnosed/excluded as it requires a distinctly different treatment approach compared to the others?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Wilson disease

Wilson disease is an important treatable cause of dystonia and basal ganglia dysfunction. Therefore, it should always be actively excluded in any young patient presenting with dystonia, movement disorders, or unexplained liver disease, as early copper-chelating therapy can halt disease progression, unlike most other neurodegenerative disorders with brain iron accumulation.

• Wilson disease is caused by mutations in the ATP7B gene, leading to copper accumulation in the liver, basal ganglia, and cornea.
• Specific treatment includes:

• D-Penicillamine or Trientine (copper chelators)
• Zinc therapy to reduce intestinal copper absorption

Why not the other options?

• A. Pantothenate Kinase-Associated Neurodegeneration (PKAN): A form of NBIA (Neurodegeneration with Brain Iron Accumulation); treatment is mainly supportive.
• B. PLA2G6-Associated Neurodegeneration (PLAN): Another NBIA disorder with no disease-modifying therapy.
• D. Kufor-Rakeb syndrome: A juvenile Parkinsonism syndrome (ATP13A2 mutation); managed symptomatically with dopaminergic therapy.

An elderly patient with fever, confusion, tachypnea, and rales indicates severe community-acquired pneumonia requiring hospital admission. Severe CAP warrants dual therapy with a β-lactam (ceftriaxone) plus a respiratory fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin) for broad coverage. Score ≥2 → Hospital admission required

Severe CAP → Broad-spectrum IV combination therapy

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 35-year-old man has had persistent hypercalcemia for the past 1.5 years, with parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels within the normal range. What is the most likely underlying cause of his hypercalcemia?
questions.explanation: Chronic hypercalcemia with a normal or low Parathyroid Hormone (PTH) level indicates a PTH-independent cause of calcium elevation. In Sarcoidosis, activated macrophages within non-caseating granulomas express the enzyme 1-alpha-hydroxylase. This enzyme converts 25-hydroxyvitamin D into its active form, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol), leading to increased intestinal calcium absorption and persistent hypercalcemia. Malignancy (Option A) often causes acute, symptomatic hypercalcemia through bone metastasis or PTHrP secretion, but the chronic, stable 1.5-year history is more typical of a granulomatous disease. Parathyroid hyperplasia (Option C) would result in primary hyperparathyroidism, characterized by an inappropriately elevated PTH level. Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) (Option D) typically presents with hypocalcemia in the early stages and secondary hyperparathyroidism (high PTH) later on. Thus, the extra-renal production of calcitriol in Sarcoidosis best explains this metabolic profile
questions.learning: Chronic hypercalcemia with a normal or low Parathyroid Hormone (PTH) level indicates a PTH-independent cause of calcium elevation. In Sarcoidosis, activated macrophages within non-caseating granulomas express the enzyme 1-alpha-hydroxylase.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A pregnant woman presented with complaints of passing grape-like vesicles vaginally. A USG scan was done and is shown below. Which of the following hormonal levels need to be checked in this patient? hCG - Human Chorionic Gonadotropin
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. hCG

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of molar pregnancy and beta hCG levels need to be measured.

Molar pregnancy may present with bleeding per vaginum or an acute discharge of vesicular mass per vaginum. On examination, the uterine size is more than the corresponding period of amenorrhea. It shows a characteristic snowstorm appearance on USG.

Suction and evacuation is the treatment of choice. The patient is followed up every week till the hCG levels normalize, after which follow-up is done monthly for 6 months.

Post-evacuation recommendations:

* Anti-D immune globulin if Rh D-negative

* Initiate effective contraception (IUD contraindicated)

* Review pathology report

* Serum hCG levels: within 48 h of evacuation, weekly until undetectable, then monthly for 6 months.

Pregnancy is allowed after 6 months following a negative hCG titer. However, it is advised to avoid pregnancy for 1 year, preferably 2 years, as a fresh pregnancy will interfere with the hCG titers.
questions.learning: hCG The given clinical scenario is suggestive of molar pregnancy and beta hCG levels need to be measured. Molar pregnancy may present with bleeding per vaginum or an acute discharge of vesicular mass per vaginum.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient underwent cholecystectomy for gallstones over 2 years ago. She now presents with symptoms of obstructive jaundice. Investigation reveals a stone in the common bile duct. What is the stone most likely to be?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Primary

This patient has a history of cholecystectomy done for gallstones 2 years ago. Thus, in this patient with choledocholithiasis, the stones found in the common bile duct would most likely be primary stones.

Choledocholithiasis or common bile duct stones are classified based on their point of origin:

• Primary stones are brown pigment stones that arise de novo in the bile duct and are composed of bile pigments and cholesterol.
• Secondary stones (option B) are usually cholesterol stones, which originate in the gall bladder and pass down into the common bile duct. Since this patient has already undergone cholecystectomy more than 2 years ago, secondary stones are unlikely.
• When stones are found in the common bile duct within 2 years of history of cholecystectomy, they are termed retained stones (option D).
• If they are found more than 2 years after cholecystectomy, they are known as recurrent stones (which are mostly primary).

Clinical features: Mostly clinically silent, but may present with biliary colic and even obstructive jaundice. When there is fever, jaundice, and associated right upper quadrant abdominal pain, it is known as Charcot’s triad, seen in cholangitis.

Management of choledocholithiasis:
ERCP +/- sphincterotomy followed by laparoscopic cholecystectomy is the most preferred management of choledocholithiasis.

If stones cannot be removed through ERCP and sphincterotomy, then common bile duct exploration is carried out intraoperatively either in an open procedure or via laparoscopy. A T-tube is left in place after choledochotomy.
questions.learning: Primary — This patient has a history of cholecystectomy done for gallstones 2 years ago. Thus, in this patient with choledocholithiasis, the stones found in the common bile duct would most likely be primary stones.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 67-year-old patient with diabetes presents with knee swelling, restricted joint movement, and minimal pain. An X-ray of the knee is shown. Based on the clinical features and radiographic findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical scenario of a diabetic patient with a "severely swollen joint" that is "painless" (out of proportion to its appearance) is the classic presentation of "Charcot arthropathy" or neuropathic joint. Chronic diabetic neuropathy leads to a loss of protective sensation, resulting in repetitive microtrauma and progressive, painless joint destruction. The provided X-ray shows the "6 Ds" of Charcot joints: Distension, Density (sclerosis), Disorganization, Debris (fragmentation), Dislocation, and Destruction. Rheumatoid arthropathy (Option A) typically involves symmetric, painful, small joint inflammation. Osteoarthritis (Option B) involves asymmetric joint space narrowing and osteophytes but not massive bone destruction and fragmentation. Psoriatic arthropathy (Option D) is characterized by "pencil-in-cup" deformities and skin lesions. Charcot arthropathy is a debilitating condition that can lead to limb deformity and amputation if not managed early with strict offloading (e.g., total contact casting). Maintaining tight glycemic control is also essential to slow the progression of underlying neuropathy
questions.learning: The clinical scenario of a diabetic patient with a "severely swollen joint" that is "painless" (out of proportion to its appearance) is the classic presentation of "Charcot arthropathy" or neuropathic joint.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A primigravida delivers a healthy baby via normal delivery. After how many hours should she initiate breastfeeding?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Within 1 hour

In this scenario of a healthy mother and infant, breastfeeding should be started within 1 hour.

Breastmilk is the ideal and exclusively food for infants in the first 6 months. It reduces the infant mortality rate, neonatal hypocalcaemia and hypomagnesemia hence  should be started as soon possible.

The standard essential newborn care include:

* Maintain the airway and breathing

* Maintain the body temperature and prevent hypothermia

* Initiate breastfeeding within one hour

* Cleaning of baby and care to prevent infection

* Cord care and care of the eyes

* Administering vitamin K

* Performing a thoroiugh examination.

Pearl PF0003: Baby-friendly hospital initiative (revised 2018)

Ten steps to successful breastfeeding (Revised 2018)

Critical management procedures

1  a. Comply fully with the International Code of Marketing of Breast-milk Substitutes and relevant World Health Assembly resolutions.

b. Have a written infant feeding policy that is routinely communicated to staff and parents.

c. Establish ongoing monitoring and data-management systems.

2. Ensure that staff has sufficient knowledge, competence, and skills to support breastfeeding.

Key clinical practices

3. Discuss the importance and management of breastfeeding with pregnant women and their families.

4. Facilitate immediate and uninterrupted skin-to-skin contact and support mothers to initiate breastfeeding as soon as possible after birth.

5. Support mothers to initiate and maintain breastfeeding and manage common difficulties.

6. Do not provide breastfed newborns any food or fluids other than breast milk, unless medically indicated.

7. Enable mothers and their infants to remain together and to practice rooming-in 24 hours a day.

8. Support mothers to recognize and respond to their infants’ cues for feeding.

9. Counsel mothers on the use and risks of feeding bottles, teats, and pacifiers.

10. Coordinate discharge so that parents and their infants have timely access to ongoing support and care.
questions.learning: Within 1 hour — In this scenario of a healthy mother and infant, breastfeeding should be started within 1 hour. Breastmilk is the ideal and exclusively food for infants in the first 6 months.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Which nerve injury is most commonly responsible for the deformity seen in a patient with leprosy?
questions.explanation: Leprosy (Hansen's disease) is a chronic infectious disease that has a predilection for the peripheral nerves. The ulnar nerve is the most common nerve affected in the upper limb in leprosy patients (Option A) . Damage to the ulnar nerve at the elbow or wrist leads to the classic "claw hand" deformity, characterized by hyperextension of the metacarpophalangeal joints and flexion of the interphalangeal joints of the ring and little fingers. Median nerve injury (Option C) leads to "ape thumb" deformity and is the second most common upper-limb nerve affected. Radial nerve injury (Option B) causing wrist drop is much less frequent. The posterior interosseous nerve (Option D) is a branch of the radial nerve. Because the ulnar nerve is uniquely susceptible to the thickening and inflammation caused by Mycobacterium leprae in its superficial course, it is the definitive answer for the primary neuro-orthopedic deformity in this population
questions.learning: Leprosy (Hansen's disease) is a chronic infectious disease that has a predilection for the peripheral nerves. The ulnar nerve is the most common nerve affected in the upper limb in leprosy patients (Option A) .

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: The arterial blood gas findings of a patient are pH = 7.12, pCO2 = 50, HCO3 = 28. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Respiratory acidosis with metabolic compensation

The above findings give the diagnosis of respiratory acidosis with metabolic compensation.

Interpretation of the ABG:

Step 1: pH is reduced (7.12), hence acidosis.

Step 2: Since pCO2 is raised (50 mmHg), it is respiratory acidosis.

Step 3: HCO3 is raised (28 mEq/L) suggesting there is metabolic compensation.

Pearl PF1719: Interpretation of Acid-Base Disorders

pH<7.35 is acidosis

pH>7.45 is alkalosis

A primary change in HCO3- is termed metabolic

If the change in HCO3- is in keeping with the pH (i.e. if there are acidosis and HCO3- is decreased) the problem is metabolic.

If the change in HCO3- is opposite with the pH (i.e. if there is acidosis and HCO3- is increased or normal) the problem is compensatory metabolic.

A primary change in CO2 is termed as respiratory

If the change in CO2 keeping in line with the pH (if in acidosis CO2 is raised) the problem is termed respiratory

If the change in CO2 is in the opposite direction of that of the pH (i.e. if there are acidosis and CO2 is decreased or normal ) the problem is termed compensatory respiratory

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 31-year-old lady with diabetes mellitus delivers a term neonate. Which of the following problems is associated with a baby born to this lady?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hypoglycemia

The condition associated with an infant born to a mother with diabetes mellitus is hypoglycemia.

In pregestational diabetes and gestational diabetes mellitus, maternal hyperglycemia causes a higher amount of blood glucose to pass through the placenta into the fetal circulation. It results in fetal hyperglycemia leading to fetal hyperinsulinism. These increased insulin levels continue to persist after delivery which leads to hypoglycemia. Extra glucose in the fetus is stored as body fat causing macrosomia. These newborns are at risk of developing various complications due to fetal hyperglycemia. They are:

* Gastrointestinal: These infants may demonstrate abdominal distention caused by a transient delay in the development of the left side of the colon due to fluctuations in maternal and fetal glucose resulting in small left colon syndrome.

* Metabolic: Hypoglycemia, hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia

* Neural: Neural tube defects like caudal regression syndrome, encephalocele, anencephaly

* Respiratory: Respiratory distress syndrome, transient tachypnea of newborn, persistent pulmonary hypertension

* Cardiac: Cardiomegaly, cardiac malformations like a ventricular or atrial septal defect, transposition of the great vessels(most specific), truncus arteriosus, double-outlet right ventricle, tricuspid atresia, coarctation of the aorta

* Haematological: Polycythemia, renal vein thrombosis

* Others: Hyperbilirubinemia, insulin resistance, diabetes, sudden intrauterine death

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: An elderly patient presents to the outpatient department with the deformity shown. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The hand in the image shows ulnar deviation (ulnar drift) of the fingers at the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints, along with joint deformity and muscle wasting, which are classic features of rheumatoid arthritis (RA). RA is a chronic inflammatory autoimmune disease that primarily affects the MCP and PIP joints, leading to progressive deformities such as ulnar deviation, swan neck, and boutonnière deformities. Unlike osteoarthritis, which causes hard bony nodules at DIP joints (Heberden’s nodes), this image shows joint misalignment rather than isolated nodules, pointing toward RA. The deformity appears more inflammatory and deforming, rather than just degenerative. Why Other Options Are Wrong (A) Rickets: Seen in children, not elderly (B) Osteomalacia: Causes bone softening, no joint deformity (C) Osteoarthritis: Primarily affects DIP with nodules, not ulnar deviation
questions.learning: The hand in the image shows ulnar deviation (ulnar drift) of the fingers at the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints, along with joint deformity and muscle wasting, which are classic features of rheumatoid arthritis (RA).
